claim: Multimodal Model Diffing (MMDiff - arXiv 2026): primary inspiration for SAE-based feature discovery; uses multimodal SAEs and contrastive token firing to isolate behavioral features in MLLMs. Operates on static VQA/OCR; we extend to continuous temporal driving VLA rollouts.
correct_value: Title: "Multimodal Model Diffing for Feature Discovery and Control" (MMDiff). arXiv:2608.09928 [cs.CV], v1 submitted 10 Aug 2026. Authors: Hunar Batra*, Lachin Naghashyar*, Ashkan Khakzar, Philip Torr, Christian Schroeder de Witt, Constantin Venhoff†, Ronald Clark† (*equal contribution, †equal advising). Affiliations: University of Oxford (PIXL lab, Dept. of Computer Science; Torr Vision Group / Engineering) and Microsoft (Naghashyar). Project page: pixl.cs.ox.ac.uk/mmdiff. Repo: github.com/hunarbatra/MMDiff (code 'will be released'; as of 2026-09-28 only README + pretrained SAE weights on Hugging Face at OX-PIXL/MMDiff_SAEs). Precursor: Naghashyar, Batra et al., "Towards Understanding Multimodal Fine-Tuning: A Case Study into Spatial Features", NeurIPS 2025 Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop / arXiv:2602.08713.
details: MMDiff trains sparse autoencoders on the language-model residual stream of multimodal LLMs and 'diffs' a base-LM SAE against its multimodal-adapted counterpart (index-aligned features) to find features that were rotated or became vision-preferring during multimodal training (roughly 5-20% of the dictionary). It then isolates task-specific features through per-token contrastive firing against a generic VQA baseline, with a filter that drops features that only track the wording of the prompt. Finally it removes or steers the discovered directions (MMDiff-CAA steering at feature-associated layers). SAEs were trained for LLaVA-MORE (LLaMA-3.1-8B backbone; TopK k=50, 32 layers, width 32,768), PaliGemma 2 (Gemma-2-2B; JumpReLU, 26 layers, width 16,384) and InternVL3.5 (Qwen3-1.7B; TopK). Removing the discovered features lowers spatial accuracy (VSR) by about 12% on average and OCR (OCRBench) by about 17%, and cuts multimodal jailbreak attack success by about 24%, with at most about 1.5% change on generic VQA. Steering improves spatial and OCR accuracy by +3.6 and +1.8 points over a single-layer CAA baseline.
project_relevance: This is the closest method template for the 'Latent Discovery' stage and the right thing to cite for 'multimodal SAE + contrastive per-token firing'. How to adapt it: (a) the 'model diff' axis maps naturally to comparing a VLM-backbone SAE with the same SAE after VLA/driving fine-tuning (e.g. PaliGemma to pi0.5, or a Qwen-VL base to a driving VLA). (b) The contrastive firing step maps to failure-rollout tokens vs. nominal-rollout tokens, in place of task vs. VQA. Caveats: (1) The 'diff' in MMDiff is base model vs. multimodal-adapted model, NOT success vs. failure, so the project must describe its contrastive success/failure analysis as an adaptation. (2) It works on static single-image VQA-style inputs, with no temporal or action outputs. (3) Code is not yet released; only SAE weights are. (4) Its PaliGemma 2 SAEs will not transfer directly to pi0/pi0.5, which use the original PaliGemma (Gemma 2B), or to driving VLAs. Contact the co-first authors Hunar Batra / Lachin Naghashyar and the advisors Constantin Venhoff / Ronald Clark (Oxford), NOT Buurmeijer or Sonia Joseph.
discrepancies: The source's contact section (item 5.2) attributes MMDiff to Hugo Buurmeijer & Sonia Joseph; the real authors are Batra, Naghashyar, Khakzar, Torr, Schroeder de Witt, Venhoff, Clark (Oxford/Microsoft).

'Operates on static VQA/OCR' is imprecise: target tasks are visual-spatial reasoning (VSR), OCR (OCRBench) and multimodal safety/jailbreaks; generic VQA is used as the contrast baseline and the check that nothing else breaks.

The source implies the diffing is contrastive between behaviors; in MMDiff 'model diffing' means comparing a base-LM SAE with its multimodal-adapted SAE. Contrastive per-token firing is a separate second stage.
The source names no arXiv id or code status; arXiv:2608.09928 (Aug 2026), and code is announced but not released (SAE weights only).

claim: Observing and Controlling Features in VLAs (Buurmeijer et al. - arXiv 2026): shows intermediate VLA layers (OpenVLA, pi0, pi0.5) contain linearly observable state/action features. Validates layer-sweep protocol.
correct_value: Title: "Observing and Controlling Features in Vision-Language-Action Models". arXiv:2603.05487 (v1 March 2026; v2 dated 21 Sep 2026). Authors: Hugo Buurmeijer, Carmen Amo Alonso, Aiden Swann, Marco Pavone. Affiliations: Stanford University (Dept. of Aeronautics & Astronautics / Autonomous Systems Lab; Dept. of Mechanical Engineering for Swann); Marco Pavone is Stanford + NVIDIA Research. Models: v1 studied OpenVLA (BridgeData V2) and pi0.5 (LIBERO). The v2 abstract says 'four frontier VLA models' spanning autoregressive and transformer/flow-matching designs; the other two models could not be identified, and pi0 specifically is unconfirmed. No public code repository found as of 2026-09-28.
details: The paper defines feature-observability (a map/observer can read a feature from a transformer layer's activations) and feature-controllability (a map/controller can change the representation so the VLA's output lands in a target region). Observers are per-layer linear probes f_l(x)=W_l x + b_l, trained with supervision on known robot quantities such as end-effector x/y/z, orientation angles and gripper state. They are applied layer by layer across the transformer backbone. The controller is a minimal additive intervention g_l(x)=x+u_l with a closed-form, optimal-control-motivated solution (roughly u_l = (zeta_target - zeta_l) W_l / ||W_l||^2) that moves the observer's prediction into a prescribed interval, which gives interpretable constraints such as limiting gripper aperture or movement speed. Closed-loop experiments with pi0.5 in LIBERO and on DROID hardware improve constraint satisfaction while keeping task performance, at about 1% inference overhead and without fine-tuning. Linear observability held for both autoregressive (OpenVLA) and flow-matching (pi0.5) architectures, with OpenVLA features less robust than pi0.5's.
project_relevance: Cite as evidence that VLA hidden states linearly encode state/action quantities layer by layer. This justifies (a) the layer sweep and (b) the 'probe-residual clustering' method: fit these linear observers on nominal driving rollouts, then cluster residuals on failures. Their closed-form minimal additive controller is a cheap causal test: steer along a discovered axis and check whether the failure rate changes. Caveats: (1) Manipulation only (LIBERO/Bridge/DROID), not driving. (2) Features are SUPERVISED and known in advance, which is the opposite of unsupervised discovery of unknown failure axes; present it as the supervised-probe baseline/contrast. (3) The source's model list 'OpenVLA, pi0, pi0.5' is not verified for pi0; say 'OpenVLA and pi0.5 (plus two further VLAs in v2)'. (4) No code is public, so a code request to the authors is reasonable. Co-author Carmen Amo Alonso is an incoming UC Berkeley EECS assistant professor, the most accessible contact for a Berkeley team.
discrepancies: pi0 is not confirmed as a studied model: v1 covers OpenVLA and pi0.5; v2 says 'four frontier VLA models' without an identifiable list in the sources that could be reached.
The source omits co-authors Carmen Amo Alonso and Aiden Swann and the arXiv id (2603.05487).
'Validates layer-sweep protocol' is an interpretation: the paper does layer-resolved linear probing of known features, not unsupervised failure discovery.
The paper also contributes the controllability/steering half (closed-form minimal additive controller with ~1% overhead, LIBERO and DROID hardware), which the source does not mention.

claim: Prisma (Sonia Joseph's mechanistic interpretability library for vision/multimodal models), referenced in the contact list as 'Sonia Joseph (Oxford / Prisma)'.
correct_value: Paper: "Prisma: An Open Source Toolkit for Mechanistic Interpretability in Vision and Video", arXiv:2504.19475 (2025). Oral + tutorial at the CVPR 2025 Workshop on Mechanistic Interpretability for Vision (MIV). Authors: Sonia Joseph, Praneet Suresh, Lorenz Hufe, Edward Stevinson, Robert Graham, Yash Vadi, Danilo Bzdok, Sebastian Lapuschkin, Lee Sharkey, Blake Aaron Richards. Code: github.com/Prisma-Multimodal/ViT-Prisma (MIT license, ~390 stars). Sonia Joseph: PhD candidate at McGill University / Mila (Blake Richards' lab) and researcher at Meta FAIR (JEPA team). NOT Oxford.
details: Prisma is an open-source toolkit, built around HookedTransformer-style hooks, for mechanistic interpretability of vision and video transformers. It gives one interface to 75+ vision/video models from Hugging Face and OpenCLIP (ViT, CLIP, DINO, JEPA-family). It supports SAE, transcoder and crosscoder training; ships 80+ pretrained SAE weights, including SAEs for all layers of CLIP and DINO and CLIP transcoders; and includes activation caching, circuit-analysis and visualization tools plus tutorials. The paper reports that effective vision SAEs can be much less sparse than language SAEs, and that SAE reconstructions sometimes lower model loss.
project_relevance: Useful as infrastructure for the vision-encoder side of a driving VLA: hook and cache activations, and train or borrow SAEs on ViT/CLIP/DINO-style encoders (e.g. the DINOv2+SigLIP encoders in OpenVLA). Check which exact encoders are supported before relying on it. Its published vision-SAE sparsity findings are useful for choosing hyperparameters. Caveats: it targets vision/video transformers, not the LLM backbone or action head of a VLA, so the language/action-token SAEs will need SAELens/dictionary_learning-style tooling. It is NOT related to MMDiff. Contact Sonia Joseph (Meta FAIR / Mila) about Prisma and vision-SAE practice, not about MMDiff hyperparameters.
discrepancies: The contact list gives Sonia Joseph's affiliation as Oxford; she is at McGill/Mila and Meta FAIR.
Prisma is a vision/video toolkit (CVPR 2025 MIV workshop), not a multimodal-LLM diffing tool, and has no connection to MMDiff.

claim: Extra related work: SAEs on VLA hidden states (Swann, ..., Buurmeijer, ... 2026) - 'Sparse Autoencoders Reveal Interpretable and Steerable Features in VLA Models'.
correct_value: "Sparse Autoencoders Reveal Interpretable and Steerable Features in VLA Models" (DR.VLA). arXiv:2603.19183 (March 2026). Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026 per the authors' repo. Authors: Aiden Swann, Lachlain McGranahan, Hugo Buurmeijer, Monroe Kennedy III, Mac Schwager (Stanford: Multi-Robot Systems Lab, ARM Lab, Autonomous Systems Lab). Code: github.com/swannaiden/drvla (release announced for 1 Oct 2026). Project page: drvla.github.io.
details: The authors train SAEs on hidden-layer activations of pi0.5 (PaliGemma backbone plus action expert), e.g. PaliGemma layer 5 and averages over layers 0/5/11/17. They collect activations on LIBERO (simulation) and DROID (real robot). Most SAE features are episode-specific memorization: about 32 general features out of ~2,044 active on LIBERO, and 104 out of ~2,046 on DROID. A minority are general, interpretable motion primitives and semantic properties. The paper proposes a metric that separates general, transferable features from memorized ones, and notes that small training datasets yield far fewer general features. Steering experiments show causality: amplifying general/semantic features induces predictable actions across tasks and scenes, while ablating them destroys performance. The planned code release covers SAE training, the pi0.5 activation-collection pipeline, and the generality metric/classifier.
project_relevance: This is the closest precedent for 'SAEs on VLA activations'. It must be cited and differentiated: they discover interpretable, steerable features, while this project ties features to failure outcomes in driving. Their generality-vs-memorization metric is directly useful as a filter before the VLM describability gate, since memorized, episode-specific latents would otherwise look like spurious 'failure axes'. The pi0.5 activation pipeline (release 1 Oct 2026) could be reused if a pi0.5-style driving policy is used. Caveats: manipulation only; the CoRL 2026 venue is taken from the authors' README.

claim: Extra related work: SAE-based interpretability inside an end-to-end driving policy - 'Driving the Wrong Way: Leveraging Interpretability in End2End Autonomous Driving Models' (2026).
correct_value: "Driving the Wrong Way: Leveraging Interpretability in End2End Autonomous Driving Models", arXiv:2607.06328 (7 July 2026). Authors: Franz Motzkus, Sebastian Bernhard. Motzkus is listed with AUMOVIO (Germany) and the University of Bamberg (Dept. of Applied Computer Science), previously Fraunhofer HHI; Bernhard's affiliation was not independently verified. No code link found.
details: The paper inserts a TopK sparse autoencoder, trained post hoc on the frozen model's latents, into the latent space of the GTRS end-to-end driving model (Generalized Trajectory Scoring). It decomposes GTRS's trajectory-scoring logic into semantically meaningful concept directions such as 'car ahead', 'intersections' and 'lane markings'. Circuit-style analysis traces how these concepts causally influence individual driving decisions, including erroneous ones such as wrong-direction driving. Suppressing a few (three) selected SAE neurons corrects erroneous behavior without retraining and improves NAVSIM metrics, notably drivable-area compliance and driving-direction compliance. The evaluation is open-loop (NAVSIM), not closed-loop simulation.
project_relevance: This is the most direct driving-domain precedent for SAEs inside a driving policy, and a must-cite 'nearest neighbor'. The project should position itself as (a) VLA rather than a trajectory-scoring planner, (b) unsupervised discovery of failure axes over many rollouts rather than case-by-case concept analysis, and (c) closed-loop validation (CARLA) rather than NAVSIM open-loop only. Their neuron-suppression result offers a cheap causal-validation baseline for discovered axes. Caveats: affiliation details are medium confidence; check them against the PDF before citing.

Project page: vla-mech-interp.github.io.
details: The authors project the feed-forward (FFN) value vectors in VLA transformer layers onto the token-embedding basis. This finds sparse semantic directions (e.g. speed, direction, 'carefulness') that are causally linked to action selection. They then steer at the activation level in real time, without fine-tuning, reward signals or environment interaction. Evaluation covers pi0 / pi0-FAST (OpenPI) and OpenVLA, zero-shot, in LIBERO simulation and on a physical UR5 arm. The code provides value-vector instrumentation and intervention hooks for OpenVLA and pi0.
project_relevance: This is the Berkeley precedent for VLA mechanistic steering, and its hooks for OpenVLA/pi0 can be reused for activation logging and causal steering tests on discovered axes. It is also a natural on-campus contact (Tomlin lab: Häon, Stocking, Chuang). Use it as the 'supervised/vocabulary-projection' contrast to unsupervised SAE discovery. Caveats: manipulation only, and its directions are found through token-vocabulary projection, which assumes action/semantic tokens align with the LM vocabulary. That fits token-based VLAs (OpenVLA, pi0-FAST) better than continuous-action driving heads.

claim: Cross-Axis Routing Diagnostics (CARD - arXiv 2026): blueprint for diagnostic activation steering. Steers intermediate representations along one axis (e.g., belief) and reads out predictions on another (e.g., action) on a 2D gridworld. We adapt CARD's projection-removal controls and steering hooks to verify a discovered axis causally drives action failures. (Elsewhere in Source A: 'Authors of CARD - AAAI 2026', 'Stuttgart ToM Lab', 'Relay Chain diagnostic evaluation scripts'.)
correct_value: Souptik Kumar Majumdar, Fabian Kögel, Andreas Bulling. "CARD: Diagnosing Belief to Action Routing Failures in Vision Language Models." arXiv:2608.20763 [cs.CV, cs.AI], submitted 21 Aug 2026 (announced 24 Aug 2026). The acronym expands to Cross-Axis Routing DiagnosTIC (singular, not 'Diagnostics'). Affiliation: University of Stuttgart, Collaborative Artificial Intelligence group (Prof. Andreas Bulling). Preprint only: the arXiv comment field is empty and no venue is listed. It is not an AAAI 2026 paper. No public code repository found as of 2026-09-28.
details: CARD asks whether mental-state information that VLMs represent internally (linear probes can decode beliefs, knowledge and intentions) is actually used by predictions on a different axis. For each axis (belief, intent, knowledge) the authors fit L2-regularised logistic-regression probes per (layer, attention head) on paired matched/negated statements. The top-K=56 (layer, head) pairs by held-out accuracy become the steering pool. A forward hook on each relevant layer's self-attention output adds a scaled probe direction to those heads' slices at the last-token position only. The effect is measured on another axis's prediction, and steering in the opposite direction serves as a control. The testbed is Relay Chain, a new cooperative gridworld the authors introduce: 11x11 grids with three agents (two lever-holders and a traveller), two gates and a goal, 444 scenario bases, and True-Belief vs False-Belief conditions, fed to the models as keyframes of 16-32-step trajectories. Four open-weight VLMs are tested: Qwen2-VL-7B, Gemma-4-E4B-it, LLaVA-NeXT-Video-7B and InternVL2.5-8B. The main result is negative, a 'routing failure': steering along the belief direction clearly shifts belief and knowledge predictions but leaves the cooperative next-action prediction essentially unchanged. Ablations, including projection-removal (which rules out an amplitude limit) and a prompt-resistance test (which rules out a prompting artefact), exclude other explanations.
project_relevance: Use it as a methods template for Stage-4 causal checks, not as a baseline. CARD's protocol can be copied to test whether a discovered failure direction causally drives the driving policy's action outputs: probe-derived direction, per-head or residual forward hooks, bidirectional steering control, and projection-removal ablation. Caveats: (1) it was run on general VLMs over static gridworld keyframes with text answers, not on VLAs with continuous action heads or closed-loop driving, so hooks and readouts need re-engineering; (2) its headline finding is that a linearly decodable direction can have NO causal effect on action. That supports the project's need for causal verification, but it also means a null steering result on a discovered axis is ambiguous, so plan positive controls such as a planted-gap axis known to matter. (3) No public code or 'Relay Chain evaluation scripts' were found, so any code must come from contacting the authors. Cite it as an arXiv 2026 preprint, not AAAI 2026, and fix the name to 'Cross-Axis Routing Diagnostic'.
discrepancies: Venue given as 'AAAI 2026' in the contacts section: wrong. The paper first appeared on arXiv on 21 Aug 2026 with no venue comment, seven months after AAAI-26 (Jan 20-27, 2026). The 'arXiv 2026' label in the literature section is the correct one.

Name given as 'Cross-Axis Routing Diagnostics'. The paper says 'Cross-Axis Routing Diagnostic' (singular), and the title is 'CARD: Diagnosing Belief to Action Routing Failures in Vision Language Models'.
Authors attributed to a 'Stuttgart ToM Lab'. No group by that name exists. The authors are in the Collaborative Artificial Intelligence group (Andreas Bulling) at the University of Stuttgart.
The source implies usable 'steering hook codebase' and 'Relay Chain diagnostic evaluation scripts'. No public code was found; availability is unverified.

The source frames CARD as a blueprint for verifying that an axis 'causally drives action failures'. CARD's actual finding is the opposite case (belief steering does not move action), and it was done on VLMs, not VLAs.

claim: PHASER (Phase-Aware & Semantic Experience Replay - arXiv 2026): continual learning engine; phase-centric capacity allocation and VLM-verified change-point detection (Auto-PC) to prevent catastrophic forgetting during VLA fine-tuning.
correct_value: Ziyang Chen, Shaoguang Wang, Weiyu Guo, Qianyi Cai, He Zhang, Pengteng Li, Yiren Zhao, Yandong Guo. "PHASER: Phase-Aware and Semantic Experience Replay for Vision-Language-Action Models." arXiv:2606.03598 [cs.RO, cs.AI, cs.CV], June 2026 (announced 3 Jun 2026; a v2 exists); comment '12 pages, 5 figures'. Listed affiliations include HKUST (Guangzhou) and AI² Robotics (per-author mapping not verified). Domain: robotic MANIPULATION (LIBERO), not driving. No public code repository found as of 2026-09-28.
details: PHASER targets catastrophic forgetting when a VLA learns new manipulation tasks one after another (continual learning), using experience replay. It argues that uniform replay sampling causes 'phase starvation': brief but critical sub-skills such as grasping are under-sampled. It also ignores that historical tasks forget at different rates. PHASER has two parts: (1) phase-centric capacity allocation, which gives each sub-skill phase an equal replay frame budget; (2) multi-modal interference routing, which uses language, vision and action signals to prioritise replay of historical phases at high risk of forgetting, with no extra training-loop overhead. Auto-PC finds phase boundaries automatically: unsupervised change-point detection on the action signal, verified semantically by a VLM, performing comparably to human annotation. It is evaluated on LIBERO-Goal and LIBERO-Long continual-learning suites with three backbones (OpenVLA-OFT-7B, QwenGR00T-3B, QwenOFT-3B), against baselines ER, MIR and iCaRL. Reported results: up to +31% Average Success Rate over matched-budget experience replay; 87.8% final ASR on LIBERO-Goal and about 85.8% on LIBERO-Long with OpenVLA-OFT-7B.
project_relevance: Optional related work for the Stage-4 retraining and no-regression step; do not treat it as a ready-made 'engine'. The general lesson carries over to driving: replay should be stratified by trajectory phase so that rare, short, critical segments are not drowned out. Driving analogues would be approach, merge, yield and the moments before a collision, with Auto-PC-style change-point detection on steering/throttle signals plus a VLM check to segment them. Caveats: (1) manipulation-only (LIBERO), with no driving or closed-loop CARLA evidence; (2) it addresses sequential multi-task continual learning, whereas the project does targeted LoRA fine-tuning on synthesized scenarios, which is closer to a single corrective update where mixing in nominal data may suffice; (3) no public code was found, so reimplementation would compete for Person 5's time in a 3-month sprint. Recommend starting with a uniform or nominal-mixing replay baseline and citing PHASER as the phase-aware alternative, adding it only if forgetting on nominal driving is observed.
discrepancies: Minor: the source's 'Phase-Aware & Semantic' is correct but the official title is 'PHASER: Phase-Aware and Semantic Experience Replay for Vision-Language-Action Models'.

Minor/omission: the source does not say PHASER is a manipulation (LIBERO) method evaluated in sequential continual learning, not driving-VLA fine-tuning. It also omits the second core component, multi-modal interference routing.
Implied availability as an 'engine' to plug in: no public code found.

claim: RoboART (Predictive Red-Teaming - arXiv 2025): Primary head-to-head baseline. Uses VLMs to score policy degradation across human-enumerated factor lists (lighting, weather). [references.bib: 'RoboART: Predictive Red Teaming and Targeted Data Collection for Robotic Policies', author={Anonymous}, arXiv:2502.06575]
correct_value: Title: 'Predictive Red Teaming: Breaking Policies Without Breaking Robots' (RoboART = 'Robotics Automated Red Teaming', the name of the pipeline, not the paper title). Authors: Anirudha Majumdar, Mohit Sharma, Dmitry Kalashnikov, Sumeet Singh, Pierre Sermanet, Vikas Sindhwani. Affiliations: Google DeepMind and Princeton University (the project page shows both logos; Majumdar is Princeton faculty, the others are Google DeepMind). Venue: Proceedings of the 9th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2025), PMLR vol. 305, pp. 1615-1635; arXiv:2502.06575 (v1 Feb 2025); OpenReview id qAGHsCsA1O. Domain: robot manipulation, not driving. Code: none released; the GitHub repos only host the project website.
details: The paper defines 'predictive red teaming': find a policy's weak spots with respect to environmental factors and predict how much performance drops, without running hardware trials under those off-nominal conditions. The RoboART pipeline has two steps. (1) Imagen 3, a generative image editor, edits a set of nominal RGB observations (overhead and wrist cameras) using language instructions, e.g. 'add a person close to the table'. (2) A simple policy-specific anomaly detector measures the distance, in the policy's own embedding space, between each edited observation and a set of nominal observations, with the anomaly threshold calibrated by conformal prediction. The predicted success rate for a factor is 1 minus the anomaly rate on that factor's edited observations. The factor list is fixed by the authors. The 12 listed conditions are: person by table, green or red background, black or white trash can, candle, laptop, red, green or blue lighting, table-height change, plus nominal. No VLM or LLM scores anything, and nothing proposes factors automatically. Experiments ran 500+ hardware trials on two visuomotor diffusion policies with different architectures, on a bimanual Kuka IIWA platform using the left arm, a Weiss gripper, and overhead plus wrist cameras. Predicted and real success rates differed by less than 0.19 on average (the project page reports about 0.1 and a Spearman rank correlation of about 0.8). For targeted data collection, co-finetuning with data from the 3 conditions predicted to be most adverse improved performance 2-7x in those conditions and 2-5x in untested conditions.
project_relevance: Keep it as the 'enumerated-factors' head-to-head baseline, with three corrections. (a) Fix references.bib: title, the six real authors, and CoRL 2025/PMLR 305 instead of arXiv only. (b) Source A says it 'uses VLMs to score degradation'. That is wrong: it uses Imagen 3 edits plus an anomaly detector in the policy's own embedding space. (c) Because RoboART already reads policy embeddings, the project cannot claim to be the first to use policy internals. The defensible difference is that RoboART only scores a fixed, human-chosen factor list, while this project discovers the axes. A faithful driving re-implementation needs six parts. (1) Nominal front-camera frames (or the VLA's full camera set) from successful CARLA/Bench2Drive rollouts. (2) A factor list frozen before any discovery results are seen, written as language edit instructions. Make it a standard taxonomy (CARLA weather/time presets, glare, fog, added pedestrians or cones, road-surface changes) and do not tune it toward the planted gaps. (3) An open image editor in place of the proprietary Imagen 3, such as InstructPix2Pix, FLUX.1-Kontext or Qwen-Image-Edit, applied to single frames. Document the substitution, because driving policies use temporal and multi-view context that RoboART never edited. (4) The VLA's embedding at a stated layer (e.g. vision-encoder output or the LLM hidden state at the action tokens), a kNN or nearest-neighbour distance to the nominal bank, and a conformal threshold at a fixed alpha on held-out nominal frames. (5) Predicted success per factor = 1 minus the anomaly rate, ranked, then checked against real closed-loop CARLA success when the same factor is rendered natively in the simulator. (6) Optionally, targeted data collection: expert data (e.g. PDM-Lite) under the top-k predicted-adverse factors, then LoRA fine-tuning. Caveats: image editing cannot express interaction factors such as occluded merges at particular relative speeds, so RoboART's recall on 'complex interactional holdouts' is limited by design. That supports the project's hypothesis, but reviewers may call it a strawman unless the factor list is chosen fairly and in advance. Also, in simulation you can render factors directly, so RoboART's main selling point (avoiding hardware evaluation) mostly disappears. Consider reporting a 'sim-rendered factors' variant as well.
discrepancies: references.bib title 'RoboART: Predictive Red Teaming and Targeted Data Collection for Robotic Policies' is wrong; the real title is 'Predictive Red Teaming: Breaking Policies Without Breaking Robots'.
references.bib author 'Anonymous' is wrong; the authors are Majumdar, Sharma, Kalashnikov, Singh, Sermanet, Sindhwani (Google DeepMind / Princeton).
Venue is not just 'arXiv 2025'; it was published at CoRL 2025 (PMLR 305:1615-1635).

'Uses VLMs to score policy degradation' is false; degradation is predicted by a conformal anomaly detector in the policy's own embedding space applied to Imagen 3-edited images (success = 1 - anomaly rate).
'lighting, weather' is only partly right: the factors are lighting colour, background colour, distractor objects, a person near the table, and table height. There is no weather (indoor manipulation).
Domain is robot manipulation (bimanual Kuka IIWA, diffusion policies), not driving; no code released.

claim: VILTA (VLM-in-the-Loop Adversary - AAAI 2026): Secondary adversarial baseline. Uses an external VLM to edit surrounding vehicle trajectory waypoints in CARLA closed-loop training; operates at scene-graph level without inspecting ego-policy neural states.
correct_value: Title: 'VILTA: A VLM-in-the-Loop Adversary for Enhancing Driving Policy Robustness' (in the text VILTA expands to 'VLM-In-the-Loop Trajectory Adversary'). Authors: Qimao Chen, Fang Li, Shaoqing Xu, Zhiyi Lai, Zixun Xie, Yuechen Luo, Shengyin Jiang, Hanbing Li, Long Chen, Bing Wang, Yi Zhang, Zhi-Xin Yang. Affiliations: Tsinghua University, University of Macau, Xiaomi EV, Peking University; corresponding authors Yi Zhang (Tsinghua) and Zhi-Xin Yang (U. Macau). Venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence 40(4):2984-2992 (AAAI 2026), DOI 10.1609/aaai.v40i4.37290; arXiv:2601.12672. Code: no public repository found (GitHub search returns nothing relevant; aggregators list 'Code: None').
details: VILTA puts a VLM (Gemini-2.5-Flash) directly into the closed-loop reinforcement-learning training of a driving agent. Earlier approaches were two-stage: a VLM or LLM describes a scene and a separate model generates the trajectories. Here the VLM does it in one step, which the authors call 'Vision-Language-Editing'. At each adversarial episode the current scene (a BEV representation plus vehicle states) goes to the VLM. The VLM picks one surrounding vehicle as the 'risky agent' and directly edits that vehicle's future trajectory to create a hazard. Post-processing enforces kinematic feasibility, and the edited trajectory then drives that agent in CARLA. The ego policy is trained with PPO on a 4:1 alternation of normal and challenging scenarios. claim: Reviewer-expected baseline: KING (adversarial safety-critical scenario generation in CARLA).

details: KING optimizes the trajectories of background traffic by gradient descent to make a given driving policy collide. It backpropagates through a differentiable kinematic bicycle model that stands in for CARLA's true dynamics. It generates safety-critical scenarios about 20% more often than black-box optimization baselines. It was applied to the imitation-learning agents AIM-BEV and TransFuser. The generated scenarios were analysed and grouped into 6 failure modes (e.g. cut-ins, rear-ends, unsafe unprotected turns). Fine-tuning AIM-BEV on KING scenarios cut the collision rate on held-out safety-critical scenarios from 100% to 28.57%, and on the Town10 intersection benchmark from 17.48% to 8.13%.
project_relevance: This is the canonical CARLA adversarial-scenario baseline, with public code, and reviewers will expect it. Its hand-analysed 6 failure-mode clusters are an early example of 'behavioural failure clustering', so cite it for the behaviour/output-only clustering baseline. claim: Reviewer-expected baseline: slice discovery (Domino). [references.bib entry eyuboglu2022domino lists 7 authors]
correct_value: 'Domino: Discovering Systematic Errors with Cross-Modal Embeddings', Sabri Eyuboglu, Maya Varma, Khaled Saab, Jean-Benoit Delbrouck, Christopher Lee-Messer, Jared Dunnmon, James Zou, Christopher Ré (Stanford). ICLR 2022 (oral); arXiv:2203.14960. Code: github.com/HazyResearch/domino.
details: Domino is a slice discovery method (SDM). It then uses the shared text-image space to generate natural-language descriptions of each slice. The paper also introduces an evaluation framework with synthetic planted slices across many settings. Domino identified the planted slices better than prior SDMs and was the first SDM to generate slice descriptions, naming the exact slice in 35% of settings, a 12-percentage-point improvement over prior methods.
project_relevance: This is the key input-embedding baseline ('Baseline 4' in PUBLISHABLE_PROPOSALS.md). Its planted-slice evaluation protocol is also the methodological precedent for the planted-gap harness, so cite it for that too. Fix references.bib: add James Zou. Wright, Kevin Leyton-Brown, FAccT 2022, DOI 10.1145/3531146.3533240. claim: SOURCE A: 'Tesla Data Engine (Karpathy Fleet Architecture, HW2/HW3 Shadow Mode): trigger-based fleet data engines; manual trigger classifiers (disengagements, radar/camera conflicts).'
correct_value: Andrej Karpathy described Tesla's 'data engine' publicly at Autonomy Day (Apr 22, 2019), ScaledML 2020, the CVPR 2020 Scalability in Autonomous Driving workshop, the CVPR 2021 WAD keynote (Jun 20, 2021) and AI Day (Aug 19, 2021). Shadow mode was announced with the HW2 'Full Self-Driving hardware' launch on Oct 19, 2016: the software runs silently, compares its outputs with the human driver and logs disagreements. The HW3 FSD Computer was unveiled by Pete Bannon at Autonomy Day 2019. At CVPR 2021 Karpathy said 221 manually implemented triggers were used for the vision-only dataset. Examples include radar-vision mismatch, bounding-box jitter, detection flicker, driver entering or exiting a tunnel, objects on a car's roof, and brake lights detected as on while acceleration is positive. At ScaledML 2020 he also described learned 'approximate triggers' trained offline and shipped to the fleet. Interventions and disengagements are also used as data-collection signals.
details: The loop is: deploy a network, and when it fails or fleet triggers fire, upload clips. Then label (increasingly auto-label), retrain, validate in shadow mode, and redeploy. For the 2021 vision-only depth and velocity release, Karpathy said the dataset went through the shadow-mode loop seven times and contained 1M ten-second clips, 6B labeled objects and 1.5 PB. 'Karpathy Fleet Architecture' is not an established term. Tesla's triggers mix hand-written rules (the 221 at CVPR 2021) with learned detectors used as triggers. Source A's 'manual trigger classifiers' is roughly right for the CVPR 2021 set.
project_relevance: This is the classic example of a trigger-based data engine and the main contrast with the project. Tesla's triggers are hand-specified symptoms, so they only catch what engineers anticipated. The project proposes unsupervised discovery of failure axes in the policy's own activations. Cite the talks as @misc with dates and video links. Karpathy's '221 triggers' slide is a good concrete number for the introduction.
discrepancies: 'Karpathy Fleet Architecture' is not a real named architecture.
Shadow mode predates HW3: it was introduced with HW2 in October 2016. HW3 (FSD Computer) came in 2019.
The 221 triggers were described as manually implemented rules, not trained 'classifiers'. Learned 'approximate triggers' were described separately (ScaledML 2020).

claim: Karpathy CVPR 2021 workshop talk: number of trigger classifiers cited.
correct_value: Andrej Karpathy (Tesla, Sr. Director of AI), keynote at the CVPR 2021 Workshop on Autonomous Driving (WAD), held virtually on June 20, 2021. Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g6bOwQdCJrc ('[CVPR'21 WAD] Keynote - Andrej Karpathy, Tesla'). Figures given: 221 triggers, 7 shadow-mode loops, about 1M ten-second clips, 6B labeled objects, 1.5 PB.
details: The talk explains Tesla's move to vision-only Autopilot (radar removed) and how it trained networks to predict depth, velocity and acceleration from cameras alone. It describes auto-labeling offline with future frames and larger models, and a data engine using 221 manually implemented triggers across the customer fleet. Examples include radar-vision mismatch, bounding-box jitter, detection flicker, tunnel entry and exit, objects on the roof, and brake lights on while acceleration is positive. The final dataset went through the shadow-mode loop seven times. Karpathy argued that when radar and vision disagree it is better to double down on vision than to fuse them.
project_relevance: The main citation for 'trigger-based industrial data engines rely on hand-specified symptoms' (the 221 manual triggers). Use it in the introduction and related work as the example of symptom-level (not representation-level) failure mining.

claim: Tesla Autonomy Day 2019 (Karpathy data engine, shadow mode; HW3).
correct_value: Tesla Autonomy Day, investor event livestream, April 22, 2019 (Palo Alto). Video: https://www.youtube.com/live/Ucp0TTmvqOE. Pete Bannon presented the FSD Computer (HW3). Karpathy presented the neural-network and data-engine segment.
details: Karpathy described fleet-based active learning, which he called the data engine. When the network does something wrong (for example a bike mounted on a car's back detected as two objects), Tesla trains a detector for similar images, asks the fleet for more examples, labels them and retrains. He used a 'cut-in' predictor as the example: it is trained on fleet data and validated in shadow mode before release. Shadow mode means the network runs silently, compares its predictions with the human driver, and triggers snapshot uploads when they disagree. Interventions and disengagements are also logged as signals.
project_relevance: The earliest primary public source for the 'data engine' concept. Cite it together with the CVPR 2021 keynote. HW3 facts come from the Bannon segment.

claim: Karpathy talks on Tesla data engine (learned triggers, fleet sourcing).
correct_value: Andrej Karpathy, 'AI for Full-Self Driving at Tesla', ScaledML Conference 2020. Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hx7BXih7zx8 (circulated April 2020).
details: Karpathy used stop signs (including occluded ones and ones with modifiers) to show the long tail. His workflow: train an 'approximate trigger' offline, ship it to the roughly 1M-car fleet to source images of failing cases, label them, retrain, and repeat. He also described 'Operation Vacation', the goal of automating data collection, labeling, training and testing so the model keeps improving without the core team.
project_relevance: The best citation for learned trigger classifiers, as opposed to the hand-written triggers at CVPR 2021. Useful for describing the 'engineer names a failure, then mines for it' workflow that the project aims to replace.

claim: Karpathy CVPR 2020 workshop talk.
correct_value: Andrej Karpathy, keynote at the CVPR 2020 Workshop on Scalability in Autonomous Driving (virtual, mid-June 2020; talk reported as 2020-06-15, Electrek coverage June 18, 2020). Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=X2CpuabzRaY.
details: Karpathy gave an update on Tesla's program and argued that its vision-based, fleet-scale approach is harder but scales better. He described multi-task learning with a large 'data engine' that collects rare examples, which he called the essence of the long-tail problem. The example was stop signs occluded by foliage.
project_relevance: An optional extra citation for the data-engine and long-tail framing. The CVPR 2021 and Autonomy Day sources are stronger.

claim: Tesla AI Day 2021 (Karpathy data engine).
correct_value: Tesla AI Day, livestream on August 19, 2021. Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j0z4FweCy4M.
details: The event covered Tesla's multi-camera vector-space networks, a manual labeling team of more than 1,000 people, offline 3D auto-labeling, simulation ('a video game with Autopilot as the player') for data that is hard to source or label, and the Dojo training computer. It restated the data-engine loop: deploy networks in shadow mode, use triggers to find inconsistencies and special scenarios, auto-label, retrain. The Tesla Bot was also unveiled.
project_relevance: Cite it for the auto-labeling and simulation stages of an industrial data engine, which correspond to the project's retrain-and-verify loop (SimLoop).

claim: BMW as a Physical AI data-engine exemplar (SOURCE A comparative synthesis).
correct_value:
BMW has public data-engine material in three places:
- High Performance D3 (Data-Driven Development) platform, launched March 27, 2019 with DXC, near the Autonomous Driving Campus in Unterschleißheim. It reprocesses about 2M real-world km and 240M virtual km, with more than 230 PB of storage, over 100,000 CPU cores and more than 200 GPUs.
- SORDI (Synthetic Object Recognition Dataset for Industries), released March 2022 with Microsoft, NVIDIA and idealworks: more than 800,000 photorealistic synthetic images in 80 categories of production resources, made with NVIDIA Omniverse.
- A 2026 'Center of Competence for Physical AI in Production', with humanoid-robot pilots at Spartanburg and Leipzig.
details: For automated driving, BMW's D3 platform ingests fleet sensor data and makes it available for AI training and simulation-based validation. In production, BMW uses synthetic data (Omniverse Replicator, Isaac Sim) to train detection, segmentation and 6D-pose models; it reports detector training for new parts with very few real images. The Physical AI center is about deploying AI and robotics in factories. None of this material describes the 8-stage loop.
project_relevance: Minor. Of BMW's material, D3 is the only piece relevant to driving (data infrastructure at scale); SORDI is relevant only as an example of synthetic data. Cite at most once, as an example of industrial synthetic-data and fleet-data infrastructure.

claim: Carbon Robotics as a Physical AI data-engine exemplar.
correct_value: Carbon Robotics (LaserWeeder) announced the 'Large Plant Model' (LPM) in early February 2026 (TechCrunch, Feb 2, 2026). It is a plant detection and identification foundation model trained on about 150M labeled plant images from more than 175 LaserWeeder units operating in over 100 crops across 15 countries. Field data continuously feeds back into the model and updates are deployed to the whole fleet over the air. Labeling has been done with iMerit since 2020.
details: Carbon Robotics describes a fleet 'data flywheel'. Deployed machines capture labeled plant and weed imagery every pass. The data feeds the centralized LPM, which generalizes across crops and regions so that new fields need little or no retraining. The loop is capture, label (with iMerit), train a foundation model, then deploy fleet-wide. No trigger mechanism or failure-naming stage is described publicly.
project_relevance: Low relevance for driving VLAs. Could appear in one sentence as a non-driving example of a fleet data flywheel. Not evidence for any '8-stage loop'.

claim: Ocado as a Physical AI data-engine exemplar.
correct_value: Ocado's On-Grid Robotic Pick (OGRP) combines computer vision, machine learning and smart sensors. The arms 'learn from every pick', including from human demonstrations, and what one robot learns is shared across the system. Ocado reports more than 30M items picked with OGRP in 2024. Related patents are titled 'Training artificial networks for robotic picking' (US 11,911,901; US 12,491,629).
details: Public material describes fleet-shared learning from real warehouse operation, with generalization across product packaging, weight and shape. It also describes learning from failures with fewer training data sets than conventional approaches. The public material is at the level of marketing and patents. No detailed data-engine stages (triggers, failure naming, synthetic generation, regression checks) are published.
project_relevance: Low relevance. At most a one-line non-driving example of fleet learning. Not a source for an 8-stage loop.

Its products include MCP gateways to statute corpora in dozens of jurisdictions (EU, German, Dutch, UK and Polish law), CVE/ATT&CK/OWASP intelligence, and compliance workflows (DPIA, threat modeling, TARA). It is listed in the CSA STAR Registry. It has no robotics, autonomous-driving or physical-AI data-engine activity.

A search for any physical-AI or data-engine connection found nothing. Its presence in Source A's list is most likely a hallucination or a mixed-up source from the notebook tool.
