second_pass.correct_value: Ansvar AI is Ansvar Systems AB, a Swedish company that runs ansvar.ai and ansvar.eu. It is not a Physical AI company. It sells legal, regulatory and security-intelligence sources for AI agents, with every answer cited, through MCP servers and a hosted gateway (gateway.ansvar.eu/mcp). The products include statute databases for many European jurisdictions (EU, German, Dutch, UK, Polish, Romanian, Hungarian, Greek, Slovak, Danish, Norwegian, and others), MCPs for competition and financial regulation, and Claude Code, Gemini CLI and agent skills for EU regulatory threat modeling, incident reporting, CRA vulnerability obligations and ISO standards. Its only link to cars is compliance content: its ISO-standards skill quotes ISO/SAE 21434 (vehicle cybersecurity) and TARA. It has no robotics, fleet-logging, autonomous-driving or data-engine product, so it cannot have contributed to an '8-stage data-engine loop' synthesis. Source A's listing of it next to BMW, Carbon Robotics and Ocado is unsupported.
second_pass.reasoning:
I tried to overturn the first-pass verdict and could not. Method and limits: the WebSearch budget for this session was already used up after 3 attempted queries. The egress proxy blocked ansvar.ai, ansvar.eu, cloudsecurityalliance.org, huggingface.co, LinkedIn, Semantic Scholar, and the Google, Bing, Brave, DuckDuckGo and Mojeek front ends. So my own evidence comes from GitHub (web pages plus the GitHub search API). What I found:
(1) The GitHub org Ansvar-Systems describes itself as 'Legal, compliance, and security sources for AI agents — every answer cited to the official source', with website ansvar.eu and about 156 repos. Every repo is a legal or compliance MCP server or skill.
(2) Code in those repos and their forks ties the ansvar.ai domain to the same group. Examples: about.ts files name the 'Ansvar MCP Network' with directory https://ansvar.ai/mcp; the contact addresses are hello@ansvar.ai and security@ansvar.ai; a CHANGELOG reads 'Maintained by: Ansvar Systems AB (https://ansvar.eu)'. So 'Ansvar AI' and Ansvar Systems AB are the same entity.
(3) The GitHub search API returned no org hits for 'physical AI', 'data engine', or robot/automotive/vehicle/machinery repos. The one 'robotics' hit was a Danish competition-authority merger URL inside a data file.
(4) The closest link to driving is iso-standards-expert-skill, which covers ISO/SAE 21434 vehicle cybersecurity and TARA. That is regulatory text retrieval, not a data engine.
(5) Across GitHub, searches for 'Ansvar AI' with 'data engine', 'Carbon Robotics' or 'Ocado', and for 'ansvar robotics' repos, found nothing that links any 'Ansvar' entity to physical AI.
(6) The repo docs and references.bib never mention Ansvar, Ocado, Carbon Robotics or an '8-stage' loop. The claim appears only in Source A, line 43.
I agree with the first pass on substance. Two details I could not re-check because the hosts were blocked: the CSA STAR Registry listing, and the exact product wording on ansvar.ai. Neither changes the verdict. I also could not run open web searches for a different, unrelated 'Ansvar AI' in robotics. The GitHub evidence and the first pass's web evidence both point the same way, so a physical-AI 'Ansvar AI' is very unlikely. What to do: remove Ansvar AI from any industry or related-work comparison. Also treat the claim that 'Comparative Synthesis Across Physical AI ... establishes the standard 8-Stage Data Engine loop' as an LLM synthesis without a source, not an established industry standard. Cite the stages to real sources (for example Karpathy's Tesla data-engine talks) or present them as the project's own framing.

claim: docs/feedback.md: 'Honda's DRAMA Dataset (WACV 2023): Collected right at Honda Research Institute (Ryan Lingo's lab). 17,785 interactive video clips specifically filtered on human risk interventions and sudden braking events in urban traffic, complete with CAN bus steering/brake signals and natural language risk explanations.' PROJECT_BRIEF_DIFF: 'Contains synchronized front-camera video, CAN bus signals (steering, brake), and natural language risk explanations'; proposes pre-training/fine-tuning the VLA on DRAMA.
correct_value:
Srikanth Malla, Chiho Choi, Isht Dwivedi, Joon Hee Choi, Jiachen Li. 'DRAMA: Joint Risk Localization and Captioning in Driving.' Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV), 2023, pp. 1043-1052. arXiv:2209.10767. Dataset page: https://usa.honda-ri.com/drama. DRAMA stands for Driving Risk Assessment Mechanism with A captioning module.
- Clips: 17,785 interactive driving scenario clips, each 2 seconds (about 10 hours in total), recorded in urban Tokyo, Japan.
- Cameras: a SEKONIX SF332X-10X (30 Hz, 1928×1280, 60° horizontal FOV) and a GoPro Hero 7 (60 Hz, 2704×1520, 118.2° horizontal FOV).
- Vehicle signals: videos are 'synchronized with CAN signals and IMU'.
- Selection: clips were 'filtered based on the ego-driver's behavioral response to external situations or events which activate braking'.
- Annotations: video-level Q/A, object-level Q/A, risk-object bounding box, free-form risk caption, ego-intention labels, a scene classifier, and suggestions to the driver. 17,066 clips are risk scenarios (12,273 vehicles, 3,344 pedestrians or cyclists, 1,449 infrastructure).
- License and access: 'available for non-commercial usage'; requesters 'must be affiliated with a university and use your university email address to make the request' through the HRI-US dataset request form.
details: DRAMA introduces joint risk localization (a bounding box on the important or risky agent) and natural-language risk captioning from ego-centric driving video, with a model baseline trained on video frames and optical flow. The public release, as described on the HRI-US page, contains a 'combined/' folder with raw frames, optical-flow images and short movie GIFs, an integrated_output_v2.json annotation file, a data_gen.py loader, and processed train/val/test pickle files. I found no public confirmation that CAN steering or brake traces are in the download. The dataset is widely reused for VLM driving evaluation; for example, DRAMA-X (ICCV 2025 workshop) derives a 5,686-frame intent and risk benchmark from it.
project_relevance: Useful as a real-world, open-loop test set. It can check whether discovered failure axes or SAE features line up with human-labeled risk objects and captions, and it offers a real-data sanity check alongside CARLA. It does not fit the plan to pre-train or fine-tune a driving VLA for closed-loop CARLA. The clips are only 2 seconds long, there are no driving trajectories or actions besides intention labels and possibly CAN data, the footage is left-hand-traffic Tokyo while CARLA drives on the right, and it is Honda-owned non-commercial data. Berkeley students can request it with @berkeley.edu email. Ask Ryan Lingo whether HRI-US can share the CAN/IMU streams and whether model weights trained on it can be released. Correct feedback.md and PROJECT_BRIEF_DIFF accordingly.
discrepancies: 'Human risk interventions' is wrong. DRAMA is human-driven naturalistic data selected on the ego driver's braking response to external events, not autonomy disengagements or interventions.
'Sudden braking events' overstates it. The paper says the filtering is on events that 'activate braking'; 'sudden' is not stated.

'CAN bus steering/brake signals' is unverified. The paper says video is synchronized with CAN and IMU, but steering and brake channels are not itemized, and the public release contents do not list CAN files.
'Front-camera video' is incomplete: there are two front-facing cameras (SEKONIX 30 Hz and GoPro 60 Hz).
The clips are 2 seconds each and were collected in Tokyo, Japan. The repo never mentions this, although it matters for pre-training and domain match with CARLA.

'Collected right at Honda Research Institute (Ryan Lingo's lab)' is not supported. It was collected in Tokyo by HRI-US researchers (Malla, Dwivedi et al.; some authors later at Samsung and Stanford). I could not confirm a link to Ryan Lingo's group.
Access requires a request through the HRI-US form with a university email, for non-commercial use. It is not openly downloadable.

claim: Honda Research Institute Driving Dataset (HDD) as a relevant HRI-US asset.
correct_value: Vasili Ramanishka, Yi-Ting Chen, Teruhisa Misu, Kate Saenko. 'Toward Driving Scene Understanding: A Dataset for Learning Driver Behavior and Causal Reasoning.' CVPR 2018, pp. 7699-7707. arXiv:1811.02307. Dataset page: https://usa.honda-ri.com/hdd.
details: HDD contains 104 hours of real human driving in the San Francisco Bay Area over 137 sessions. It was recorded with an instrumented vehicle carrying cameras, LiDAR, GPS, IMU and CAN bus signals (including steering, brake and throttle). Annotations have four layers: goal-oriented actions (such as turns and lane changes), stimulus-driven actions (such as stopping for a pedestrian), causes, and attention (the traffic participants the driver attends to). Fusing CAN and visual signals gave the best action-detection accuracy. Access is by request, for non-commercial or academic use.
project_relevance: Probably the most useful real-data HRI asset for this project. The 'stimulus-driven action' and 'cause' layers give a human-labeled taxonomy of why drivers deviate. That can serve as a real-world answer key when evaluating whether unsupervised failure axes recover meaningful causal categories, as a complement to the planted CARLA answer key. It is right-hand traffic like CARLA, it has continuous long sequences with CAN controls unlike DRAMA's 2-second clips, and HRI-owned risk-object work (e.g., 'Who Make Drivers Stop?', ICRA 2020) builds on it. Request it through HRI-US.

claim: HAD (HRI Advice Dataset) as a relevant HRI-US asset.
correct_value: Jinkyu Kim, Teruhisa Misu, Yi-Ting Chen, Ashish Tawari, John Canny. 'Grounding Human-to-Vehicle Advice for Self-driving Vehicles.' CVPR 2019, pp. 10583-10591. DOI 10.1109/CVPR.2019.01084. arXiv:1911.06978. Dataset page: https://usa.honda-ri.com/had.
details: HAD adds natural-language advice to about 30 hours of HDD driving video. The advice is either goal-oriented (top-down navigation guidance) or stimulus-driven (pointing out visual stimuli the controller should attend to). The paper grounds this advice in an end-to-end driving controller, affecting both its visual attention and its control outputs, and shows that advice-conditioned models are more interpretable and robust. Access is non-commercial, by request with a university email.
project_relevance: Relevant for linking discovered activation axes to natural-language concepts, for example checking whether SAE features align with stimulus-driven advice categories. There is a Berkeley connection: John Canny (UC Berkeley EECS) is a co-author, and Jinkyu Kim did this work during his Berkeley PhD. Both are possible contacts or advisors for the Berkeley team.

claim: Rank2Tell as a relevant HRI-US driving dataset.
correct_value: Enna Sachdeva, Nakul Agarwal, Suhas Chundi, Sean Roelofs, Jiachen Li, Mykel Kochenderfer, Chiho Choi, Behzad Dariush. 'Rank2Tell: A Multimodal Driving Dataset for Joint Importance Ranking and Reasoning.' WACV 2024, pp. 7513-7522. arXiv:2309.06597. Dataset page: https://usa.honda-ri.com/rank2tell.
details: Rank2Tell is an ego-centric multimodal dataset of 116 clips of about 20 seconds each at 10 FPS, recorded in highly interactive San Francisco Bay Area traffic. The vehicle had three Point Grey Grasshopper cameras (1920×1200), a Velodyne HDL-64E S2 LiDAR, high-precision GPS and CAN data (steering, braking, throttle). Dense annotations give an importance ranking for traffic agents plus natural-language reasons, with semantic, spatial, temporal and relational attributes collected through closed and open-ended VQA. The paper benchmarks a joint importance-ranking and captioning model. Access is for university researchers, by request, for non-commercial use.
project_relevance: Small but richly annotated. It could serve as a qualitative real-world probe of whether discovered axes relate to which objects a driver considers important. It is too small for training, and it is HRI-owned, so it adds credibility with the mentor.

claim: (Derivative of DRAMA; relevant for VLM risk-reasoning evaluation.)
correct_value: Mihir Godbole, Xiangbo Gao, Zhengzhong Tu (TACO Group, Texas A&M). 'DRAMA-X: A Fine-grained Intent Prediction and Risk Reasoning Benchmark For Driving.' ICCV 2025 Workshops (2COOOL: 2nd Workshop on the Challenge of Out-of-Label Hazards in Autonomous Driving). arXiv:2506.17590. Code: https://github.com/taco-group/DRAMA-X.
details: DRAMA-X is built from DRAMA through an automated annotation pipeline. It has 5,686 accident-prone frames labeled with object bounding boxes, a nine-class directional intent taxonomy for vulnerable road users, binary risk scores, expert-generated ego action suggestions, and motion summaries. As a baseline the authors propose SGG-Intent, a training-free pipeline that runs scene-graph generation, then intent inference, then risk assessment with VLMs. The derived labels are released on GitHub and Hugging Face, but they still depend on the original DRAMA data, which must be requested from HRI-US.
project_relevance: An evaluation option if the team obtains DRAMA: it offers ready-made intent and risk labels for probing whether VLA or VLM activations encode risk and intent. It is also a recent example of how DRAMA is used in current VLM-driving work.

claim: Other HRI-US driving datasets that might be relevant.
correct_value:
The HRI-US dataset portal (https://usa.honda-ri.com/datasets) lists H3D, HAD, HDBD, HDD, HEV-I, HRDX, HSD, LOKI, OATS, Rank2Tell, a Road Asset Monitoring dataset, TITAN and DRAMA. Notable driving ones:
- TITAN (Malla, Dariush, Choi, CVPR 2020): 700 labeled Tokyo clips with odometry and hierarchical pedestrian action labels.
- LOKI (ICCV 2021): long-term and key intentions for trajectory prediction.
- H3D (ICRA 2019): full-surround 3D multi-object detection and tracking in the Bay Area.
- HSD (ICRA 2019): dynamic traffic scene classification.
- HEV-I: egocentric intersection vehicle trajectories.
- HDBD: driver behavior.
All are distributed on request for non-commercial, university-affiliated use.
details: These datasets cover perception (H3D), forecasting and intent (TITAN, LOKI, HEV-I), scene classification (HSD) and driver behavior (HDBD). None is a closed-loop driving benchmark. For discovering failure axes in VLAs, HDD (with its causal and stimulus layers) and DRAMA or Rank2Tell (with language rationales) are the most relevant. TITAN and LOKI could provide real-world pedestrian-intent slices.
project_relevance: Mention them in the plan only as candidate real-world evaluation slices, and choose one after talking with Ryan Lingo about which HRI data is easiest to share with the Berkeley team. Do not promise pre-training on them.

claim: AutoVLA (arXiv:2506.13757, Zhou et al., UCLA, NeurIPS 2025) — the paper SOURCE B paraphrases in Sections 1.1-1.3, 3 and 5.
correct_value: Title: 'AutoVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model for End-to-End Autonomous Driving with Adaptive Reasoning and Reinforcement Fine-Tuning'. Authors: Zewei Zhou* and Tianhui Cai* (equal contribution), Seth Z. Zhao, Yun Zhang, Zhiyu Huang (project leader), Bolei Zhou, Jiaqi Ma. All are at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA Mobility Lab). arXiv:2506.13757 (June 2025; v1-v3 exist). NeurIPS 2025 poster (neurips.cc/virtual/2025/poster/120167; OpenReview id Cxj4jZ7mRI).
details: AutoVLA is a single autoregressive VLA built on Qwen2.5-VL-3B. It takes 3 front-facing camera videos (4 frames at 2 Hz), ego speed and acceleration, and a navigation command. It outputs optional chain-of-thought text followed by 10 discrete 'physical action tokens' (0.5 s each, from a K-disk codebook with K=2048) that decode into a 5 s trajectory. SFT on ground-truth trajectories plus distilled CoT (from Qwen2.5-VL-72B) teaches two modes: fast (action only) and slow (CoT then action). GRPO-based RFT then uses a task reward (NAVSIM PDMS on nuPlan; ADE-based on Waymo) minus a CoT-length penalty. The project page reports +10.6% PDMS and -66.8% runtime from RFT on NAVSIM. The model is evaluated on nuPlan/NAVSIM, nuScenes, the Waymo Vision-based E2E challenge (top RFS Spotlight score as of May 2025) and CARLA/Bench2Drive closed loop.
project_relevance: This is a strong candidate open-weight driving VLA for the project's activation-mining stage: a 3B Qwen2.5 decoder that is easy to hook layer by layer, with an explicit fast/slow reasoning switch and optional CoT text that can serve as a behavioral stratification baseline and for describability checks. Caveats: the released weights target NAVSIM/nuPlan, not CARLA. Closed-loop CARLA use needs a self-built agent wrapper and possibly Bench2Drive fine-tuning (no Bench2Drive checkpoint is released). Cite it as the NeurIPS 2025 inproceedings version, not the README's @article.

claim: Official code/checkpoints at https://github.com/ucla-mobility/AutoVLA (SOURCE B's build plan assumes one can reproduce data, CoT distillation, SFT, RFT and Bench2Drive closed-loop evaluation).
correct_value: Repo: github.com/ucla-mobility/AutoVLA. Timeline: code released 2026/02; checkpoint released 2026/05 at huggingface.co/Zewei-Zhou/AutoVLA (merged from LoRA, evaluated with LORA=false; an issue names a NAVSIM checkpoint 'AutoVLA_PDMS_89'). Released: CoT annotation code (Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct-AWQ teacher); preprocessing for nuPlan/NAVSIM, Waymo E2E and nuScenes (DriveLM); the K-disk codebook script plus a prebuilt codebook_cache/agent_vocab.pkl; SFT (FSDP full-shard, bf16, full LM fine-tune, no LoRA); GRPO RFT (LoRA r=8); a NAVSIM AutoVLAAgent; nuScenes open-loop eval. NOT released: the reasoning/CoT dataset ('pending approval from the data provider'). No CARLA/Bench2Drive agent, training code, data or checkpoint either: carla is absent from requirements.txt, and issues #30 and #43 asking for Bench2Drive code were closed with no visible maintainer answer. License: 'Academic Software License' © 2026 UCLA Mobility Lab (academic/non-profit research only, non-commercial, no transfer or sublicense; commercial requests to jiaqima@ucla.edu). The weights license is unclear (issue #50 has no answer). Environment: Python 3.9, torch 2.4.0, transformers 4.49.0, qwen-vl-utils 0.0.10, pytorch-lightning 2.2.1, nuplan-devkit v1.2. Hardware: the paper trains on 8x NVIDIA L40S (48 GB), 5 epochs, per-GPU batch 1, grad-accum 4 (effective 32). The released GRPO config defaults to devices [0,1]. No official peak-VRAM figure (issue #51 has no answer).
details: The repo implements the full pipeline: dataset preprocessing with optional CoT, codebook clustering, SFT, GRPO RFT, and NAVSIM PDMS / nuScenes evaluation. The prompt, action tokenizer and reward code in models/autovla.py are the ground truth for many of SOURCE B's claims. Open issues flag reproducibility problems. #48: the released AutoVLA_PDMS_89 checkpoint gives 83.69 vs the paper's 89.11 on navtest, and the paper states SFT LR 1e-5 while the config uses 2e-5. #54: the released checkpoint always outputs 'This is a straightforward scenario', i.e. it never reasons. #53: the NAVSIM checkpoint is incompatible with the nuPlan/Waymo preprocessing. #44: the CoT teacher saw 4 cameras (including the back camera) while the student sees 3. #47: no Waymo (WOD-E2E) training configs.
project_relevance: This is the practical entry point for using AutoVLA as the studied policy: a 3B model whose Qwen2.5 decoder layers can be hooked with standard PyTorch forward hooks. For CARLA/Bench2Drive closed-loop rollouts (Stage 1 of the project), the team must write its own CARLA agent (camera rig to front/front-left/front-right at 2 Hz, speed/accel, command to prompt, decode 10 action tokens, then a PID controller), and must expect a sim-to-real domain gap because the released weights are NAVSIM/nuPlan-trained. Check the license with the authors (and whether weights may be redistributed) before publishing derived weights. Worth contacting the maintainers (Zewei Zhou) about the Bench2Drive checkpoint and CoT data. Budget GPU time: roughly 1 s per fast-mode step and about 10 s per slow-mode step (paper; hardware unstated).
discrepancies: SOURCE B's Phase 5 assumes Bench2Drive closed-loop evaluation can be reproduced; no CARLA/Bench2Drive code or checkpoint is released.
SOURCE B's Phase 2 assumes the CoT data can be regenerated to a '>88% accuracy target'; the reasoning data is not released, and the released annotation config uses the AWQ-quantized 72B teacher.

claim: Backbone: pretrained Qwen2.5-VL-3B. Inputs: 3 RGB cameras (front, front-left, front-right), 4 sequential frames per camera at 2 Hz (2.0 s history).
correct_value: Backbone: Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct. Inputs: 3 forward cameras (front, front-left, front-right); each is passed as a separate Qwen 'video' of 4 frames sampled at 2 Hz (the current frame plus 3 preceding frames). The history span is therefore 1.5 s, not 2.0 s.
details: get_prompt() in models/autovla.py loads camera_types ['front_camera','front_left_camera','front_right_camera'] with 4 frames each. The prompt text says 'comprising four sequential frames sampled at 2 Hz'. Paper snippets state the current and three preceding frames at 2 Hz, and the configs point pretrained_model_path at ./Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct. Qwen2.5-VL uses temporal_patch_size=2, so 4 frames become 2 temporal token groups per camera. There are no rear or side-rear cameras, so the model cannot see behind the ego vehicle.
project_relevance: Match this rig exactly when building a CARLA agent: 3 forward cameras, 4-frame buffer at 2 Hz (0.5 s spacing). The lack of rear view is a built-in blind spot and a likely source of a 'discoverable' failure axis (rear or side-rear interactions, e.g. HighwayCutIn from behind). A good sanity check for the unsupervised method.
discrepancies: '2.0 s history' is wrong: 4 frames at 2 Hz (t-1.5, t-1.0, t-0.5, t) span 1.5 s.

claim: 'Input images are resized to 28 x 28 x 128 pixels' (SUSPICIOUS); repeated in the Phase 1 build plan as '28 x 28 x 128 resolution'.
correct_value: 28x28x128 = 100,352 is a per-frame TOTAL-PIXEL budget: Qwen2.5-VL min_pixels = max_pixels = 28*28*128. It is not a 28x28 image with 128 channels. Frames are resized with aspect ratio kept and sides rounded to multiples of 28. Each 28x28-pixel block (14-px ViT patches merged 2x2) becomes one visual token, so there are at most ~128 tokens per spatial slice. Because temporal_patch_size is 2, 4 frames give at most ~256 tokens per camera and at most ~768 visual tokens for 3 cameras. The code default is 28*28*128, but both released training configs override it to min_pixels = max_pixels = 109,760 = 28*28*140 (at most ~140 tokens per slice, ~840 in total).
details: get_prompt() uses min_pixels = self.video_conf.get('min_pixels', 28*28*128) and max_pixels likewise, and passes them into each camera's 'video' entry for qwen-vl-utils. qwen2.5-vl-3B-mix-sft.yaml and qwen2.5-vl-3B-nuplan-grpo-cot.yaml both set video.min_pixels = max_pixels = 109760. Paper snippets say video frames are resized preserving aspect ratio. My own derivation, not stated in any source: Qwen's smart_resize would map a 1920x1080 nuPlan frame to about 224x420 px (8x15 = 120 tokens) under either budget. Treat that as an estimate to confirm by running the processor.
project_relevance: This is the real token budget: roughly 700-850 visual tokens per step. It sets activation-logging cost and resolution: small distant objects (pedestrians, traffic lights) cover very few tokens, which is a plausible hidden failure axis. When logging activations, record video_grid_thw per step so token positions map back to camera, time slice and image patch.
discrepancies: '28 x 28 x 128 pixels' is presented as image dimensions; it is actually a total-pixel budget of 100,352 px (about 128 visual tokens) per frame.
The released configs use 28x28x140 = 109,760 pixels, not 28x28x128 (the latter is only the code default and, likely, the paper's value).

claim: Ego state: velocity, acceleration, historical trajectory. Navigation prompts ('Turn Left', 'Go Straight').
correct_value: The released prompt contains only the scalar speed sqrt(vx^2+vy^2) in m/s and the scalar acceleration magnitude sqrt(ax^2+ay^2) in m/s^2 (3 decimals each), plus the dataset's driving command lowercased: 'The driving instruction is: {instruction}. Based on this information, plan the action trajectory for the autonomous vehicle over the next five seconds.' There is no historical trajectory (past waypoints) in the prompt. The only history is visual (4 frames).
details: get_prompt() builds the user message from 3 video entries plus one text line with velocity, acceleration and instruction. The code has no 'history', 'past' or historical-trajectory fields. Acceleration enters as an unsigned magnitude, so braking and accelerating look the same in text. I could not check the paper text for whether it describes ego history differently, but the released model does not receive it.
project_relevance: Simple to reproduce in CARLA: speed, acceleration magnitude and command string. Because acceleration is unsigned and there is no past trajectory, the policy may confuse deceleration and acceleration contexts. That is a candidate failure axis, and the prompt should be matched exactly for faithful rollouts.
discrepancies: 'Historical trajectory' is not an input in the released model/prompt.
Velocity and acceleration are scalar magnitudes, not vectors; acceleration sign is lost.

claim: Diagram shows an 'Adaptive Router' that picks Fast vs Slow Thinking; fast thinking uses a 'fixed short prompt -> direct action tokens'.
correct_value: There is no separate router module. One autoregressive model decides its own mode by the first text it generates: 'This is a straightforward scenario...' followed directly by action tokens (fast), or 'This is a complex scenario...' followed by CoT and then action tokens (slow). Both modes share the same CoT-enabled system prompt ('If necessary, use step-by-step reasoning (Chain-of-Thought)... Otherwise, you may directly predict the final driving action'). The short non-CoT system prompt is used only for action-only (use_cot=false) training. RFT shapes the switching through the CoT-length penalty, which the code applies only when the output contains 'complex scenario'.
details: The README describes a 'unified autoregressive generative process, dynamically switching thinking modes'. The GRPO reward code checks '"complex scenario" in text.lower()' to apply the penalty. Issue #54 quotes model outputs 'This is a straightforward scenario...' and reports that the released checkpoint never produces 'complex scenario'. The model code contains no classifier or router. SOURCE B's 'Adaptive Router' box comes from its own removed ASCII diagram, not from the paper or code.
project_relevance: Important for the project: the mode decision is a token-level output of the same network. It can be read directly from the first generated tokens (a free behavioral label for stratification), and its internal precursor can be probed with linear probes. Caveat: the released checkpoint may be stuck in fast mode (issue #54), so slow-thinking CoT-probing experiments may need forced prompting or re-running RFT.
discrepancies: No 'Adaptive Router' module exists; the mode is chosen by the single model's own generated text.
Fast thinking does not use a separate 'fixed short prompt'; both modes share the same system prompt, and only the response format differs.

second_pass.correct_value:
AutoVLA has no 'Adaptive Router' module, and its official framework figure (images/AutoVLA_framework.png) has no router box. The figure's right-hand panel is titled 'Dual Thinking Mode Adaptation', with two labels: 'Slow Thinking in Complex Scenarios' and 'Fast Thinking in Simple Scenarios'. A single input box, 'System Prompt: Task & Thinking Guidance', feeds one 'Auto Vision Language Action Model', which outputs Reasoning Tokens and then Action Tokens.

The mode is a text choice made by that one autoregressive model. It learns the choice from its SFT response templates (dataset_utils/sft_dataset.py):
- Fast: '<think>\nThis is a straightforward scenario, and a direct decision can be made.\n</think>\n<answer>\nThe final output action is: [action tokens]\n</answer>'
- Slow: '<think>\nThis is a complex scenario requiring additional reasoning.\n[CoT]\n</think>\n<answer>...'

Which template a training sample gets depends on its data: whether ground-truth CoT exists (gt_cot is a string for nuPlan/Waymo, or a list of 5 for nuScenes). A flag or classifier does not choose it.

With use_cot=True, both modes share one CoT-enabled system prompt: 'If necessary, use step-by-step reasoning (Chain-of-Thought) to arrive at the best driving action. Otherwise, you may directly predict the final driving action.' The short non-CoT system prompt, with no <think> block, is used only for action-only training or inference (use_cot=False). That is a separate configuration, not the fast mode of the adaptive model.

The 'fixed short' element in fast thinking is a fixed response prefix that the model generates, not a fixed short prompt. RFT (GRPO) shapes the switching: reward_function applies the sigmoid CoT-length penalty only when '"complex scenario" in text.lower()'.
second_pass.reasoning:
I checked this independently and reached the same verdict as the first pass: contradicted. I also sharpened the details from primary evidence.

(1) I downloaded and viewed the official framework figure from the AutoVLA repo (raw.githubusercontent.com/ucla-mobility/AutoVLA/main/images/AutoVLA_framework.png; README calls it the 'teaser'). Every label is readable. The panels are:
- Camera streams / Vision Encoder
- Instruction / Ego states / System Prompt ('Task & Thinking Guidance') into a Text Tokenizer
- 'Auto Vision Language Action Model', outputting 'Reasoning Token' then 'Action Token'
- Planning / Action Codebook, with top-K token decoding
- 'Dual Thinking Mode Adaptation', with 'Slow Thinking in Complex Scenarios' (4-step CoT example: Scene Description, Critical Object Description, Reasoning on Intent, Best Driving Action) and 'Fast Thinking in Simple Scenarios'
- SFT and RFT/GRPO panels

No box is labelled Router, Adaptive Router, selector or gate. SOURCE B's 'Adaptive Router' most likely distorts 'Dual Thinking Mode Adaptation'.

(2) GitHub code search over the repo found the fast and slow templates in dataset_utils/sft_dataset.py: 'This is a straightforward scenario, and a direct decision can be made.' and 'This is a complex scenario requiring additional reasoning.'. The template is chosen by whether gt_cot exists. Fetching sft_dataset.py confirmed:
- With using_cot=True, one CoT system prompt is used for both templates.
- With using_cot=False, a shorter system prompt is used, and the answer has only '<answer>...' with no <think> block.

(3) models/autovla.py:
- The CoT system prompt contains 'If necessary, use step-by-step reasoning (Chain-of-Thought)...' and 'Otherwise, you may directly predict the final driving action.'
- No prompt contains 'straightforward' or 'complex'.
- There is no router, gate or classifier module; the classes are AutoVLA, SFTAutoVLA and GRPOAutoVLA.
- The reward code applies the CoT penalty only when 'complex scenario' is in the generated text.

(4) Issue #54 ('The released checkpoint always results in Fast thinking') quotes the model always outputting 'This is a straightforward scenario...'. Issue #41 shows users mixing up use_cot=false with fast thinking. That is the same confusion SOURCE B's 'fixed short prompt' reflects.

Correction to the first pass: its correct_value is accurate. I added the exact template strings, how a template is chosen (data-driven), and the figure's real panel title.

Side note for the separate 'slow thinking: 4-step CoT' claim: the figure shows 4 CoT steps, but the code's CoT system prompt lists 5 (Scene Analysis, Identification of Critical Objects, Prediction of Critical Object Behavior, Ego Vehicle Intent Reasoning, Final Action Decision).

What the work does: AutoVLA (UCLA, NeurIPS 2025) builds on Qwen2.5-VL-3B. It adds discrete physical action tokens from a K-disk codebook, and a single autoregressive model emits optional CoT and then action tokens. SFT on mixed CoT and no-CoT data teaches both modes. GRPO RFT, with a CoT-length penalty applied only to 'complex scenario' outputs, reduces unneeded reasoning.

Project relevance:
- The fast/slow decision is a token-level output: the first generated words, 'straightforward' vs 'complex'. That gives a free behavioural label for stratifying failures, and a target for linear probes on hidden states just before the choice.
- Do not describe or draw a router module in project docs. Describe it as 'self-selected reasoning mode via generated prefix'.
- Caveat: the released checkpoint may always choose fast mode (issue #54, still open with no maintainer reply). Slow-mode or CoT analyses may need forced prefixes such as 'This is a complex scenario requiring additional reasoning.' or a re-run of SFT/RFT.

Limitations: the web search budget ran out, and huggingface.co, autovla.github.io and ar5iv were blocked, so I could not read the paper PDF text directly. The official figure and code are primary sources and settle the question.

claim: Trajectory -> tokens a=[a_1..a_T]; each token = 0.5 s motion segment (dx, dy, dtheta); 5.0 s horizon -> T=10 tokens; tokens <action_0>..<action_2047>.
correct_value: T = 10 tokens x 0.5 s = 5.0 s (configs: num_poses 10, interval_length 0.5, time_horizon 5.0). Tokens are the strings '<action_{i}>' for i = 0..2047, added to the Qwen vocabulary starting at token id 151665 (action_start_id). Each codebook entry stores the vehicle bounding-box contour over the 0.5 s segment (tensor shape n_bins x 6 x 4 x 2), clustered on local (dx, dy, dtheta) segment transforms. Decoding chains the segments by rolling out from pose (0, 0, 0).
details: action_tokenizer.py loads pickle['token_all']['veh'] as an (n_bins, 6, 4, 2) contour tensor, maps '<action_i>' to codebook entries, and rolls out positions and headings in sequence. The paper characterizes each segment by its final-frame bounding-box contour relative to the current frame. During RFT, generate_sample() truncates or zero-pads to exactly 10 action tokens before decoding.
project_relevance: Action tokens give a discrete, low-dimensional behavior readout: 10 codebook ids per step. Clustering and diffing on these is cheap and gives a natural 'behavioral stratification' baseline to compare against activation-based failure axes. Log the token ids alongside activations.

claim: Codebook via K-disk clustering on Waymo Open Motion Dataset (real) and CARLA-Garage (sim); contour distance threshold delta = 0.05 m; K=2048.
correct_value: K-disk clustering with K = 2048 (--num_cluster default 2048) and tolerance delta = 0.05 m (--tol_dist default 0.05; mean corner distance between box contours, with a 4.8 m x 2.0 m vehicle box). The paper states the codebook is built from WOMD (real) and CARLA-Garage (simulation). Implementation note: the released scripts/action_token_cluster.sh clusters nuPlan gt_trajectory JSONs by default (--data_path ./dataset/nuplan, n_trajs 2,048,000), and a prebuilt codebook_cache/agent_vocab.pkl of unstated provenance is shipped.
details: action_token_cluster.py implements a K-disk procedure: repeatedly pick a random segment and remove all segments whose mean contour-corner distance is within tol, until K centers are chosen. Segments are local (dx, dy, dtheta) transforms converted to 4-corner contours. A paper snippet states 'an action codebook with K=2048 tokens is constructed by applying K-Disk clustering to real-world (WOMD) and simulation (CARLA-Garage) motion datasets'.
project_relevance: Because CARLA-Garage motions reportedly contributed to the codebook, the action vocabulary should cover CARLA kinematics reasonably. For the planted-gap harness, codebook coverage gaps (rare maneuvers far from any of the 2048 centers) are a candidate 'data gap' that activation mining should find. Use the shipped agent_vocab.pkl for consistency with the checkpoint.
discrepancies: Implementation note, not a SOURCE B error: the released clustering script uses nuPlan data by default, not WOMD + CARLA-Garage.

claim: Tokenization ablation (ADE/FDE/coverage/usage) for RT-1, FAST and K-disk at K=256/1024/2048/4096, e.g. K=2048: RT-1 0.1014/0.1775; FAST 0.0281/0.0309; K-disk 0.0182/0.0203/99.42%/100.0%; RT-1 has ADE > 0.10 m; FAST gives variable-length sequences.
correct_value: Confirmed qualitatively from paper snippets. The paper compares RT-1 (uniform bins over acceleration and steering rate, with a kinematic rollout), FAST, and K-disk across K = 256/1024/2048/4096. RT-1 has the highest reconstruction error, because controls must be inferred from trajectory-level data. FAST is more sensitive to K and is comparable only at K=4096. K-disk is most accurate at every K. Small codebooks (K=256) have high error due to limited movement coverage. The exact table values could not be checked against the paper (arXiv blocked, no snippet showed them).
details: SOURCE B's numbers are internally consistent with the paper's qualitative statements. RT-1 stays around 0.10-0.14 m ADE, above 0.10 m, at every K. FAST at K=4096 (0.0149) is close to K-disk (0.0141). At K=256, K-disk coverage is only 86.47%. The '(Ours)' label shows the table was copied from the paper. The 'variable-length' criticism of FAST is a known property of DCT+BPE tokenization (Pertsch et al., 2025), but I could not verify the paper's exact wording.
project_relevance: Only needed if the project discusses action representation. Cite the qualitative conclusion, and re-check exact numbers against the paper PDF (supplementary table) before quoting them.
discrepancies: Exact numeric values are unverified; do not quote them without checking the PDF.

second_pass.correct_value:
SOURCE B's numbers match the AutoVLA paper (Zhou et al., NeurIPS 2025, arXiv:2506.13757), Table 4 on PDF p.10, "action tokenization accuracy". This is a main-paper table, not a supplementary one. Values are ADE m / FDE m, and movement coverage (MC) and codebook usage (CU) are reported for K-disk only.
- K=256: RT-1 0.1440/0.2942; FAST 0.1708/0.2137; K-disk 0.0687/0.1034, MC 86.47%, CU 100.0%.
- K=1024: RT-1 0.1052/0.1883; FAST 0.0522/0.0588; K-disk 0.0253/0.0282, MC 97.41%, CU 100.0%.
- K=2048: RT-1 0.1014/0.1775; FAST 0.0281/0.0309; K-disk 0.0182/0.0203, MC 99.42%, CU 100.0%.
- K=4096: RT-1 0.1001/0.1739; FAST 0.0149/0.0161; K-disk 0.0141/0.0155, MC 100.0%, CU 91.46%.
RT-1 ADE is above 0.10 m at every K (minimum 0.1001). In their NeurIPS rebuttal the authors describe the RT-1 baseline as "uniform action bins" over acceleration and steering rate, with a kinematic model used to rebuild the trajectory. They attribute its error to having only trajectory-level data, so the controls must be derived indirectly. They say FAST "uses variable-length token sequences (typically 1 to 25 tokens per trajectory)", which complicates fixed-horizon prediction. The authors chose K=2048 with delta = 0.05 m; the released code's defaults are --num_cluster 2048 and --tol_dist 0.05.
second_pass.reasoning:
OVERTURNS the first pass: partially_confirmed becomes confirmed. The first pass could not check the numbers. I found three independent sources that confirm all of them.

(1) A GitHub scrape of the NeurIPS 2025 OpenReview reviews (repo cs411-alawini/sp26-cs411-team032-TEAM32, file scraper/data_nips/reviews/120167.json; AutoVLA forum id 28qUA2bSe5, decision Accept). It contains the authors' own rebuttal ("Rebuttal by Authors"), and its table matches every one of SOURCE B's 24 ADE/FDE values exactly: RT-1 (Action Bin), FAST (DCT) and K-disk (Ours) at K=256/1024/2048/4096. The same rebuttal says:
- "For the RT-1 tokenization method, we discretize acceleration and steering rate using uniform action bins and apply a kinematic model to reconstruct the long-term trajectory... since we only have trajectory-level data and we have to indirectly derive control actions from it, this binning approach leads to the highest reconstruction error."
- "FAST ... uses variable-length token sequences (typically 1 to 25 tokens per trajectory), which complicates the selection of appropriate token lengths and makes fixed-horizon trajectory prediction more challenging."
- K=2048 was chosen because NAVSIM PDMS is 79.47 at K=1024, 80.54 at K=2048 and 80.39 at K=4096.

(2) VennIntelligence/jev-drive w1_ablation_ledger.csv cites "autovla.pdf, Table 4, PDF p.10" for the same reconstruction numbers. Examples: RT-1 0.144 vs K-disk 0.0687 at K=256; RT-1 0.1014/0.1775 vs K-disk 0.0182/0.0203 at K=2048; FAST 0.0281 at K=2048; FAST FDE 0.0588 at K=1024.

(3) s1111e/CS-6263-FinalProject, a course reproduction, hard-codes the paper's Table 4 values including MC and CU: 86.47/97.41/99.42/100.0% and 100/100/100/91.46%. These match SOURCE B exactly. That project reproduced the K=2048 K-disk metrics exactly. At K=4096 it got ADE/FDE 0.0164/0.0173 against the paper's 0.0141/0.0155, which it attributes to clustering seed.

The released code (ucla-mobility/AutoVLA, tools/action_token/action_token_cluster.py) confirms Kdisk_cluster with default tol_dist 0.05 and num_cluster 2048. The Paper-Notes summaries independently quote ADE 0.018 m, MC 99.42%, RT-1 0.101 and FAST 0.028.

Corrections to the first pass:
- The table is Table 4 in the main paper (p.10 of the PDF version used by jev-drive), not a supplementary table.
- Everything else in the first pass's qualitative summary was accurate.

Minor nuance on SOURCE B's wording: "RT-1 uniform binning compounds integration error" paraphrases the authors. Their stated cause is having to infer controls (acceleration and steering rate) from trajectory data and then roll them out with a kinematic model. Cite it as "controls must be inferred from trajectories and rolled out kinematically."

Caveats for the project:
- Evidence is strong secondary evidence: an author-written rebuttal via a scrape, plus two independent transcriptions of Table 4. I could not open the PDF directly (arXiv, OpenReview and HF are blocked).
- These are token-reconstruction errors, not driving metrics.
- Paper Table 6 (NAVSIM) gives FAST DCT vs K-disk PDMS 67.63 vs 80.54, No at-fault Collision 92.74 vs 96.89, and Progress 64.09 vs 75.82. The rebuttal gave FAST PDMS 65.04, so quote the camera-ready values.
- The released cluster script points at ./dataset/nuplan, while the paper describes codebooks from Waymo and CARLA-Garage data.

Project relevance: this is only background for action representation (why AutoVLA uses 2048 K-disk trajectory tokens, 10 tokens per 5 s). It could motivate failure axes tied to tokenization, such as codebook coverage gaps: at K=2048 about 0.58% of movements are not covered. It is not a baseline.

claim: SFT loss: L_LM + lambda_a * L_action, per-sample weight w_i = lambda_cot if CoT present else 1; lambda_a = 1, lambda_cot = 40.
correct_value: Paper form (snippet): L_SFT,i = w_i * (L_LM,i + lambda_a * L_action,i), with w_i = lambda_cot when the ground truth contains CoT, else 1. lambda_cot = 40 is hard-coded in the released code, and the action-loss weight is effectively 1. Implementation nuance: for CoT samples the code computes loss = 40 * L_LM + L_action, so the x40 does not multiply the extra action term. For non-CoT samples it uses only the standard LM cross-entropy, with no extra action term.
details: SFTAutoVLA.training_step: loss = output.loss (token-level CE over the response, including action tokens). action_loss = mean CE over positions with label >= action_start_id. Then 'if hascot[0] == True: loss = loss * 40; loss = loss + action_loss'. The paper says the weighting counters the imbalance between CoT and action-only data. The SFT config uses lr 2e-5, 5 epochs, accumulate_grad_batches 4, lr_warmup_step 500, and a frozen vision backbone. Issue #48 reports the paper states 1e-5.
project_relevance: Relevant if the project retrains or repairs the policy (Stage 4 LoRA fine-tuning). Reuse the same loss so CoT and action-only examples keep their balance. The heavy CoT weight means the language head is strongly shaped by teacher CoT, which is useful context for CoT-probing.
discrepancies: Minor: the released code applies x40 only to L_LM and adds L_action unweighted, and only for CoT samples. SOURCE B's formula describes the paper's idealized version.

claim: RFT via GRPO: clipped ratio objective with KL to SFT reference; epsilon = 0.2, beta = 0.04; advantage A_i = (r_i - mean)/std over group G; group size G = 6 (Phase 4).
correct_value: beta (KL coefficient) = 0.04: confirmed (rl.kl_beta: 0.04; k3 estimator exp(ref-logp) - (ref-logp) - 1). Advantage = (r - mean(group)) / (std(group) + 1e-4): confirmed. epsilon = 0.2: not in the released code. The loss is exp(logp - logp.detach()) * A, a single on-policy update, so the ratio is 1 and clipping has no effect; the paper's stated epsilon is unverifiable. G = 6: unverifiable. In released code the 'group' is one sampled completion per GPU for the same scenario (GroupSampler returns identical indices on every rank, generation is seeded by device index, rewards are all_gathered), so G = number of GPUs; the released nuPlan config uses devices [0,1], i.e. G = 2. The project page states only that larger groups gave better exploration and performance.
details: RFT config: LoRA r=8, lr 3e-5, 1 epoch, sampling temperature 0.9, max_length 2048, rewards scaled by 10 before normalization (the scale cancels in the normalized advantage). The reference model is the SFT checkpoint. Snippets confirm the paper includes training-reward curves for different GRPO group sizes, but the G values used were not visible.
project_relevance: If the project re-runs RFT (for example to restore slow thinking, or as a repair baseline), note that group size is tied to GPU count in this code. To get G > #GPUs you would need to modify generate_sample (num_return_sequences). Do not cite epsilon = 0.2 or G = 6 without checking the PDF.
discrepancies: epsilon = 0.2 is not present in the released implementation (no clipping); the paper value is unverified.
G = 6 is unverified; the released code uses G = number of GPUs (default 2).

second_pass.correct_value: AutoVLA (arXiv:2506.13757, NeurIPS 2025) RFT is GRPO against the SFT checkpoint as the reference policy. Paper values, from the arXiv v1 text: beta (KL weight) = 0.04; advantage A_i = (r_i - mean({r_j}_{j=1..G})) / std({r_j}); RFT learning rate 3e-5; 6,000 steps with the best checkpoint selected; LoRA rank = alpha = 8, dropout 0.1; GRPO sampling at temperature 1.0, top-p 1.0, top-k 0; reward r = r_Driving - 0.3 * r_CoT. Epsilon appears only as a symbol in the general GRPO equation and is never given a number. The paper also says: "We perform a single policy update at each step, allowing the use of a simplified objective without the need for clipping or tracking the old policy." So there is no epsilon = 0.2, and clipping is not used in practice. Group size: Fig. 5(b) compares GRPO group sizes 2, 4 and 8 over 6k steps, and 8 gives the highest training reward. G = 6 was never tested, and the text does not state which G the final model used. Released code (ucla-mobility/AutoVLA) has kl_beta 0.04, no clipping, and loss exp(logp - logp.detach()) * A with a k3 KL term. Its advantage is (r - mean)/(std + 1e-4) over rewards all_gathered across GPUs, so G = number of GPUs x batch size. The shipped nuPlan config uses devices [0,1] and batch_size 1, so G = 2. That config also uses temperature 0.9 and 1 epoch, where the paper says 1.0 and 6k steps.
second_pass.reasoning:
The first pass left epsilon and G as 'unverifiable'. I found two new sources that settle them: a full-text markdown copy of the paper (arXiv v1 HTML, in atanas1054/llm_wiki_knowledgebase) and the first-party project-page figure rl_vis.png, which is the paper's Figure 5. The verdict stays partially_confirmed, and both questions now have evidence.

CONFIRMED: (a) GRPO with KL to the SFT reference. The paper says "The KL regularization weight beta is set to 0.04", the reference policy is the SFT model, and config rl.kl_beta is 0.04. (b) The advantage formula matches the paper's equation. The code adds +1e-4 to the std.

NOT SUPPORTED / CONTRADICTED: (c) epsilon = 0.2. The paper only says "epsilon and beta are hyperparameters controlling the clipping range and the weight of the KL divergence term". No number is given anywhere, including Appendix D (D.1 KL, D.2 reward, D.3 implementation). The paper also states it does a single policy update per step, "without the need for clipping or tracking the old policy". The code matches this: the ratio is exactly 1 and there is no clip. 0.2 looks like a filled-in default: the usual PPO/GRPO convention, and the default in TRL's GRPOTrainer, which also used beta 0.04. The paper does write out the clipped formula as the general GRPO objective, so the "clipped ratio objective" wording is only nominally true. (d) G = 6. Reading Fig. 5(b) directly, the legend is "GRPO group size 2 / 4 / 8". Its caption, "Training reward curves for different GRPO group sample sizes", appears verbatim in the paper text. G = 8 reaches about 0.90 training reward, against about 0.85 for 2 and 4. G = 6 is not a value in the paper. The final model's G is not stated in the text. G = 8 is plausible, since the best curve runs the full 6k steps and SFT used 8 L40S GPUs, but that is my inference, not a stated fact.

The first pass's code analysis holds up on re-derivation. The GroupSampler gives every rank the same indices, generation is seeded with torch.manual_seed(device index), rewards are all_gathered, so the group is one sample per GPU. The config's devices [0,1] therefore give G = 2. The first-pass details (LoRA r=8, lr 3e-5, temperature 0.9, max_length 2048, reward scale 10) match the config. The config's temperature 0.9 and 1 epoch differ from the paper's 1.0 and 6,000 steps.

Side finding, outside this claim but relevant to Source B: Fig. 5(a) shows RFT cutting runtime from 3.95 s to 1.31 s (-66.8%) and raising PDMS from 80.54 to 89.11. Source B's "latency 10.518 s -> 3.49 s" is not what the figure shows.

PROJECT RELEVANCE: cite beta = 0.04, lr 3e-5, 6k steps, LoRA 8/8/0.1, and the group-size ablation {2, 4, 8} with larger groups better. Do not cite epsilon = 0.2 or G = 6, and describe the objective as unclipped single-update GRPO. If the project re-runs RFT, G equals the GPU count in the released code. G = 8 needs 8 GPUs, or a change to generate_sample to use num_return_sequences. The per-device fixed seed means sample diversity comes only from the device index, not from the step.

Caveat: the paper text came from a third-party conversion of arXiv v1. The NeurIPS camera-ready could add a G value, but the first-party figure confirms the tested set {2, 4, 8}.

claim: Reward r = r_Driving - lambda_r * r_CoT with lambda_r = 0.3; CoT length penalty r_CoT = 1/(1+exp(-(L - L_tol) gamma)), gamma = 2e-3, L_tol = 400.
correct_value: Confirmed in the released GRPO config and code: cot_penalty.weight = 0.3 (lambda_r), center = 400.0 (L_tol), coef = 0.002 (gamma). The penalty is sigmoid((L - 400) * 0.002). Implementation details: (1) the penalty applies only when the completion contains 'complex scenario' (slow-thinking outputs); fast outputs get 0. (2) In code L = len(text) of the decoded completion string, i.e. characters, not tokens (the paper may state tokens; unverified). (3) r_Driving on nuPlan is the NAVSIM PDM score (train_critic.rl_pdm_score).
details: reward_function computes the PDMS of the decoded trajectory, then subtracts 0.3 * sigmoid((len(text) - 400) * 0.002) for 'complex scenario' completions. The reward is multiplied by rl.reward.scale = 10, and a 100-step sliding-window reward buffer is kept for logging. The project page and snippets confirm the design goal: discourage unnecessary long reasoning in straightforward scenarios.
project_relevance: This length penalty pushes the policy toward fast mode, which may explain issue #54 (the checkpoint never reasons). For CoT-based failure probing, expect sparse CoT unless it is forced. The 'complex scenario' self-label is a cheap, model-internal difficulty signal to compare with discovered failure axes.
discrepancies: Nuance: the penalty is applied only to slow-thinking outputs, and in code L is measured in characters.

claim: Waymo reward: r_Driving = (delta - ADE)/kappa with delta = 2, kappa = 10.
correct_value: Paper snippets confirm that RFT on the Waymo E2E data uses an ADE-based reward and gives the best overall RFS. The functional form (delta - ADE)/kappa and the constants delta = 2 m, kappa = 10 could NOT be verified: the arXiv text is blocked and no Waymo RFT config or ADE reward code is in the released repo (issue #47 requesting WOD-E2E configs has no answer).
details: The released code implements only the nuPlan PDMS reward (models/utils/score.py wraps NAVSIM PDMScorer). A search snippet mentioned δ=2 with κ=1 in some WOD-E2E reward context, from an unclear source, so the constants are genuinely uncertain.
project_relevance: Low relevance unless the project uses Waymo E2E. If an ADE reward is needed for CARLA repair RFT, define it independently and do not attribute constants to AutoVLA without checking the PDF.
discrepancies: delta = 2 and kappa = 10 unverified; the form of the ADE reward is unverified.

second_pass.correct_value: Confirmed as stated. AutoVLA (arXiv:2506.13757; v1 HTML, Appendix D.2 "Reward Function") says: "For the Waymo dataset, we define the driving reward r_Driving based on the ADE metric: r_Driving = (δ − ADE)/κ, ADE = (1/T) Σ_{t=1..T} ||ŷ_t − y_t||_2, where δ denotes the maximum displacement error, and κ is a scaling factor to normalize the reward." Appendix D.3 "Implementation Details" says: "We also set δ=2, κ=10 in the RFT of the Waymo dataset." (δ is in meters.) The full reward is r = r_Driving − λ_r·r_CoT with λ_r = 0.3. The main text gives the reason for using ADE: "due to the limited availability of Rater Feedback Score (RFS) annotations". RFT on Waymo uses the WOD-E2E validation split.
second_pass.reasoning:
I overturned the first-pass verdict of partially_confirmed. The first pass could not see the paper text. I found a verbatim markdown copy of the AutoVLA paper, a clipping of https://arxiv.org/html/2506.13757v1 dated 2026-04-05, in a third-party GitHub knowledge-base repo (atanas1054/llm_wiki_knowledgebase, raw/papers/AutoVLA_...md). I got its exact text in two independent ways: GitHub code search, whose text_matches return the literal file content, and a raw.githubusercontent fetch.

What the verbatim text shows:
(1) The equation "r_{\text{Driving}}=\frac{\delta-ADE}{\kappa}, \text{ADE}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|\hat{y}_t-y_t\|_2", introduced by "For the Waymo dataset, we define the driving reward r_Driving based on the ADE metric".
(2) "where δ denotes the maximum displacement error, and κ is a scaling factor to normalize the reward".
(3) In D.3 Implementation Details: "To ensure that the driving reward signal is dominant, the regularization weight is set to a relatively small value, λ_r=0.3. We also set δ=2, κ=10 in the RFT of the Waymo dataset."
So the functional form and both constants in the claim match exactly.

Other facts from the same passage:
- RFT uses the WOD-E2E validation split.
- The vision encoder is frozen and training uses LoRA (rank = alpha = 8, dropout 0.1).
- γ = 2e-3, L_tol = 400, lr = 3e-5.
- Sampling uses temperature 1.0 and top-p 1.0.

What these values imply: the reward is 0.2 at ADE = 0 and 0 at ADE = 2 m, and it goes negative above 2 m. Because GRPO standardizes rewards within each group, δ only shifts the reward and does not change the gradient. The ratio 1/κ against λ_r sets how much the driving term weighs relative to the CoT penalty.

Caveats:
(a) The text I saw is arXiv v1, reached through a third-party clipping. I could not fetch arxiv.org or openreview directly (egress blocked), so I could not confirm the v2 or NeurIPS camera-ready wording. The first pass cited v2.
(b) The official repo, ucla-mobility/AutoVLA, still ships no Waymo ADE-reward code. Code search found only models/utils/score.py, which wraps the NAVSIM PDMScorer. So the constants come from the paper alone.
(c) A student reimplementation (s1111e/CS-6263-FinalProject, slurm/README.md) writes the reward in a different form, δ − ADE/κ with κ = 10. That is a misreading and should not be cited. It may explain the conflicting snippet the first pass saw.

Independent corroboration:
- Paper notes on WOD-E2E (zhaoyang97/Paper-Notes-en) state that AutoVLA used ADE rather than RFS as its GRPO reward, while Poutine used RFS and reached a higher RFS (7.986 vs 7.556).
- Qwen-Drive-1.0 uses the same affine displacement term, (δ − ADE)/κ.

Project relevance: this fact matters only if the project runs RFT on Waymo E2E, or borrows an ADE reward for CARLA repair RFT. It can be cited as "AutoVLA, Appx. D, Eq. r_Driving=(δ−ADE)/κ, δ=2, κ=10". The WOD-E2E paper's own analysis is a caveat worth noting: an ADE reward is misaligned with the RFS target metric.

claim: nuPlan reward: PDMS = NC x DAC x ((5 TTC + 2 C + 5 EP)/12).
correct_value: This is the standard NAVSIM v1 PDMS: PDMS = NC * DAC * (5*TTC + 5*EP + 2*C)/12. NC is in {0, 1/2, 1} and DAC in {0, 1} (multipliers); TTC in {0, 1}, EP in [0, 1] and C in {0, 1} are weighted 5/5/2. AutoVLA uses the NAVSIM PDM scorer as its nuPlan RFT reward and evaluation metric (navtest).
details: NAVSIM v1.1 docs give 'PDMS = NC * DAC * (5*TTC + 5*EP + 2*C + 0*DDC) / 12'. NAVSIM v2 replaces it with EPDMS (adds DDC, TLC, LK, HC, EC), so make sure comparisons use the same version. Issue #48 lists the paper's sub-scores for the 89.11 model: NC 98.4, DAC 95.6, EP 81.9, TTC 98.0, C 99.9.
project_relevance: PDMS sub-metrics (NC/DAC/TTC/EP/C) give ready-made behavioral stratification labels for the NAVSIM-side baseline. For CARLA closed-loop, use Bench2Drive DS/SR instead; PDMS is open-loop / non-reactive.

claim: Phase 3 SFT from Qwen2.5-VL-3B with FSDP, BF16; Phase 4 RFT: freeze vision encoder, LoRA r=8, alpha=8, dropout 0.1.
correct_value: RFT: LoRA r=8, alpha=8, dropout=0.1, bias none, targets q_proj/k_proj/v_proj/o_proj, train_vision_backbone false; lr 3e-5, 1 epoch. SFT: also train_vision_backbone false (the vision encoder is frozen in SFT too). SFT is full fine-tuning of the language model (train_lm_backbone true, no LoRA). Both stages use Lightning FSDPStrategy (FULL_SHARD) with bf16 MixedPrecision (param, reduce and buffer dtypes) and value gradient clipping at 1.0. Paper: 8x NVIDIA L40S, 5 SFT epochs, per-GPU batch 1, grad-accum 4 (effective batch 32).
details: Verified in configs and in run_sft.py / run_rft.py. The model code sets requires_grad=False on autovla.vlm.visual parameters when train_vision_backbone is false. Issue #41 notes the paper figure does not show the frozen encoder. The NAVSIM agent config also carries the LoRA settings (r=8, dropout 0.1) for loading LoRA checkpoints.
project_relevance: For Stage 4 repair fine-tuning, reuse this recipe: LoRA on attention projections with a frozen ViT. It matches the checkpoint lineage and keeps vision features fixed, so activation-space failure axes found in the ViT/merger stay stable across repair iterations. Full-LM SFT needs FSDP on several 48 GB GPUs; LoRA RFT runs on 2 GPUs by default.
discrepancies: The vision encoder is frozen in SFT as well, not only in RFT.
SFT uses full LM fine-tuning (no LoRA); LoRA is used only in RFT.

claim: 4-step CoT (scene description, critical objects, intention reasoning, meta-action decision); CoT distillation with a Qwen2.5-VL-72B teacher given GT meta-actions/trajectories as hints; 'manual quality checks across 3,000 randomly sampled distilled CoT instances confirmed an 88.8% annotation accuracy rate'.
correct_value: Teacher: Qwen2.5-VL-72B (the released annotation config uses Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct-AWQ), prompted with the ground-truth best driving action as a hint ('the ground truth of the best driving action is {fut_ego_action}'). Four reasoning steps: (1) scene description/analysis, (2) critical object identification/description, (3) intention reasoning of surrounding objects, (4) decision/meta-action (one lateral plus one longitudinal action). Human annotators checked 3,000 randomly selected samples and found 88.8% overall accuracy. A secondary snippet reports about 45.6k nuPlan and 7.2k Waymo CoT annotations.
details: cot_prompts.py contains the 4-step teacher prompt with the GT-action hint. The student's inference system prompt splits this into 5 numbered steps (Scene Analysis, Identification of Critical Objects, Prediction of Critical Object Behavior, Ego Vehicle Intent Reasoning, Final Action Decision), with 5 lateral and 7 longitudinal meta-action options. Issue #44 (a user report, not confirmed by maintainers) says the teacher saw 4 cameras including the back view while the student sees 3, which could create 'phantom' CoT references. The CoT dataset is not released. SOURCE B's qualitative failure cases (stop-sign handling, construction detours, lane-level traffic-light misreading) could not be checked.
project_relevance: Because the CoT is distilled with GT-action hints, it tends to be post-hoc rationalization. For the project's CoT-probing and VLM-describability gate, treat CoT as possibly unfaithful: compare CoT claims against activations, and check whether CoT mentions objects outside the 3-camera view (the #44 mismatch). The 88.8% figure measures annotation quality, not student reasoning faithfulness.
discrepancies: Minor: the student's system prompt uses 5 numbered steps (critical-object behavior prediction is a separate step); the 4-step structure is the teacher annotation format.

claim: Fast thinking latency Min 0.997 s | Max 1.116 s | Avg 1.072 s; Slow thinking Min 7.607 s | Max 13.706 s | Avg 10.518 s.
correct_value: The paper has a table titled 'Runtime Analysis of Fast & Slow Thinking Modes', and says slow thinking incurs significantly higher runtime because of CoT generation. One secondary search result (source unclear) cites AutoVLA latencies of about 1,072 ms fast and about 10,518 ms slow, matching SOURCE B's averages. The min/max values (0.997/1.116 and 7.607/13.706 s), the GPU and the batch setting could not be verified.
details: I could not open the arXiv/NeurIPS text. Evidence is limited to snippets confirming the table exists and one secondary mention of the averages. SOURCE B does not state the hardware. The numbers imply roughly 1 Hz decision rate in fast mode and about 0.1 Hz in slow mode, well below the 2 Hz input rate. This fits autoregressive decoding of ~800 visual tokens plus long CoT with a 3B model.
project_relevance: Key for rollout budgeting. Closed-loop CARLA must run in synchronous mode (the simulator waits for the model). Thousands of seeds in slow mode are expensive: about 10 s per step, e.g. a 30-60 s route at 2 Hz is 60-120 steps, i.e. 10-20 min per route. Plan most rollouts in fast mode and measure latency on the team's own GPUs rather than relying on these numbers.
discrepancies: Min/max latencies and measurement hardware are unverified; the averages are only secondarily supported.

second_pass.correct_value: AutoVLA (Zhou et al., arXiv 2506.13757, NeurIPS 2025), Table 2, "Runtime Analysis of Fast & Slow Thinking Modes". Fast thinking: min 0.997 s, max 1.116 s, avg 1.072 s. Slow thinking: min 7.607 s, max 13.706 s, avg 10.518 s. That makes slow mode about 9.8x slower on average. All six numbers in the claim match exactly. The measurement GPU is not confirmed. One secondary source says Table 2 does not name an inference device. A student reproduction repo says the paper used an A100, but that is unverified.
second_pass.reasoning:
I am upgrading the first-pass verdict from partially_confirmed to confirmed. The first pass could not support the min/max values. I found them in two independent secondary sources that both attribute the numbers to AutoVLA's Table 2, and both match SOURCE B's line 12-13 exactly.

Evidence:
(1) The GitHub repo s1111e/CS-6263-FinalProject tries to reproduce AutoVLA. Its files are evaluation_results/paper_tables_nuscenes.md, results.md, print_results.py, reproduce_paper_tables_nuscenes.py and README.md. They list "Paper Table 2" as Fast 0.997/1.116/1.072 s and Slow 7.607/13.706/10.518 s (min/max/avg), with a slow/fast ratio of 9.8. Their own V100 run with max_new_tokens=64 got very different numbers: fast avg 4.618 s, slow avg 2.929 s. So the paper's numbers depend on hardware and on how long the CoT is.
(2) The GitHub repo VennIntelligence/jev-drive, file research/survey-thin-head.md, lists AutoVLA [13] (arXiv 2506.13757) with "verifiable latency" of fast 1.072 s and slow 10.518 s. It also notes that "Table 2 is not bound to an inference device" (Table 2 未绑定推理设备).
(3) The first pass already confirmed that the paper has a table titled "Runtime Analysis of Fast & Slow Thinking Modes" and found a snippet with ~1,072 ms and ~10,518 ms.
The official README of ucla-mobility/AutoVLA confirms the paper's title and authors (Zewei Zhou, Tianhui Cai, Seth Z. Zhao, Yun Zhang, Zhiyu Huang, Bolei Zhou, Jiaqi Ma; UCLA), that it appeared at NeurIPS 2025, that the backbone is Qwen2.5-VL-3B, and that it has fast (trajectory-only) and slow (CoT) modes. The README gives no runtime numbers.

Limits: I could not read the primary PDF or HTML. arxiv, papers.nips.cc, huggingface, openreview, semanticscholar and neurips.cc were all blocked by the egress proxy, and the web-search budget was used up. Exact six-number matches across independent sources make fabrication very unlikely. The claim does not state hardware or batch settings, and they stay unverified; the two secondary sources disagree on whether the paper names a GPU.

What AutoVLA does: it is a VLA built on Qwen2.5-VL-3B that turns trajectories into discrete physical action tokens (5 s horizon encoded as 10 tokens). It is trained with SFT on both action-only and CoT data, then with GRPO reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT), including a length penalty so it learns when to skip CoT. It was evaluated on nuPlan/NAVSIM, nuScenes, Waymo E2E and CARLA/Bench2Drive. Per SOURCE B and secondary sources, RFT raises NAVSIM PDMS from 80.54 to 89.11.

How the project should use it: cite these as per-sample inference times reported in AutoVLA Table 2, with an unspecified or unconfirmed GPU. Do not treat them as closed-loop step latency on the team's hardware. Implications for rollout budgets:
- Fast mode is about 1 s per decision and slow mode about 10.5 s, both slower than real time at a 2 Hz control rate.
- CARLA must run in synchronous mode.
- Plan most seed sweeps in fast mode or RFT-adaptive mode.
- The reproduction shows timings change a lot with GPU type (V100 vs the likely A100) and the max_new_tokens cap, so measure latency on the team's own GPUs.

claim: Text waypoints vs action tokens (nuPlan): Text: PDMS 71.31, L2 0.89 m, collision 0.36%, runtime 7.65 s; Action tokens: PDMS 80.54, L2 0.70 m, collision 0.31%, runtime 3.95 s; 'reducing runtime latency by 48.4%'.

FIRST-PASS RED FLAGS

WHAT THE WORK ACTUALLY DOES
AutoVLA (Zhou, Cai, Zhao, Zhang, Huang, Zhou, Ma; UCLA; NeurIPS 2025) is a Qwen2.5-VL-based driving VLA. It discretizes trajectories into 2048 physical action tokens, clustered with K-disk from WOMD, with a separate codebook for CARLA. It generates reasoning and action tokens in one autoregressive sequence. SFT trains both fast (action-only) and slow (chain-of-thought) modes. RFT with GRPO adds a penalty on chain-of-thought length, which raises NAVSIM PDMS from 80.54 to 89.11 and cuts runtime by 66.8%. The ablation shows that outputting waypoints as text is worse and slower than action tokens, and the authors attribute this to LLMs' weakness at precise numerical decoding. The size of the gap depends on how well the text baseline is tuned: v1 showed a gap of 21 PDMS, the revised version 9.2 PDMS. A user report and the S4Driver work suggest text waypoints can be competitive.

- Cite it as motivation for studying a token-action VLA: action tokens were better and roughly 2x faster in AutoVLA's own ablation.
- Cite the revised version (Table 5) and give both versions' numbers or none.
- Label the 48.4% as a derived figure, not a quote.
- Do not present this as settled evidence that text waypoints are inferior, since the baseline was re-tuned between versions and a user disputed the result.
- Do not compare the 3.95 s runtime with other AutoVLA latency figures.
- Limitation: I could not open the primary PDF or v2 HTML (arXiv and HF are blocked). The v2 numbers rest on four consistent secondary sources, one of which cites the PDF table and page.

Abilities (scenario counts): Merging 16, Overtaking 9, Emergency Brake 12, Give Way 2, Traffic Sign 18; a scenario can count toward more than one ability. DS = (1/n_total) * sum_i RouteCompletion_i * prod_j p_i,j. Efficiency = mean of Speed Percentage = ego speed / average speed of nearby vehicles, checked every 5% of the route (20 checkpoints instead of 4); values above 1000% are dropped; the speed check is excluded from DS. Comfort thresholds follow nuPlan: lon accel [-4.05, 2.40] m/s^2, |lat accel| 4.89 m/s^2, |yaw rate| 0.95 rad/s, |yaw accel| 1.93 rad/s^2, |lon jerk| 4.13 m/s^3, |jerk magnitude| 8.37 m/s^3; trajectory split into 20-frame segments; score = smooth segments / total segments.
details: Bench2Drive is a closed-loop CARLA benchmark for end-to-end driving that isolates driving abilities. Instead of long Leaderboard-2.0 routes (7-10 km, scenarios packed densely, harsh multiplicative infraction penalties), it runs 220 short (~150 m) routes, each with one of 44 interactive scenarios (cut-ins, overtaking, detours, and so on), spread over towns and weathers. Training data were collected by the world-model RL expert Think2Drive, with full annotations (3D boxes, depth, segmentation, HD map, expert features). Metrics are Driving Score, Success Rate (route completed with no infraction and in time), Efficiency and Comfortness (nuPlan-style smoothness), plus per-ability success for Merging, Overtaking, Emergency Brake, Give Way and Traffic Sign. The paper benchmarks AD-MLP, UniAD, VAD, TCP variants, ThinkTwice and DriveAdapter trained on the base set. Versions: v0.0.2 removed the minimum-speed penalty and extended ticks from 2000 to 4000 (the v0.0.1 results are deprecated); v0.0.3 fixed ability-calculation typos and is the version most 2025 papers report. v0.0.4 (2026-08-06) added a strictly uniform 1,100-route training set, a 3D-occupancy modality and a separate 220-route validation set, and re-evaluated the baselines.
project_relevance: Bench2Drive is the obvious closed-loop testbed for failure-axis discovery. The 44 scenario types and 5 abilities give a ready-made supervised taxonomy to compare unsupervised clusters against, and the per-route infraction logs give failure labels. Caveats: (1) always state which version you use (v0.0.3 vs v0.0.4), because numbers are not comparable across versions; (2) models trained on PDM-Lite data (SimLingo, TF++) and on Think2Drive data (UniAD, VAD, ORION, AutoVLA) differ in expert distribution; (3) Bench2Drive DS is not comparable to official CARLA LB2.0 DS; (4) the 5-ability grouping overlaps across scenarios. Cite the NeurIPS D&B version (references.bib entry jia2024bench2drive is correct).
discrepancies: Clip count: 13,638 (arXiv v1 abstract; README counts Full + supplementary) versus 10,000 short clips (NeurIPS proceedings abstract; README 'Full' split). Either can be cited but should be qualified.
The CARLA version is 0.9.15 (called 'CARLA v2'); Source B names no numbered version.

Comfort thresholds are borrowed from nuPlan's comfort protocol. Lateral acceleration, yaw rate, yaw acceleration, longitudinal jerk and jerk magnitude are bounds on absolute values; Source B's symmetric-interval notation is equivalent.
Bench2Drive's text says the CARLA Leaderboard v2 has 39 new scenarios. Source B does not give a count, but some secondary sources say 38.

WHAT THE WORK DOES. AutoVLA (NeurIPS 2025, UCLA) is a Qwen2.5-VL-3B VLA. It discretizes 5 s trajectories into 10 physical action tokens drawn from a K-disk codebook of size 2048. correct_value: SimLingo: Vision-Only Closed-Loop Autonomous Driving with Language-Action Alignment. Katrin Renz, Long Chen, Elahe Arani, Oleg Sinavski (Wayve; Renz interning from Univ. Tübingen). CVPR 2025 (highlight). arXiv:2503.09594; preliminary CARLA Challenge report arXiv:2406.10165 (CarLLaVA). Code: github.com/RenzKa/simlingo (Apache-2.0). Checkpoint: huggingface.co/RenzKa/simlingo (released 2025-06-25). Dataset: huggingface.co/datasets/RenzKa/simlingo (released 2025-05-26, Wayve non-commercial licence). CARLA 0.9.15.
details: SimLingo is a camera-only VLA built on InternVL2-1B: an InternViT-300M-448px vision encoder plus a Qwen2-0.5B-Instruct LLM, about 1B parameters in total. The front camera image is split into 448px tiles and pixel-unshuffled. Speed and navigation (GPS target points or a language command) go in through the prompt. Learnable path and speed query tokens feed MLPs that output disentangled geometric-path waypoints and temporal speed waypoints; PID controllers turn these into steering, throttle and brake. The model also produces commentary (chain-of-thought), DriveLM-style VQA answers and 'Action Dreaming' instruction following. Training data is 3.1M samples at 4 fps from the PDM-Lite expert in CARLA 0.9.15 (Leaderboard 2.0 Town12/13 routes split into single-scenario segments, plus Town01-10 routes, with random weather). Training samples from buckets, 650k samples per epoch. Per the paper, training is 14 epochs on 8xA100-80GB at global batch 96, about 24 h, with DeepSpeed; the vision encoder is fully fine-tuned and the LLM uses LoRA (r=32, alpha=64, dropout 0.1). Bench2Drive results: DS 85.07±0.95 and SR 67.27±2.11 over 3 seeds. SimLingo-BASE (CarLLaVA) scored DS 6.87 / RC 18.08 / IS 0.42 on the official Leaderboard 2.0 sensor track. Language results: DriveLM-VQA GPT score 58.48 and Commentary GPT score 78.94.
project_relevance: Recommended primary policy. It is the only candidate that releases all of the following together: weights, the full training dataset with language labels, Hydra training configs (e.g. simlingo_seed1.yaml: InternVL2-1B, LoRA r32/α64, use_town13: True, gpus: 8), SLURM train and eval launchers, Bench2Drive closed-loop agent code, and PDM-Lite data-collection scripts for generating repair data. Its small size makes activation hooking cheap. Caveats: (1) The dataset licence (LICENCE_Dataset, Wayve) is non-commercial and forbids operational or vehicle use. Models trained on it may be distributed only on an academic basis and free of charge, so check this against the 99P Labs/Honda sponsorship. (2) Community reproductions vary. Issue #43 reports DS 75.50 / SR 67.12 with the released code versus the paper's 85.94 for SimLingo-BASE; issue #72 relays a maintainer figure of about 87.5 when Town13 is included in training. Re-baseline locally before planting gaps. (3) The released checkpoint has already seen every slice, so a planted gap needs retraining from InternVL2-1B on filtered data; LoRA fine-tuning the release cannot create one. (4) Contact: Katrin Renz, who is also a co-author of Fail2Drive.
