**Project use.** Use Drive-π0 or DriveMoE, SimLingo, or Qwen2.5-VL via Bench2Drive-VL (non-commercial, no training pipeline) as closed-loop CARLA policies. Treat OpenVLA and π0 only as methodological references for layer-sweep probing, e.g. Buurmeijer et al. Do not plan to LoRA-tune OpenVLA or DriveVLM for driving: that means building a new action head and a CARLA agent, which is a separate project.

**Confidence.** Medium, because Hugging Face model search and general web search were unavailable. A small unreported OpenVLA driving fine-tune could exist on HF, but no maintained, CARLA-integrated one showed up anywhere I could reach.

claim: Candidate (f)/(d): a π0-based open driving VLA with CARLA closed-loop support and released training code (Drive-π0 / DriveMoE).
correct_value: DriveMoE: Mixture-of-Experts for Vision-Language-Action Model in End-to-End Autonomous Driving. Zhenjie Yang, Yilin Chai, Xiaosong Jia, Qifeng Li, Yuqian Shao, Xuekai Zhu, Haisheng Su, Junchi Yan (SJTU). CVPR 2026, pp. 10678-10688. arXiv:2505.16278. Code: github.com/Thinklab-SJTU/DriveMoE (no licence file). Model and data: huggingface.co/rethinklab/DriveMoE. CARLA 0.9.15 + Bench2Drive.
details: Drive-π0 adapts the π0 recipe (built on open-pi-zero/openpi) to driving: a PaliGemma-3B VLM plus a flow-matching action expert (hidden size 1024). It takes a 10-dimensional ego-state input, predicts a 10-step horizon with 2-D actions, and uses 10 denoising steps at inference. DriveMoE adds a scene-specialised vision MoE (camera-view selection) and a skill-specialised action MoE. The released closed-loop Drive-π0 config does full fine-tuning (no LoRA): bf16/AMP, 12 epochs, global batch 1024 (8 per device), lr 5e-5, on Bench2Drive data. Released evaluation on Bench2Drive (run on 8xH200) gives DS/SR: DrivePi0-Base-bf16 55.85/30.00, DrivePi0-Base-fp32 65.85/42.27, DrivePi0-Full-fp32 67.41/44.09, DriveMoE-Base-bf16 74.22/48.64. Training compute is not stated in the docs I could reach.
project_relevance: Recommended secondary policy. Its training data is the open Bench2Drive dataset, organised as scenario_name/Town_weather_route, so withholding slices is a folder filter. It is a π0-family VLA, which ties to the OpenVLA/π0 interpretability literature, and it has a ready CARLA closed-loop agent. Caveats: full fine-tuning a ~3B flow-matching model at global batch 1024 needs A100-80GB/H100-class GPUs (openpi puts full fine-tuning above 70 GB per GPU), so plan to reuse the released weights for rollouts and do gapped retraining only on a cluster. fp32 inference noticeably beats bf16 (65.85 vs 55.85 DS), which raises rollout cost. There is no licence file, so ask the authors before redistributing.

claim: Candidate (e): ORION, a driving VLA evaluated on Bench2Drive (Source B lists 'Orion (generative VLM planner) DS 77.74 / SR 54.62').
correct_value: ORION: A Holistic End-to-End Autonomous Driving Framework by Vision-Language Instructed Action Generation. Haoyu Fu, Diankun Zhang, Zongchuang Zhao, Jianfeng Cui, Dingkang Liang, Chong Zhang, Dingyuan Zhang, Hongwei Xie, Bing Wang, Xiang Bai (HUST & Xiaomi EV). ICCV 2025. arXiv:2503.19755. Code: github.com/xiaomi-mlab/Orion (Apache-2.0; inference code April 2025, training code and data August 2025). Weights: HF poleyzdk/Orion (Orion.pth). Chat-B2D data: HF poleyzdk/Chat-B2D. Bench2Drive DS 77.74 / SR 54.62.
details: ORION combines an EVA-02 ViT image encoder (640x640) with a QT-Former (query transformer with history memory) and an LLM (LlavaLlamaForCausalLM with PEFT LoRA r=16, initialised from OmniDrive's pretrain_qformer checkpoint). It also has a generative trajectory planner conditioned on a planning token, so language reasoning and action generation are aligned. Training has three stages, using Chat-B2D VQA data and then Bench2Drive. Every released stage config sets num_gpus = 32, batch_size = 4 and num_epochs = 6 over 234,769 samples. Inference needs an A100-class GPU with more than 32 GB in FP32 or more than 17 GB in FP16. Closed-loop evaluation runs in the Bench2Drive/CARLA toolchain. On Fail2Drive, ORION drops from DS 53.0 in-distribution to 51.2 and SR from 52.0 to 46.0 (−11.5%).
project_relevance: Usable as a rollout-only comparison policy on an A100 (open weights and closed-loop agent), for example to test whether discovered axes transfer across VLAs. Not practical for planted-gap retraining: 7B-class, three stages, configs assuming 32 GPUs. Source B's DS/SR numbers are correct.

claim: Candidate (f): an open E2E driving model with CARLA closed-loop support and released training code/data (LEAD / TransFuser v6).
correct_value: LEAD: Minimizing Learner-Expert Asymmetry in End-to-End Driving. Long Nguyen, Micha Fauth, Bernhard Jaeger, Daniel Dauner, Maximilian Igl, Andreas Geiger, Kashyap Chitta. CVPR 2026. arXiv:2512.20563. Code: github.com/kesai-labs/lead (MIT). Dataset: HF ln2697/lead-123d (~1 TB; 8,930 routes, 43 scenario types, all 12 CARLA towns; organised in scenario-type folders). Checkpoints: HF ln2697/transfuser-carla-123d (v1.5.1, 2026-09-13). CARLA 0.9.16 for data collection; 0.9.15 supported for evaluation.
details: LEAD is imitation-learning infrastructure for CARLA that reduces the asymmetry between the privileged expert and the learner. It includes a faster data generator (about 10 steps/s on a consumer GPU) and TransFuser v6 (TFv6) policies. The docs report TransFuser training on 4xH100-80GB at 23.9–42.0 h total for pre-training plus post-training, depending on settings, with Bench2Drive DS about 93.6–93.8 and Longest6 v2 DS about 52–54. Its self-reported Bench2Drive leaderboard entry is TFv6 DS 95.28 / SR 86.81. Sensors include RGB, depth, semantics, LiDAR and radar. A third-party repo (lloitesa013/bench2drive-failure-taxonomy) reproduces TFv6 at mean DS 93.36 over 202 clean routes on one RTX 5090 and publishes a per-route failure taxonomy.
project_relevance: Strongest non-VLA option for planted gaps. The dataset is permissive (MIT code) and already split by scenario type, and retraining costs about 100–170 H100-hours. Use it as a non-language control policy, to test whether activation-based discovery beats output-only clustering on a non-VLA, if cluster time allows. It is not a VLA, so it cannot be the headline policy for 'Driving VLAs'. The public failure-taxonomy repo is relevant prior art for failure discovery on Bench2Drive.

claim: Candidate (f): TransFuser++ / CARLA Garage as an open E2E model with CARLA closed-loop support and released training code.
correct_value: TransFuser++: Jaeger, Chitta, Geiger, 'Hidden Biases of End-to-End Driving Models', ICCV 2023. Leaderboard-2.0 version: Zimmerlin, Beißwenger, Jaeger, Geiger, Chitta, 'Hidden Biases of End-to-End Driving Datasets', CVPR Workshops 2024. Code: github.com/autonomousvision/carla_garage, branch leaderboard_2 (MIT). CARLA 0.9.15. PDM-Lite dataset about 364 GB (CC BY 4.0). Pretrained models: 3 seeds (CC BY 4.0).
details: TF++ is a camera+LiDAR TransFuser variant trained by imitation of the PDM-Lite expert. The leaderboard_2 branch is a Leaderboard 2.0 starter kit with data collection, training and evaluation. The README reports training at about 3 days per stage on 4xA100-40GB, in two stages. It reports Bench2Drive evaluation of TF++ at about 4 h on 8x2080Ti, which gives a useful throughput reference: roughly 220 routes in about 32 GPU-hours. TF++ has LB2.0 sensor-track DS 5.18 (from the SimLingo paper's Table 1) and Bench2Drive DS 84.21 / SR 67.27 on the Bench2Drive leaderboard.
project_relevance: A permissively licensed non-VLA fallback. For new work it is superseded by LEAD/TFv6 from the same group, which is faster to train and scores higher. Its evaluation-speed figure is a good lower bound for rollout budgeting; VLAs will be slower.

claim: Candidate (f): CarLLaVA as a separate open driving VLA with CARLA closed-loop support and released training code.
correct_value: CarLLaVA is the CARLA Challenge 2024 tech report (arXiv:2406.10165) of the model that the SimLingo paper renames 'SimLingo-BASE'. Its training code is in the SimLingo repo (simlingo_base_training/). No SimLingo-BASE/CarLLaVA checkpoint appears to be public: GitHub issue #92 (Jan 2026) asks for it and has no reply, and issue #84 asks for SimLingo-Base evaluation support.
details: Per the SimLingo appendix, SimLingo-BASE uses the LLaVA-Next CLIP-ViT encoder on two 336x336 front-image patches. Its language model is a 50M-parameter LLaMA-architecture transformer decoder trained from scratch, and it has no language input or output. It is trained for 30 epochs with L2 loss and uses the same disentangled path/speed outputs as SimLingo. It was the 2024 LB2.0 sensor-track entry: DS 6.87, RC 18.08, IS 0.42 (paper Table 1). On Bench2Drive it reaches DS 85.94 / SR 66.82. It is not a VLA in the language sense.
project_relevance: A cheap-to-train ablation twin of SimLingo: same data, heads and code base, with a 50M decoder instead of a 0.5B LoRA LLM. It could be the compute-light planted-gap model if full SimLingo retraining proves too expensive. The trade-off is losing the 'VLA' framing and the language channel, and the team would have to train it itself because no checkpoint is released.
discrepancies: Not a separate project or repository: CarLLaVA = SimLingo-BASE, code inside RenzKa/simlingo.
No public checkpoint found (issue #92 unanswered).

claim: Candidate (f): LMDrive as an open language-driving model with CARLA closed-loop support and released training code.
correct_value: LMDrive: Closed-Loop End-to-End Driving with Large Language Models. Hao Shao, Yuxuan Hu, Letian Wang, Steven L. Waslander, Yu Liu, Hongsheng Li. CVPR 2024. Code: github.com/opendilab/LMDrive (Apache-2.0); data CC BY-NC 4.0 (about 64K clips, 2–20 s each; HF/OpenXLab). CARLA 0.9.10.1. Checkpoints: LLaVA-v1.5-7B, Vicuna-v1.5-7B and LLaMA-7B variants with a ResNet50 vision encoder. Benchmark: LangAuto (long, short and tiny).
details: LMDrive feeds multi-view camera and LiDAR tokens from a pretrained vision encoder, plus natural-language navigation and notice instructions, into a 7B LLM. The LLM predicts waypoints and whether the instruction is complete. Training has two stages: vision-encoder pre-training and instruction fine-tuning, each about 2–3 days on 8xA100-80GB according to the README, so roughly 770–1,150 A100-hours in total. It is evaluated on its own LangAuto benchmark built on CARLA 0.9.10.1 (the Leaderboard 1.0 era).
project_relevance: Not recommended. It is 7B-class, expensive to retrain, and tied to CARLA 0.9.10.1 rather than the 0.9.15 Bench2Drive/Leaderboard-2.0 stack used by SimLingo, Drive-π0, ORION and LEAD, and the data is non-commercial. Cite as related work on instruction-following closed-loop driving.

claim: Candidate (f): DriveTransformer as an open E2E model with CARLA closed-loop (Bench2Drive) support and released training code.
correct_value: DriveTransformer: Unified Transformer for Scalable End-to-End Autonomous Driving. Xiaosong Jia, Junqi You, Zhiyuan Zhang, Junchi Yan (SJTU). ICLR 2025. Code: github.com/Thinklab-SJTU/DriveTransformer (no licence file). DriveTransformer-Large checkpoint via Google Drive/Baidu. Bench2Drive DS 63.46 / SR 35.01; reported latency 211.7 ms.
details: DriveTransformer is a unified transformer that jointly performs perception, prediction and planning with task-parallel attention and sparse queries, trained and evaluated closed-loop on Bench2Drive in CARLA. Training configs and a Large checkpoint are released; training compute is not stated in the README. It is not a language or VLA model.
project_relevance: Low priority. It is a non-VLA baseline with lower closed-loop scores than TFv6 or SimLingo and no licence file. Useful only as another architecture for cross-policy transfer of discovered axes.

claim: Other open driving VLA considered: NVIDIA Alpamayo (open-weight reasoning VLA) as a possible policy.
correct_value: NVIDIA Alpamayo 1 (nvidia/Alpamayo-R1-10B; github.com/NVlabs/alpamayo): 10B Cosmos-Reason backbone plus action expert. Weights under OpenMDW-1.1; inference code Apache-2.0. Needs at least 24 GB VRAM. SFT and RL fine-tuning recipes are in NVlabs/alpamayo-recipes (2026). Training data (Physical AI AV dataset) is gated. No CARLA closed-loop support is documented. Alpamayo 1.5 (10B) and Alpamayo 2 Super (34B) also exist.
details: Alpamayo pairs driving trajectory prediction with 'Chain-of-Causation' reasoning. The README describes it as not a fully fledged driving stack and lacking automotive-grade validation. It targets real-world multi-camera data, not CARLA.
project_relevance: Not suitable for the planted-gap design. Its training data is gated, it has no CARLA integration, and 10B is too heavy to retrain. Its permissive weight licence makes it a candidate for later open-loop activation-probing on real data if the sponsor wants a real-world angle.

claim: Source A: rollouts 'in CARLA or Drake'; 'Drake / CARLA physics & safety parameter bounds' — i.e., Drake (TRI's robotics toolbox) is a reasonable simulator for camera-based driving VLA rollouts.
correct_value: Drake (RobotLocomotion/drake; describes itself as 'Model-Based Design and Verification for Robotics') is a multibody-dynamics, optimisation and systems toolbox. It has generic camera rendering (systems/sensors/RgbdSensor; VTK, GL and glTF-client render engines), but its former drake/automotive driving code was deprecated in June 2019 with removal 'on or after 2019-09-01' (issue #11603). It ships no road networks, towns, traffic agents, pedestrians, traffic lights, weather, driving scenario tooling or driving benchmarks, and no driving VLA I found targets it.
details: Every candidate driving VLA or E2E policy in scope (SimLingo, Drive-π0/DriveMoE, ORION, LEAD/TFv6, TF++, DriveTransformer) ships CARLA 0.9.15 Leaderboard-2.0/Bench2Drive agents. LMDrive uses CARLA 0.9.10.1. Using Drake would mean building maps, actors, sensors, a photoreal rendering pipeline and expert data from scratch, and no pretrained policy has seen Drake imagery, so the domain shift would dominate any failure analysis. Drake is appropriate for manipulation or vehicle-dynamics verification, not camera-based urban driving.
project_relevance: Remove Drake from the plan and standardise on CARLA 0.9.15 with Bench2Drive's leaderboard/scenario_runner fork, as bundled by SimLingo and DriveMoE. If a cheap non-photoreal sandbox is needed for early SAE and clustering prototyping, MetaDrive or HighwayEnv (already listed in repo docs) are closer fits, but a VLA trained on CARLA imagery will not transfer to them. Drake likely entered Source A through a mistaken Toyota Research Institute association; the orchestrator notes the mentor is at Honda Research Institute / 99P Labs.
discrepancies: Drake has no driving-world assets or traffic/scenario tooling; its automotive module was deprecated for removal in 2019.
No driving VLA has a Drake integration; all candidates target CARLA.

second_pass.correct_value: Drake (RobotLocomotion/drake; its README tagline is "Model-Based Design and Verification for Robotics") is a toolbox for multibody dynamics, optimisation and systems. It has generic camera rendering: RgbdSensor, "a meta-sensor that houses RGB, depth, and label cameras", with VTK, GL and glTF-client render engines, and a Blender backend through RobotLocomotion/drake-blender, which its README calls "relatively new". Drake core has no driving content. The master examples/ directory has no car, vehicle or driving example. The old drake/automotive module (promoted from examples/Cars in issue #3406, 2016) was deprecated on 2019-06-10, with removal "on or after 2019-09-01" (issue #11603). One caveat the first pass left out: TRI's automotive work continued outside Drake. Delphyne ("a traffic level simulator for autonomous driving") and maliput (a road-network API) now live under github.com/maliput; the old ToyotaResearchInstitute/delphyne URL redirects there. Delphyne builds on drake_vendor plus Ignition, targets Ubuntu 20.04, and had commits as recently as Sep 2025. It is a traffic-level simulator of ego and other cars. Its GUI is a visualiser built on ignition-rendering3/Ogre, and neither its README nor its package manifests mention camera sensors, perception, towns, pedestrians or weather. No driving VLA or end-to-end camera policy I could find targets Drake or Delphyne. SimLingo and the other candidates target CARLA 0.9.15 with Bench2Drive and the Leaderboard. So Drake is not a reasonable rollout simulator for camera-based driving VLAs.
second_pass.reasoning:
I tried to overturn the first pass and could not. The verdict stands with one refinement. My WebSearch budget was used up, and drake.mit.edu, huggingface.co, semanticscholar and openreview were blocked by egress, so I relied on GitHub pages, raw files and GitHub code search.

Evidence for the claim (the strongest case for Drake):
(1) Drake can render RGB, depth and label images through RgbdSensor, and can do Blender-quality rendering through the glTF client and drake-blender. In principle it could produce camera frames.
(2) Drake does have a driving lineage. drake/automotive existed from 2016 (#3406), and the Drake-based traffic simulator Delphyne plus the maliput road-network stack still exist under github.com/maliput. Delphyne's package.xml depends on drake_vendor, the maliput road backends and py_trees, and its last commit was 2025-09-23.
(3) Drake models contact and friction, so "physics parameter bounds (friction, accel limits)" is a physically meaningful phrase for Drake.

Evidence against:
(a) Drake master has no automotive, car or driving example; the examples/ list covers acrobot, atlas, kuka, quadrotor and similar.
(b) drake/automotive was deprecated on 2019-06-10 and slated for removal after 2019-09-01. The issue tells users to copy the files if they want them.
(c) Delphyne calls itself a "traffic level simulator". It targets Ubuntu 20.04, and its GUI is a road-network and traffic visualiser. Neither its README nor its package manifests mention camera sensors or perception. It ships no photoreal towns, pedestrians, traffic lights, weather or scenario suites comparable to CARLA or Bench2Drive, and has no expert driving data.
(d) GitHub code search for pydrake together with CARLA, "autonomous driving" or vehicle-mounted RgbdSensor returned no driving-policy repos.
(e) The flagship candidate VLA, SimLingo, uses CARLA 0.9.15 with Bench2Drive and the Leaderboard and does not mention Drake.
(f) Where the Drake mention likely came from: Source A calls the mentor "RYAN LINGO — TOYOTA RESEARCH INSTITUTE" (TRI develops Drake). The repo's docs/refined proposals.md says Ryan Lingo is at Honda Research Institute / 99P Labs. That looks like a misattribution that pulled in TRI's toolbox.

Changes to the first pass: none to the verdict. I add Delphyne/maliput as the only real Drake-based driving simulator, which is traffic-level only, and the exact deprecation date (2019-06-10, by jwnimmer-tri).

Recommendation for the project: remove Drake. Use CARLA 0.9.15 with Bench2Drive's leaderboard and scenario_runner, as the SimLingo and DriveMoE releases do. If a mentor-facing physics discussion is still wanted, frame the friction and acceleration bounds in terms of CARLA vehicle physics control parameters. Delphyne/maliput can at most be cited as the TRI-origin traffic simulator on top of Drake, not as a VLA rollout environment. The BibTeX below is Drake's self-recommended citation; I could not re-fetch drake.mit.edu to reconfirm it.

claim: CARLA ScenarioRunner / Bench2Drive support programmatic, parameterised generation of targeted scenarios (needed to invert discovered failure axes into scenario configs and to generate repair data).
correct_value:
ScenarioRunner (MIT) supports:
- Python scenario classes.
- OpenSCENARIO 1.0, including ParameterDeclarations and the --openscenarioparams 'p1: v1, p2: v2' command-line override of global parameters.
- Route-based (Leaderboard) scenarios.
The README also mentions OpenSCENARIO 2.0. Its latest release (0.9.16) matches CARLA 0.9.16; Bench2Drive and SimLingo bundle 0.9.15-compatible forks. Leaderboard-2.0/Bench2Drive route XML sets per-scenario parameters (e.g., <scenario type="ParkingCutIn"><trigger_point .../><direction value="right"/>, plus flow_speed and source_dist_interval for actor flows) and per-route weather blocks (cloudiness, precipitation, deposits, wetness, wind, sun azimuth/altitude, fog). Bench2Drive has 44 scenario types, 220 evaluation routes (bench2drive220) and datasets foldered as scenario_name/Town[id]_weather[id]_route[id].
details: Targeted scenarios can be generated by writing route XML files programmatically: pick the scenario type, trigger location, scenario parameters and weather/sun values, then run them through the leaderboard evaluator with the agent, or through the PDM-Lite expert to collect repair data (SimLingo's collect_dataset_slurm.py; LEAD's faster data generator). autonomousvision/carla_route_generator offers a GUI route and scenario editor. Limits: each Leaderboard-2.0 scenario class exposes only a few parameters. New axes such as pedestrian speed distributions, occluder geometry or novel assets need edits to the scenario classes or blueprint changes; Fail2Drive shows how to add novel assets. OpenSCENARIO parameter sets and stochastic distributions are not documented as supported.
project_relevance: This supports the 'activation cluster → scenario parameters' inversion step without writing a new simulator. Recommended implementation: a Python generator that emits Bench2Drive-style route XML with weather × scenario-parameter grids. It gives exact control over planted-slice definitions (scenario type × weather × town) for the sealed answer key, and the same generator produces LoRA repair data through the PDM-Lite expert. Budget engineering time for any failure axis that is not a native scenario parameter.

claim: Bench2Drive (CARLA v2) provides the scenario-structured open training data and 220-route closed-loop protocol that the planted-gap design would use.
correct_value: Bench2Drive: Towards Multi-Ability Benchmarking of Closed-Loop End-To-End Autonomous Driving. Xiaosong Jia, Zhenjie Yang, Qifeng Li, Zhiyuan Zhang, Junchi Yan. NeurIPS 2024 Datasets & Benchmarks. Code and data: github.com/Thinklab-SJTU/Bench2Drive (default branch 0.0.4). CARLA 0.9.15. Dataset: mini 10 clips (~4 GB), base 1,000 clips (~400 GB), full 13,638 clips (~4 TB); v0.0.4 adds 1,100 uniformly distributed routes (44 scenarios × 25) with 3D occupancy. Evaluation set bench2drive220 (44 × 5 routes). Licence: CC-BY-NC-ND.
details: Bench2Drive supplies expert (Think2Drive RL expert) demonstrations as short clips, each centred on one of 44 interactive scenarios, across towns and weathers. It also defines a closed-loop evaluation on 220 short routes with Driving Score, Success Rate, Efficiency, Comfortness and five multi-ability scores (merging, overtaking, emergency brake, give way, traffic sign). Multi-GPU parallel evaluation scripts are provided. The self-reported leaderboard (autonomousvision/Bench2Drive-Leaderboard, v0.0.3 numbers, updated 2026-09-24) lists SimLingo 85.07/67.27, AutoVLA 78.84/57.73, ORION 77.74/54.62, DriveMoE 74.22/48.64, TFv6 95.28/86.81, and privileged PDM-Lite 97.02/92.27.
project_relevance: Use bench2drive220 as the nominal no-regression suite. Use Bench2Drive's scenario/Town/weather folder structure to define withheld slices for Drive-π0 (or any model trained on Bench2Drive). Note the NC-ND licence, which restricts redistributing modified data; share generation scripts, not data.

claim: (Found during feasibility check) A CARLA benchmark of unseen scenarios can serve as naturally held-out 'gaps' for released driving policies, including SimLingo.
correct_value: Fail2Drive: Benchmarking Closed-Loop Driving Generalization. Simon Gerstenecker, Andreas Geiger, Katrin Renz. IROS 2026 (to appear); arXiv:2604.08535. Code: github.com/autonomousvision/fail2drive. CARLA 0.9.15. 100 route pairs, 17 unseen scenarios, 30 novel assets (animals, visual noise, adversarial obstacles).
details: Fail2Drive pairs each generalisation route with an in-distribution counterpart, so the generalisation gap per scenario can be measured directly. Models are not allowed to train on its scenarios. The README lists SimLingo, TransFuser++, ORION, PlanT2, HiP-AD and Bench2DriveZoo as evaluated. The public leaderboard .tex shows, for example, ORION DS 53.0 → 51.2 (SR −11.5%), BridgeDrive 91.6 → 81.9 (SR −21.1%), UniAD SR −24.0%, and the PDM-Lite expert only −1.7%. Custom agents run through leaderboard_evaluator_local.py with Fail2Drive route XMLs.
project_relevance: This is a strong fallback or complement to planted gaps. For the released SimLingo checkpoint, whose training data is public and can be checked for absence, Fail2Drive scenarios are held-out slices with known identity, a ready ground truth for discovery precision and recall without any retraining. It also shows the 'discover failure axes' framing is timely. Contact: Katrin Renz (SimLingo first author, Fail2Drive senior author).

claim: Source A: 'Execute open-weight driving VLA rollouts (e.g., DriveVLM, SimLingo, or OpenVLA/pi0 variants) across thousands of simulated trajectory seeds in CARLA or Drake' and 'Targeted Retraining & Policy Repair: fine-tune the VLA on synthesized scenarios using LoRA'.
correct_value: Of the named policies, only SimLingo is an open-weight driving VLA with CARLA closed-loop code and released training data. DriveVLM has no public weights. OpenVLA has no driving variant. For π0 there is only a third-party driving variant, Drive-π0 (DriveMoE). Drake is unsuitable; use CARLA 0.9.15 (Bench2Drive/Leaderboard 2.0). LoRA repair is natively supported by SimLingo, whose LLM is already LoRA-trained (r=32, α=64). Drive-π0's released recipe uses full fine-tuning.
details: Thousands of rollouts are feasible, but the cost is dominated by CARLA plus VLA inference speed. SimLingo runs at about 0.05x real time on an RTX 4060 Ti with about 11 GB GPU memory in use (issue #95). TF++ needs about 4 h on 8x2080Ti for the 220 Bench2Drive routes. DriveMoE reports evaluation on 8xH200.
project_relevance: Replace the list with: primary SimLingo; secondary Drive-π0; optional non-VLA control LEAD/TFv6; simulator CARLA 0.9.15 with Bench2Drive and ScenarioRunner route XML. Budget rollouts and activation storage explicitly.
discrepancies: DriveVLM is not open-weight.
No OpenVLA driving variant exists; π0 only via third-party Drive-π0.
Drake is not a driving simulator (automotive module removed after 2019).

second_pass.correct_value:
The plan is only partly feasible as written. SimLingo (Renz et al., CVPR 2025) is the only named policy that is an open-weight driving VLA with CARLA closed-loop code. It ships checkpoints (HF RenzKa/simlingo, released 2025-06-25), its dataset (released 2025-05-26), Bench2Drive eval scripts, CARLA 0.9.15 and an Apache-2.0 code license. The problems with the rest of the list:
- DriveVLM (Tsinghua/Li Auto) has no public code or weights. The official repo has only a github-pages branch, and its "Question about code release" issue (#1, March 2024) is still open and unanswered.
- I found no public OpenVLA-derived driving checkpoint. The repo "olh2012/OpenVLA-Drive" does not use OpenVLA weights (it is phi-2/LLaVA + LoRA), and OpenDriveVLA is Qwen2.5-based, not OpenVLA.
- The only public π0-style driving policy I found is Drive-π0 in the DriveMoE repo (Thinklab-SJTU, CVPR 2026, arXiv 2505.16278; checkpoints at HF rethinklab/DriveMoE). It reimplements π0 on top of open-pi-zero/openpi but starts from PaliGemma-3B weights, not Physical Intelligence π0 weights. It is trained and evaluated closed-loop on Bench2Drive.
- Drake is a robotics dynamics toolbox, not a driving simulator. drake/automotive was deprecated in issue #11603 (June 2019), with removal "on or after 2019-09-01", and no automotive path exists on master today.
- Use CARLA 0.9.15 with Bench2Drive / Leaderboard 2.0 routes instead.

correct_value: SAFE: Multitask Failure Detection for Vision-Language-Action Models. Qiao Gu, Yuanliang Ju, Shengxiang Sun, Igor Gilitschenski, Haruki Nishimura, Masha Itkina, Florian Shkurti. NeurIPS 2025 (Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38, pp. 40041-40076). arXiv:2506.09937. Code: github.com/vla-safe/SAFE. Hosted on a Toyota Research Institute page (TRI co-authors).
details: SAFE introduces the 'multitask failure detection' problem for generalist VLA policies: a detector must flag failures on unseen tasks without task-specific training. The authors analyse VLA feature space, find that internal features carry high-level, task-generic success/failure information, and train a small sequential detector (MLP/LSTM-style) on VLA internal features to output a single scalar failure likelihood per timestep. Thresholds are calibrated with functional conformal prediction, trading off accuracy and detection time. They evaluate on OpenVLA, pi0, pi0-FAST and pi0* in LIBERO and SimplerEnv, plus real Franka and WidowX robots, and report state-of-the-art failure detection against diverse baselines. It is squarely about VLAs, but only robot manipulation, not driving; nothing about crashes or collisions.
project_relevance: The best-matched prior work for 'scalar failure detection from VLA activations'. Use it as the canonical example of 'detection ≠ discovery', and run the SAFE-style detector (public code) as a scalar baseline on driving-VLA rollouts, since its outputs could seed which episodes to cluster. Caveats: manipulation only; the repo docs' claims that SAFE predicts crashes, or fits linear probes with AUROC for collisions 15 steps ahead, are unsupported and should be removed.

Venue missing: published at NeurIPS 2025 (proceedings vol. 38)

correct_value: VLA-FAIL: Efficient Task Failure Detection for Finetuned Vision-Language-Action Models. Florian Seligmann, Emiliyan Gospodinov, Enes Ulas Dincer, Gerhard Neumann (KIT, Autonomous Learning Robots lab). arXiv:2606.21386, v1 19 Jun 2026, preprint (cs.LG/cs.CV). details: VLA-FAIL is a lightweight runtime failure detector for fine-tuned VLAs. It needs no failure rollouts, no external models and no expensive action sampling. It combines two signals. LLMD (last-layer Mahalanobis distance) flags out-of-distribution states from token-wise deviations in last-layer features relative to training demonstrations. ACC (action-chunk consistency) exploits the temporal overlap of receding-horizon action chunks and flags failures when consecutive chunks disagree. It also proposes AUCPDT, a threshold-free metric that jointly scores precision, recall and detection time. Experiments use flow-matching VLAs pi0.5 and X-VLA on LIBERO-Plus and six real tabletop tasks, reportedly matching 32-sample baselines at about 2 ms per step. correct_value: ProbeAct: Probe-Guided Training-Free Failure Recovery in Vision-Language-Action Models. Fan Zhang, Seongbin Park, Baharan Mirzasoleiman, Shahriar Talebi, Nader Sehatbakhsh (UCLA). arXiv:2606.09740, 8 Jun 2026, under review. No CVPR 2025 paper with this name was found.
details: ProbeAct is a training-free, inference-time failure-recovery layer for a frozen VLA (OpenVLA-OFT). A multi-target hidden-state probe (PCA plus a small MLP on an intermediate layer, reported as layer 8, of the visual trunk) decodes 3D object positions with high accuracy (reported R² ≈ 0.97). This reveals that perception features stay intact while the action endpoint drifts, a 'memory trap' in which the action head, not perception, fails. A rule-based kinematic state machine uses gripper width, end-effector pose and probe coordinates to detect empty or soft grasps, drops and placement failures. A hierarchical control-barrier-function filter then steers actions away from repeatedly failed locations via a closed-form QP. On LIBERO-plus perturbations it lifts OpenVLA-OFT from 69.6% to 74.1% success, with the largest gains under geometric shifts. It is a manipulation paper; it does not output a scalar P(failure) or predict collisions.
project_relevance: Useful as evidence that VLA hidden states carry task-relevant information that the action output loses. That supports probing trunk vs. action-head activations in a driving VLA and naming 'perception intact / action drifted' as a candidate failure axis. Cite it as a recent arXiv preprint (2026), not CVPR 2025. Rewrite the docs' description: it is not a linear P(failure) probe and says nothing about collisions or 15-step horizons.

claim: @article{roboart2025, title={RoboART: Predictive Red Teaming and Targeted Data Collection for Robotic Policies}, author={Anonymous}, journal={arXiv preprint arXiv:2502.06575}, year={2025}}; docs: primary head-to-head baseline, 'uses VLMs to score policy degradation across human-enumerated factor lists'
correct_value: Predictive Red Teaming: Breaking Policies Without Breaking Robots. Anirudha Majumdar, Mohit Sharma, Dmitry Kalashnikov, Sumeet Singh, Pierre Sermanet, Vikas Sindhwani. Proceedings of the 9th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2025), PMLR 305:1615-1635. arXiv:2502.06575. RoboART is the name of the proposed pipeline, not the paper title. Project page: predictive-red-team.github.io.
details: The paper defines 'predictive red teaming': finding a policy's vulnerabilities to environmental factors and predicting the resulting performance drop without hardware evaluation in off-nominal conditions. The proposed pipeline, RoboART (automated red teaming), has two steps. First, it edits nominal observations with language-conditioned generative image editing to vary factors such as lighting, distractors and object locations (a VLM critic filters edits, per secondary summaries). Second, it predicts per-factor performance by running a policy-specific anomaly detector on the policy's embeddings of the edited observations. Across 500+ hardware trials in twelve off-nominal conditions for visuomotor diffusion policies, predicted and real success rates differ by less than 0.19 on average. Fine-tuning with data collected under factors predicted to be adverse boosts performance 2-7x. It covers manipulation with diffusion policies, not VLAs and not driving, and the factor list is enumerated up front.
project_relevance: A sensible head-to-head baseline for the 'enumerated factors' condition. The project would reimplement the edit-and-predict idea on driving frames (e.g. CARLA/Bench2Drive camera images) with an anomaly detector on driving-VLA embeddings. Caveats: no public code found (the GitHub repo is only a project website); the paper evaluates diffusion policies on hardware; and the 'VLM scores degradation' framing in the docs is imprecise: prediction comes from a policy-embedding anomaly detector.
discrepancies: Title wrong: real title 'Predictive Red Teaming: Breaking Policies Without Breaking Robots' (RoboART is the method name)

details: RoboMonkey is a test-time scaling framework for VLAs in robot manipulation, not autonomous driving. correct_value: Correct as written. NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks Track; arXiv:2406.03877; Thinklab-SJTU; code github.com/Thinklab-SJTU/Bench2Drive.
details: Bench2Drive is a closed-loop benchmark for end-to-end autonomous driving in CARLA v2. The official training set has 2 million fully annotated frames from 13,638 short clips, spread evenly across 44 interactive scenarios (cut-in, overtaking, detour, etc.), 23 weathers and 12 towns. Evaluation requires passing the 44 scenarios under different locations and weathers, 220 short routes in total, giving a disentangled, per-ability assessment. It is intended to replace high-variance long-route driving scores (Town05Long, Longest6).
project_relevance: Core evaluation harness. The scenario-type × weather × town metadata of the 220 routes gives a ready-made human-labelled factor space to use as a 'known axes' control and for planted-gap experiments. Caveat: training data covers all towns, so test towns are seen during training.

What I tried:
(1) WebFetch of the claimed URL on www.mobileye.com, the bare mobileye.com domain and ir.mobileye.com. All three were blocked by the egress proxy (EGRESS_BLOCKED).
(2) WebSearch for "Mobileye Meteor Genario edge cases" and for the exact title "Diagnosing the Long Tail" Mobileye. Neither ran: the session's 200-search budget was used up.

None found anything tied to Mobileye. The Genario repositories are personal profiles and an unrelated Russian project; the "Meteor" hits are Intel Meteor Lake or ordinary dictionary words.

What I did find: a broad code search for "mobileye.com/blog" listed about 24 distinct Mobileye blog slugs cited in public repositories. These include a CES 2026 takeaways post, "compound-ai-the-framework-powering-scalable-autonomy" and two long-tail posts. The long-tail posts appear in the ledger at swaylq/master-skill (prototypes/autonomous-driving-master/references/research/01-figures.md), marked "verified_primary" and dated 2026-05-27, by Shalev-Shwartz & Shashua:

- "driving-the-long-tail", a companion post on engineering countermeasures to the long tail.

But the "diagnosing-the-long-tail" slug, the title, "Meteor", "Genario" and the "Genario Loop" appear nowhere I could reach. The first pass's corrections still hold: the entry type, the made-up journal and the placeholder author are wrong regardless of whether the page exists. It also counts against the entry that SOURCE A, the same LLM handoff prompt, bundles this claim with other vague "industrial" claims, such as an "8-Stage Data Engine loop" from BMW, Carbon Robotics, Ocado and Ansvar AI.

What the source claims the work does: Meteor, a multi-agent VLM data-mining engine, turns fleet driving videos into natural-language failure hypotheses and queries, and passes scenario parameters to Genario, which generates synthetic variations for retraining. None of this is supported by evidence I could access.

claim: @inproceedings{zhong2023ctgplusplus, title={Language-Guided Traffic Simulation via Controllable Trajectory Generation}, author={Zhong, Zhaofeng and others}, booktitle={IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)}, year={2023}}; docs propose using CTG++ 'in CARLA' with ScenarioRunner
correct_value: Language-Guided Traffic Simulation via Scene-Level Diffusion (CTG++). Ziyuan Zhong, Davis Rempe, Yuxiao Chen, Boris Ivanovic, Yulong Cao, Danfei Xu, Marco Pavone, Baishakhi Ray. 7th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2023), PMLR 229:144-177 (oral). arXiv:2306.06344. Code: github.com/NVlabs/CTG (covers CTG and CTG++). The earlier CTG paper is 'Guided Conditional Diffusion for Controllable Traffic Simulation' (ICRA 2023).
details: CTG++ is a scene-level conditional diffusion model for multi-agent traffic simulation. A spatio-temporal transformer backbone models realistic joint agent trajectories. An LLM interface translates a user's natural-language query into a differentiable loss or guidance function that steers diffusion sampling at test time. It shows realistic, controllable, query-compliant traffic behaviour on nuScenes-derived scenarios. It generates agent trajectories, not rendered sensor data, and it is not a CARLA plug-in.
project_relevance: A candidate controllable 'behaviour generator' for turning a discovered axis into scenario parameters, e.g. adversarial cut-in timing. It would need custom bridging to CARLA/ScenarioRunner (trajectory replay of actors), since it runs on nuScenes-format data via NVIDIA's tbsim/trajdata stack. It is also gated on language queries, the same 'query-space bottleneck' the docs criticise. Correct title, first author's first name and venue.

Venue wrong: CoRL 2023 (PMLR 229:144-177), not CVPR 2023

correct_value: Editable Scene Simulation for Autonomous Driving via Collaborative LLM-Agents (system name: ChatSim). Yuxi Wei, Zi Wang, Yifan Lu, Chenxin Xu, Changxing Liu, Hao Zhao, Siheng Chen, Yanfeng Wang. CVPR 2024, pp. 15077-15087. arXiv:2402.05746. Code: github.com/yifanlu0227/ChatSim.

correct_value: Correct as written. Proceedings of the 1st Annual Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2017), PMLR 78:1-16. arXiv:1711.03938. This matches the official citation in the carla-simulator/carla README.
details: CARLA is an open-source urban driving simulator with open digital assets (towns, vehicles, pedestrians), configurable sensors and environmental conditions such as weather and time of day. The original paper uses it to compare a modular pipeline, end-to-end imitation learning and end-to-end reinforcement learning. claim: Domino: Discovering Systematic Errors with Cross-Modal Embeddings. Eyuboglu, Varma, Saab, Delbrouck, Lee-Messer, Dunnmon, Ré. ICLR 2022.
correct_value: Domino: Discovering Systematic Errors with Cross-Modal Embeddings. Sabri Eyuboglu, Maya Varma, Khaled Saab, Jean-Benoit Delbrouck, Christopher Lee-Messer, Jared Dunnmon, James Zou, Christopher Ré. ICLR 2022 (oral). OpenReview FPCMqjI0jXN; arXiv:2203.14960.
details: Domino frames slice discovery as finding coherent, underperforming subsets of a validation set. Inputs are embedded with cross-modal encoders (e.g. CLIP-style models that put images or time series and text in one space). An error-aware Gaussian mixture model then models embeddings, labels and predictions together to find regions where errors cluster. Each slice gets a natural-language description by matching its prototype against text embeddings. The paper also adds a quantitative evaluation framework of 1,235 slice-discovery settings with planted slices across natural images, medical images and time series. Domino recovers 36% of those slices, 12 points better than prior methods. Code is at HazyResearch/domino.
project_relevance: Use Domino as the main input-space slice-discovery baseline. Run it on camera-frame CLIP embeddings with a per-clip failure flag (infraction or collision) in place of the class error. Its planted-slice evaluation is the model to copy for planted failure axes in CARLA. Caveats: it is built for classification, so the 'label/prediction' inputs must be redefined for driving outcomes. It looks only at input embeddings, not VLA internals, which is exactly the gap the project's activation-space methods claim to fill.
discrepancies: Author list omits James Zou (7th of 8 authors)

claim: Spotlight: Inspecting Machine Learning Models for Hidden Underperforming Subpopulations. d'Eon, Greg; d'Eon, Jason; Ullrich, Jamie R; Varma, Maya. FAccT 2022.
correct_value: The Spotlight: A General Method for Discovering Systematic Errors in Deep Learning Models. Greg d'Eon, Jason d'Eon, James R. Wright, Kevin Leyton-Brown. Proceedings of the 2022 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT '22), pp. 1962-1981. DOI 10.1145/3531146.3533240. arXiv:2107.00758.
details: The Spotlight finds systematic errors without predefined groups. It works in the model's final hidden-layer representation space. It learns a soft 'spotlight', a truncated kernel with a learnable center and precision, that maximizes weighted mean loss subject to a minimum total weight. Adam optimizes it in linear time, and later spotlights discount losses already covered. On FairFace, ImageNet, Amazon polarity, MovieLens, SQuAD and chest x-rays it surfaced coherent high-loss groups, such as profile faces, children and Spanish-language reviews. The authors caution that finding nothing proves nothing. The official code is gregdeon/spotlight.
project_relevance: This is the most direct representation-space baseline for the project. Run it on VLA hidden states from failure and nominal rollouts, with per-frame or per-clip driving loss (e.g. an infraction-weighted L2 to the expert trajectory). It is a cheap, strong comparison to SAE-based or probe-residual clustering. The current bib entry would be flagged in review: two of the four authors are wrong (not real co-authors) and the title is wrong.
discrepancies: Title is wrong: real title is 'The Spotlight: A General Method for Discovering Systematic Errors in Deep Learning Models'
Authors 3-4 are wrong: 'Ullrich, Jamie R' and 'Varma, Maya' should be 'Wright, James R.' and 'Leyton-Brown, Kevin'
Pages (1962-1981), DOI and arXiv id are missing

claim: No Subclass Left Behind: Fine-Grained Robustness in Rough-Grained Classifiers. Sohoni, Dunnmon, Angus, Gu, Ré. NeurIPS 2020, vol 33, pp. 19339-19352.
correct_value: No Subclass Left Behind: Fine-Grained Robustness in Coarse-Grained Classification Problems. Nimit S. Sohoni, Jared A. Dunnmon, Geoffrey Angus, Albert Gu, Christopher Ré. NeurIPS 2020, vol. 33, pp. 19339-19352. arXiv:2011.12945.
details: GEORGE targets 'hidden stratification': unlabeled subclasses inside coarse classes that a model does badly on. Step one trains an ERM model and takes penultimate-layer features, optionally reduced with UMAP. It then clusters within each superclass with Gaussian mixtures, choosing k by silhouette score. Step two treats the cluster assignments as groups and trains with group DRO. It raises worst-group accuracy, e.g. Waterbirds robust accuracy from about 63% to 76% as reported. The clusters recover rare subclasses with high recall but low precision.
project_relevance: Use GEORGE as a 'cluster the activations' baseline: cluster VLA penultimate or bottleneck features within outcome classes (success vs failure, or per scenario type), then check whether clusters match planted axes. The GDRO second stage is also a simple retraining baseline for the repair step. Caveat: it clusters within each class, so it cannot find failure modes that cut across classes, which Spotlight points out.
discrepancies: Title is wrong: 'Rough-Grained Classifiers' should be 'Coarse-Grained Classification Problems'

claim: SliceLine: Fast, Linear-Algebra-based Slice Finding for ML Model Debugging. Sagadeeva, Elena; Boehm, Matthias. Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment 14(11):2246-2254, 2021.
correct_value: SliceLine: Fast, Linear-Algebra-based Slice Finding for ML Model Debugging. Svetlana Sagadeeva, Matthias Boehm. SIGMOD '21: Proceedings of the 2021 International Conference on Management of Data (Virtual Event, China), pp. 2290-2299. DOI 10.1145/3448016.3457323.
details: SliceLine enumerates 'slices': conjunctions of predicates over categorical or binned features where a model's error is much higher than average. It uses a scoring function that trades off slice error against slice size. Enumeration and pruning run as sparse linear-algebra operations with sound pruning bounds, which makes exact top-K slice finding fast on large tabular data. It is implemented in Apache SystemDS, and a reproducibility package is in damslab/reproducibility (sigmod2021-sliceline-p218).
project_relevance: Use SliceLine as the metadata-only baseline. Run it over scenario metadata such as town, weather, time of day, Bench2Drive scenario type, speed bin and actor counts to show which failures can already be explained by human-named attributes. The project's claim to find 'unnamed' axes is only convincing if the discovered axes beat or complement this baseline. Caveat: it needs discrete features and cannot see images or activations.
discrepancies: First author's given name is wrong: Svetlana, not Elena
Venue is wrong: it is SIGMOD 2021 (ACM), pp. 2290-2299, not PVLDB 14(11):2246-2254

claim: Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning. Bricken, Templeton, Batson, Chen, Jermyn, Conerly, Turner, Henighan, Drain, Ray, others. Transformer Circuits Thread 2023.
correct_value: Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning. Trenton Bricken, Adly Templeton, Joshua Batson, Brian Chen, Adam Jermyn, Tom Conerly, Nicholas L. Turner, Cem Anil, Carson Denison, Amanda Askell, Robert Lasenby, Yifan Wu, Shauna Kravec, Nicholas Schiefer, Tim Maxwell, Nicholas Joseph, Zac Hatfield-Dodds, Alex Tamkin, Karina Nguyen, Brayden McLean, Josiah E. Burke, Tristan Hume, Shan Carter, Tom Henighan, Chris Olah. Transformer Circuits Thread, October 4, 2023. https://transformer-circuits.pub/2023/monosemantic-features
details: Anthropic trained sparse autoencoders (ReLU encoder, L1 sparsity penalty) on MLP activations of a one-layer transformer, using about 8B tokens. Dictionary sizes ranged from 512 to 131,072 features. They argue neurons are polysemantic because of superposition, while the learned features are much more monosemantic and interpretable, judged by human raters and automated interpretability. Case studies cover Arabic-script, DNA, base64 and Hebrew features. They also report 'feature splitting' as dictionary size grows and universality of features across independently trained models. This is the canonical reference for SAE-based dictionary learning on transformer activations.
project_relevance: Cite it as the foundational SAE and dictionary-learning reference for decomposing VLA bottleneck activations. Its feature-splitting result bears directly on choosing dictionary size when looking for failure axes: coarse versus fine axes will split. Caveat: the method (ReLU plus L1) is now superseded in practice by TopK, JumpReLU or BatchTopK SAEs, so cite it for the concept and cite Gao et al. or Rajamanoharan et al. for the architecture actually trained.

claim: Scaling and Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders. Gao, Leo; Goh, Gabriel; Sutskever, Ilya; others. arXiv:2406.04093, 2024.
correct_value: Scaling and Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders. Leo Gao, Tom Dupré la Tour, Henk Tillman, Gabriel Goh, Rajan Troll, Alec Radford, Ilya Sutskever, Jan Leike, Jeffrey Wu. arXiv:2406.04093 (June 2024). Published at ICLR 2025 (oral), OpenReview tcsZt9ZNKD.
details: This is the TopK SAE paper (OpenAI). Only the k largest latents are kept, which sets sparsity (L0) directly and removes the L1 shrinkage problem. Together with initialization tricks and an auxiliary 'AuxK' loss, this sharply reduces dead latents. The authors derive clean scaling laws in autoencoder size and sparsity, and train a 16M-latent SAE on GPT-4 activations. They also propose feature-quality metrics beyond MSE: downstream loss, probe loss for hypothesized features, explainability, and sparsity of ablation effects. Code and GPT-2-small SAEs are released at openai/sparse_autoencoder.
project_relevance: This is the recommended default SAE architecture: TopK, or its BatchTopK successor, as implemented in SAELens. It makes sparsity an explicit, sweepable hyperparameter (k) and gives an evaluation protocol worth reusing, especially the probe-loss and downstream-loss metrics, adapted to driving-action loss. Cite the ICLR 2025 version. The 'TopK SAE' citation for the project is this entry; no separate record is needed.
discrepancies: Author order is wrong: Gabriel Goh is 4th author, not 2nd; co-authors Dupré la Tour, Tillman, Troll, Radford, Leike and Wu are omitted or misplaced

claim: Evidence-Based Scientific Question Discovery: A Framework with Historical Backtesting. Author 'Research Team, Scientific AI'. arXiv:2608.01234, 2026.
correct_value: Evidence-Based Scientific Question Discovery: A Framework with Historical Backtesting. Hui Mao (sole author). arXiv:2608.09968 [cs.DL; cross-listed cs.AI], submitted ~July 29, 2026, announced Aug 11-12, 2026. Companion paper by the same author: 'Historical Backtesting for Scientific Question Discovery: A Protocol and Astronomy Pilot', arXiv:2608.16795 (Aug 17, 2026). NOTE: arXiv:2608.01234 is an unrelated paper: 'Learning What to Remember and What to Internalize in LLM Self-Evolution via Adaptive Memory-Parameter Coordination' (COVE) by Tianyun Ji, Zhenya Huang, Jiayu Liu, Zirui Liu, Yu Su, Hongbin Pei.
details: The paper describes a framework that turns a traceable, reproducible, scope-controlled research corpus into ranked, falsifiable research questions. Evidence is represented as provenance-carrying claims. Cross-paper tensions are detected, typed and adjudicated by humans. Surviving signals are refined into questions and ranked by a two-stage protocol that separates scientific priority from execution priority. It is instantiated on exoplanet atmospheres, combining literature, structured catalogs and space-telescope archives. In a historical backtest, every question generated from pre-2021 evidence was substantively engaged by 2021-2026 literature the system never saw: two were answered (one with a premise later refuted), and the top-ranked question was independently posed and remains open. The companion 2608.16795 formalizes backtesting as a model-agnostic benchmark protocol with astronomy instances and four reference baselines.
project_relevance: This is the key methodological anchor for the SpecGap proposal (claim-provenance graphs, tension detection, historical backtesting). Fix the arXiv id and author immediately: the current id points to an unrelated paper, which a reviewer would take as a fabricated citation. Also cite 2608.16795 for the backtesting protocol and its falsifiable 'denominator' framing. Contact: Hui Mao. Caveats: it is a single-author, very recent, unreviewed preprint in astronomy, not mobility or engineering literature. Repo text claiming 'verbatim quote grounding' was not confirmed from the abstract; check against the PDF before paraphrasing.
discrepancies: arXiv id is wrong: 2608.01234 should be 2608.09968 (2608.01234 is the unrelated COVE paper by Ji et al.)
Author is a placeholder: 'Research Team, Scientific AI' should be Hui Mao
Primary category (cs.DL) and application domain (exoplanet atmospheres) are not stated

claim: The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery. Lu, Lu, Lange, Foerster, Clune, Ha. arXiv:2408.06292, 2024.
correct_value: The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery. Chris Lu, Cong Lu, Robert Tjarko Lange, Jakob Foerster, Jeff Clune, David Ha. arXiv:2408.06292 (2024). Follow-ups: The AI Scientist-v2 (Yamada et al., arXiv:2504.08066, 2025), and a Nature paper 'Towards end-to-end automation of AI research' (Nature, March 2026, DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10265-5; author list not verified here).
details: Sakana AI's AI Scientist is an end-to-end LLM agent pipeline. It generates research ideas, checks novelty against the literature, writes and runs experiment code from a template, writes a full LaTeX paper, and scores it with an automated LLM reviewer calibrated against ICLR reviews. It was shown on three ML templates (diffusion models, transformer language modelling, grokking), at a reported cost of roughly $15 per paper. The v2 system removed templates via agentic tree search; one fully AI-generated paper passed peer review at an ICLR 2025 workshop before being withdrawn by prior agreement. The bib entry matches the official README citation exactly.
project_relevance: Cite it as the main contrast for SpecGap: ungrounded, LLM-judged ideation with no falsifiable 'answer key'. Its automated reviewer is an example of the LLM-as-judge circularity the project wants to avoid. Consider also citing the 2026 Nature version (verify authors first) and v2 for the current state of the art.

claim: SciMon: Scientific Inspiration Machines for Generating Novel Research Ideas. Wang, Qingyun and others. ACL 2024.
correct_value: SciMON: Scientific Inspiration Machines Optimized for Novelty. Qingyun Wang, Doug Downey, Heng Ji, Tom Hope. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the ACL (Volume 1: Long Papers), 2024, pp. 279-299. DOI 10.18653/v1/2024.acl-long.18. arXiv:2305.14259.
details: SciMON generates natural-language scientific ideas grounded in the literature. Given a background context, it retrieves 'inspirations' from semantic neighbours, knowledge-graph neighbours and citation neighbours. It then generates ideas with fine-tuned T5 and GPT-3.5/GPT-4 models. An iterative novelty-boosting loop compares each idea against retrieved prior work and revises it until it is sufficiently different. It was evaluated in NLP and biochemistry. The authors found that even GPT-4 ideas tend to lack technical depth and novelty, which retrieval and novelty optimization partly fix. Code is at EagleW/CLBD.
project_relevance: Use SciMON as a literature-grounded ideation baseline for SpecGap, and as a contrast: it optimizes for novelty relative to prior work, not for evidence tensions or backtested predictive validity. Its novelty-checking loop is a reusable component.
discrepancies: Title is wrong: real title is 'SciMON: Scientific Inspiration Machines Optimized for Novelty'
Co-authors Doug Downey, Heng Ji and Tom Hope are hidden behind 'others'

claim: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning. Shinn, Noah; Labash, Beck; Gopinath, Ashwin. NeurIPS 2023.
correct_value: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning. NeurIPS 2023 proceedings authors: Noah Shinn, Federico Cassano, Ashwin Gopinath, Karthik Narasimhan, Shunyu Yao. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36, pp. 8634-8652. arXiv:2303.11366; the latest arXiv/README version lists Noah Shinn, Federico Cassano, Edward Berman, Ashwin Gopinath, Karthik Narasimhan, Shunyu Yao.
details: Reflexion improves LLM agents without weight updates. After each trial, the agent turns task feedback (scalar reward, unit-test results or self-evaluation) into a natural-language self-reflection. These reflections are stored in an episodic memory buffer and conditioned on in later trials, a form of 'verbal reinforcement learning'. It was evaluated on sequential decision-making (AlfWorld), reasoning (HotpotQA) and programming (HumanEval, MBPP, LeetcodeHardGym). It reported 91% pass@1 on HumanEval against 80% for the GPT-4 baseline at the time.
project_relevance: Cite it as the mechanism for the self-critique loop, e.g. an LLM that iteratively names or describes discovered failure axes, or refines generated open questions, using feedback from probes or closed-loop tests. The v1 author list (with Beck Labash) is outdated. Use the NeurIPS proceedings author list and @inproceedings.
discrepancies: Author list is outdated: 'Labash, Beck' appears only on early arXiv versions; the NeurIPS 2023 version is Shinn, Cassano, Gopinath, Narasimhan, Yao
Entry type is @article with journal=NeurIPS; it should be @inproceedings with volume 36 and pages 8634-8652

claim: Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback. Madaan, Tandon, Gupta, Hallinan, Gao, Wiegreffe, Alon, Dziri, Prabhumoye, Yang, others. NeurIPS 2023.
correct_value: Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback. Aman Madaan, Niket Tandon, Prakhar Gupta, Skyler Hallinan, Luyu Gao, Sarah Wiegreffe, Uri Alon, Nouha Dziri, Shrimai Prabhumoye, Yiming Yang, Shashank Gupta, Bodhisattwa Prasad Majumder, Katherine Hermann, Sean Welleck, Amir Yazdanbakhsh, Peter Clark. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (NeurIPS 2023), pp. 46534-46594. arXiv:2303.17651.
details: In Self-Refine, one LLM produces an initial output, critiques it with self-generated feedback, and refines it, repeating until a stopping condition. No extra training, supervised data or RL is needed. It was evaluated on seven tasks, including dialogue response, code optimization, code readability, math reasoning, sentiment reversal, acronym generation and constrained generation, with GPT-3.5, ChatGPT and GPT-4. Humans and automatic metrics preferred its outputs, with about 20% absolute average improvement over one-step generation.
