claim: JumpReLU SAEs (Rajamanoharan et al. 2024)
correct_value: Jumping Ahead: Improving Reconstruction Fidelity with JumpReLU Sparse Autoencoders. Senthooran Rajamanoharan, Tom Lieberum, Nicolas Sonnerat, Arthur Conmy, Vikrant Varma, János Kramár, Neel Nanda (Google DeepMind). arXiv:2407.14435, July 2024.
details: JumpReLU SAEs replace ReLU with a JumpReLU activation: each latent has a learned threshold below which it outputs zero. They train an L0 sparsity penalty directly, using straight-through estimators to get gradients through the discontinuous threshold and step function. On Gemma 2 9B activations they report state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity at a given sparsity against Gated and TopK SAEs, without worse interpretability. This is the architecture behind DeepMind's Gemma Scope SAE release.
project_relevance: JumpReLU is a strong candidate architecture next to TopK or BatchTopK. SAELens labels it state-of-the-art and supports training it (JumpReLUTrainingSAEConfig). Include it in the architecture ablation for VLA bottleneck SAEs. Caveat: the thresholds add training hyperparameters (bandwidth, L0 coefficient) that need tuning.

claim: Gated SAEs
correct_value: Improving Sparse Decomposition of Language Model Activations with Gated Sparse Autoencoders (NeurIPS 2024). arXiv version titled 'Improving Dictionary Learning with Gated Sparse Autoencoders', arXiv:2404.16014. Senthooran Rajamanoharan, Arthur Conmy, Lewis Smith, Tom Lieberum, Vikrant Varma, János Kramár, Rohin Shah, Neel Nanda.
details: Gated SAEs split the encoder into two parts. A gating path decides which latents are active, and a magnitude path estimates how large they are. The L1 penalty is applied only to the gating path. This removes the 'shrinkage' bias that L1-penalized ReLU SAEs have. The authors report a Pareto improvement over standard SAEs on language models up to 7B parameters: about half as many active features for similar reconstruction fidelity, with comparable interpretability in a blinded human study.
project_relevance: Gated SAEs are a historical, intermediate architecture. Cite them in the SAE background and optionally in an architecture ablation, but SAELens now calls Gated SAEs 'legacy' in favour of JumpReLU and BatchTopK. Use the NeurIPS 2024 title when citing the published version.
discrepancies: Note: the NeurIPS 2024 proceedings title differs from the arXiv title

claim: SAELens library
correct_value: SAELens. Joseph Bloom, Curt Tigges, Anthony Duong, David Chanin. 2024. https://github.com/decoderesearch/SAELens (formerly jbloomAus/SAELens).
details: SAELens is an open-source PyTorch library for training, loading and analysing sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability. Supported training architectures are standard L1, Gated, TopK (marked legacy), JumpReLU, BatchTopK and Matryoshka BatchTopK (marked state-of-the-art), and Matching Pursuit (marked research). It uses TransformerLens models by default, can use any HuggingFace AutoModelForCausalLM, and can train from cached activations. It also gives access to many pretrained SAEs and integrates with Neuronpedia.
project_relevance: Use SAELens as the SAE training and evaluation library. Caveat: its model-hooking pipeline assumes TransformerLens or AutoModelForCausalLM models, while driving VLAs (e.g. InternVL-based SimLingo or Qwen2.5-VL-based AutoVLA) are multimodal. The practical route is to dump bottleneck activations with custom hooks and train from cached activations (use_cached_activations=True), or use the SAE classes with a custom loop. Pin the version, because architecture names and configs have changed across releases.

claim: LoRA (Hu et al. 2021)
correct_value: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. Edward J. Hu, Yelong Shen, Phillip Wallis, Zeyuan Allen-Zhu, Yuanzhi Li, Shean Wang, Lu Wang, Weizhu Chen. arXiv:2106.09685 (2021); ICLR 2022 (OpenReview nZeVKeeFYf9).
details: LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and adds trainable low-rank matrices (W + BA, rank r much smaller than d) to selected weight matrices, typically attention projections. For GPT-3 175B it cuts trainable parameters by about 10,000x and GPU memory by about 3x compared with full fine-tuning, while matching or beating fine-tuning quality. The low-rank update can be merged into the weights, so inference latency does not increase. The official implementation is microsoft/LoRA (loralib), and it is widely available via HuggingFace PEFT.
project_relevance: LoRA is the planned fine-tuning mechanism for targeted retraining and repair on synthesized failure-axis scenarios. It pairs naturally with replay to limit regression on nominal driving. Cite the ICLR 2022 version, since the official README uses it. Caveat: LoRA alone does not prevent forgetting, so nominal-driving regression must be measured explicitly.
discrepancies: Year: arXiv 2021, peer-reviewed ICLR 2022; cite the ICLR version

claim: GRPO (DeepSeekMath, Shao et al. 2024)
correct_value: DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models. Zhihong Shao, Peiyi Wang, Qihao Zhu, Runxin Xu, Junxiao Song, Xiao Bi, Haowei Zhang, Mingchuan Zhang, Y. K. Li, Y. Wu, Daya Guo. arXiv:2402.03300 (Feb 2024).
details: DeepSeekMath 7B continues pre-training DeepSeek-Coder-Base-v1.5 7B on 120B math-related tokens mined from Common Crawl. It reaches 51.7% on the competition-level MATH benchmark without tools or voting, and 60.9% with self-consistency over 64 samples. The paper introduces Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a PPO variant that drops the learned value function. It samples a group of outputs per prompt, uses group-normalized rewards as advantages, and adds a KL penalty to a reference policy directly in the loss, which saves memory compared with PPO. GRPO produced DeepSeekMath-RL 7B.
project_relevance: GRPO is the RL fine-tuning algorithm used by AutoVLA (source literature review: G=6, clipped ratio epsilon=0.2, KL beta=0.04). Cite DeepSeekMath whenever the project describes or reuses GRPO-based reinforcement fine-tuning of the driving VLA. Note that the official README's BibTeX drops two authors (Xiao Bi, Haowei Zhang); use the full arXiv author list.
discrepancies: The official GitHub README BibTeX omits Xiao Bi and Haowei Zhang; arXiv metadata lists 11 authors

claim: Activation steering / ActAdd (Turner et al.)
correct_value: Steering Language Models With Activation Engineering (earlier arXiv versions titled 'Activation Addition: Steering Language Models Without Optimization'). Alexander Matt Turner, Lisa Thiergart, Gavin Leech, David Udell, Juan J. Vazquez, Ulisse Mini, Monte MacDiarmid. arXiv:2308.10248 (Aug 2023, revised through 2024).
details: ActAdd builds a steering vector from the difference in residual-stream activations between a pair of contrasting prompts (e.g. 'Love' vs 'Hate'). It adds the vector, scaled by a coefficient, to a chosen layer's activations during the forward pass. No gradient optimization or labelled data is needed. It controls high-level properties of the output such as sentiment and topic while keeping off-target performance. The work framed 'activation engineering' as an inference-time alternative to fine-tuning and prompting.
project_relevance: Use ActAdd as the simplest causal test for a discovered failure axis: add or subtract the axis direction, whether an SAE decoder vector or a contrastive mean difference, in the VLA's bottleneck during closed-loop rollouts, and measure the change in failure rate. Cite it with CAA. Use the current arXiv title and note the earlier one, since the repo may cite either.
discrepancies: The title changed across arXiv versions: 'Activation Addition: Steering Language Models Without Optimization' became 'Steering Language Models With Activation Engineering'

claim: Contrastive Activation Addition (Rimsky et al. CAA)
correct_value: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition. Nina Rimsky (now listed as Nina Panickssery in the ACL Anthology), Nick Gabrieli, Julian Schulz, Meg Tong, Evan Hubinger, Alexander Matt Turner. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the ACL (Volume 1: Long Papers), 2024, pp. 15504-15522. DOI 10.18653/v1/2024.acl-long.828. arXiv:2312.06681.
details: CAA builds steering vectors by averaging, over many contrastive pairs, the difference in residual-stream activations between positive and negative examples of a behavior. Examples of behaviors are sycophancy, hallucination, refusal and corrigibility, using A/B multiple-choice datasets. At inference the vector is added with a positive or negative coefficient at every token position after the user prompt. On Llama 2 Chat, CAA changed behavior substantially and worked on top of fine-tuning and system prompts with minimal capability loss. It was also analyzed with activation-space interpretation methods.
project_relevance: CAA is the right template for 'diagnostic activation steering' of a discovered axis. Compute a mean-difference vector between failure and matched nominal rollouts, or use an SAE feature direction. Inject it at the VLA bottleneck with a range of coefficients, and check for a dose-response in closed-loop failure rate. Include projection-removal (ablation) controls. Caveat: in a VLA, the right token positions (vision tokens, language tokens or action queries) need an ablation.
discrepancies: Author name: the ACL Anthology now lists the first author as Nina Panickssery; the paper was originally published as Nina Rimsky

claim: Linear probing (Alain & Bengio 2016)
correct_value: Understanding Intermediate Layers Using Linear Classifier Probes. Guillaume Alain, Yoshua Bengio. arXiv:1610.01644 (Oct 2016); ICLR 2017 Workshop Track.
details: The paper introduces linear classifier 'probes': linear classifiers trained on the frozen features of each intermediate layer of a trained network to predict the target label. Probe training does not affect the model. Probe accuracy per layer measures how linearly separable the task information is at each depth. Experiments, including on Inception v3 and ResNet-50, show linear separability rising monotonically with depth in trained models. It is the standard citation for linear probing of representations.
project_relevance: Cite it for the probe-residual clustering method: fit linear probes on nominal driving representations, e.g. to predict expert waypoints or speed, then cluster the probe residuals on failure rollouts. Also cite it for layer sweeps that locate where failure-relevant information becomes linearly decodable. Caveat: probe accuracy shows information is decodable, not that the model uses it. Pair probes with steering or ablation for causal claims.
discrepancies: Venue: usually cited as arXiv 2016 or ICLR 2017 Workshop; it is not a main-track paper

claim: HDBSCAN (Campello et al. 2013)
correct_value: Density-Based Clustering Based on Hierarchical Density Estimates. Ricardo J. G. B. Campello, Davoud Moulavi, Jörg Sander. Advances in Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (PAKDD 2013), LNCS vol. 7819, Springer, pp. 160-172. DOI 10.1007/978-3-642-37456-2_14. (Extended journal version: Campello, Moulavi, Zimek, Sander, ACM TKDD 10(1), 2015.)
details: HDBSCAN builds a hierarchy of density-based clusters from a minimum spanning tree over the mutual-reachability distance, for all density levels at once. It then extracts a flat clustering by choosing the most stable clusters in the condensed tree. The main parameter is the minimum cluster size; the number of clusters is not fixed in advance. Low-density points are labelled noise. It improves on DBSCAN by handling clusters of varying density without a global epsilon.
project_relevance: Use HDBSCAN to cluster failure-rollout representations (SAE codes, probe residuals, embeddings) because the number of failure axes is unknown and many failures are one-off noise. Cite Campello et al. for the algorithm and McInnes et al. for the implementation. Caveat: it works poorly in very high dimensions, so reduce dimensionality first (PCA or UMAP), and report stability across min_cluster_size.

claim: HDBSCAN (McInnes et al. 2017)
correct_value: hdbscan: Hierarchical density based clustering. Leland McInnes, John Healy, Steve Astels. Journal of Open Source Software 2(11):205, 2017. DOI 10.21105/joss.00205.
details: This JOSS paper describes the scikit-learn-contrib 'hdbscan' Python package, a fast implementation of Campello et al.'s HDBSCAN. It adds soft-clustering membership vectors, GLOSH outlier scores and prediction for new points. A companion paper (McInnes & Healy, 'Accelerated Hierarchical Density Based Clustering', IEEE ICDMW 2017, pp. 33-42) describes the accelerated algorithm. scikit-learn now also ships sklearn.cluster.HDBSCAN, and its documentation cites Campello et al. 2013.
project_relevance: Cite it as the implementation used for density-based clustering of failure representations. Soft membership and outlier scores are useful for ranking which failures are 'on-axis' versus idiosyncratic. Cite both McInnes and Campello when using the package.

claim: Hungarian algorithm (Kuhn 1955)
correct_value: The Hungarian Method for the Assignment Problem. Harold W. Kuhn. Naval Research Logistics Quarterly 2(1-2):83-97, 1955. DOI 10.1002/nav.3800020109.
details: Kuhn's paper gives a combinatorial, polynomial-time algorithm for the linear assignment problem: find a minimum-cost (or maximum-weight) perfect matching in a bipartite graph. It builds on earlier work by König and Egerváry, which is why it is called the 'Hungarian' method. Munkres (1957) later proved its polynomial complexity, hence 'Kuhn-Munkres'. Modern implementations include scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment.
project_relevance: Use it in evaluation to match discovered clusters or SAE features one-to-one with planted ground-truth failure axes, or with human-labelled scenario categories, before computing matched precision, recall or accuracy. This is the standard way to score unsupervised discovery against an answer key. Report the implementation used (e.g. scipy's linear_sum_assignment).

claim: Experience replay for continual learning (Rolnick et al. 2019)
correct_value: Experience Replay for Continual Learning. David Rolnick, Arun Ahuja, Jonathan Schwarz, Timothy P. Lillicrap, Gregory Wayne. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 32 (NeurIPS 2019). arXiv:1811.11682.
details: The paper proposes CLEAR, a replay-based method for continual reinforcement learning. It mixes on-policy learning from new experience (for plasticity) with off-policy learning from replayed old experience, plus behavioural-cloning losses on the replay data (for stability). Across sequential Atari and DMLab tasks, CLEAR greatly reduces catastrophic forgetting. It does not need task identities and matches or exceeds methods such as EWC and Progress & Compress. The takeaway is that simple replay is a strong, often underrated baseline against forgetting.
project_relevance: Cite it as the basis for replay during targeted retraining: mix replayed nominal-driving data with synthesized failure-axis data when LoRA fine-tuning, so the model keeps nominal performance. The source prompt's 'PHASER phase-centric replay' should be framed as building on this and similar replay work. Caveat: page numbers differ between bib sources, so cite volume 32 without pages or check the proceedings page.
discrepancies: Page numbers are inconsistent across third-party bib files (348-358 vs 350-360); the official proceedings BibTeX omits pages

claim: Catastrophic forgetting (Kirkpatrick et al. EWC 2017)
correct_value: Overcoming Catastrophic Forgetting in Neural Networks. James Kirkpatrick, Razvan Pascanu, Neil Rabinowitz, Joel Veness, Guillaume Desjardins, Andrei A. Rusu, Kieran Milan, John Quan, Tiago Ramalho, Agnieszka Grabska-Barwinska, Demis Hassabis, Claudia Clopath, Dharshan Kumaran, Raia Hadsell. PNAS 114(13):3521-3526, 2017. DOI 10.1073/pnas.1611835114. arXiv:1612.00796.
details: The paper introduces Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC). When a network learns a new task, a quadratic penalty anchors each parameter to its old value, weighted by its importance to earlier tasks as estimated by the diagonal Fisher information. This slows learning on important weights. On permuted MNIST and sequential Atari 2600 games, EWC lets one network learn tasks in sequence with much less catastrophic forgetting than plain SGD. It is the canonical regularization baseline in continual learning.
project_relevance: Cite it for the catastrophic-forgetting problem when fine-tuning the VLA on failure-axis data, and optionally use EWC as a regularization baseline next to replay. Caveat: combining EWC with LoRA needs care, because Fisher estimates would be over the adapter parameters only. Replay is usually the stronger and simpler baseline, per Rolnick et al.

claim: Model diffing with crosscoders (Lindsey et al. 2024, Transformer Circuits)
correct_value: Sparse Crosscoders for Cross-Layer Features and Model Diffing. Jack Lindsey, Adly Templeton, Jonathan Marcus, Thomas Conerly, Joshua Batson, Christopher Olah. Transformer Circuits Thread, October 25, 2024. https://transformer-circuits.pub/2024/crosscoders/index.html
details: Crosscoders generalize SAEs: one sparse dictionary reads from and reconstructs activations at several layers, or in several models, at once. This yields features shared across layers or models. For model diffing, the authors trained a crosscoder jointly on Claude 3 Sonnet base and fine-tuned activations. Features fell into base-specific, fine-tune-specific and shared groups; fine-tune-specific features included refusal- and code-review-related ones. Some shared features changed direction or correlation between models. The authors caution that many model-exclusive features were uninterpreted and that crosscoder features may not match the models' actual mechanisms. Anthropic later posted a 2025 update note on crosscoder diffing.
project_relevance: This is the reference method for 'model diffing': comparing the VLA before and after targeted retraining to see which features appeared, vanished or rotated. It can also diff a base VLM against its driving-fine-tuned VLA to locate driving-specific features. It is also the right citation for the 'MMDiff-style diffing' planned in the source prompt, since MMDiff builds on this line of work. Caveat: joint training needs both models' activations on the same inputs, and the exclusive-feature labels can be artifacts of the sparsity loss; see the 2025 update before relying on them.

claim: Prior-art candidate (not cited in Source A/B): SAE-based discovery of behavior-linked features from closed-loop VLA rollouts, with optional VLM labels and causal validation.
correct_value: Event-Grounded Sparse Autoencoders for Vision-Language-Action Policies. Xinchen Jin, Aditya Chatterjee, Pranav Kumar, Rohan Paleja (Purdue). arXiv:2605.17204 [cs.RO], submitted 17 May 2026. Code: github.com/xc-j/Event-SAE, plus an openpi fork (xc-j/openpi-event-sae). No peer-reviewed venue found.
details: The authors train sparse autoencoders on hidden activations of OpenVLA and π0.5 (openpi) in LIBERO. They extract end-effector kinematic keyframes from closed-loop rollouts, then cluster those keyframes within each task using visual, state and temporal cues, which gives 'behavioral events'. SAE features are ranked against these events, and the clusters can optionally be annotated by a VLM to add semantic context. Each ranking is checked with residual-preserving zero-out interventions in closed loop, in two simulation architectures and one real-robot study. Event-grounded ranking gives the strongest causal effects on OpenVLA and transfers to π0.5's continuous action chunks. The authors say the SAE is a sparse but imperfect basis for intervention: usefulness varies with architecture and intervention site, and aggressive interventions expose safety limits. The paper does not study failures, planted data gaps, scenario generation or retraining, and it covers manipulation only, not driving.
project_relevance: THREAT: MEDIUM-HIGH. This is the closest methodological precedent for Stage 3 plus the describability gate (SAE on VLA rollouts, VLM naming, closed-loop causal check). The paper must differentiate on four points: (1) discovery conditioned on failure (success vs failure rollouts), not general behavior-event labeling; (2) ground-truth planted gaps scored by precision and recall; (3) a closed-loop driving VLA (SimLingo/CARLA/Bench2Drive), not LIBERO; (4) discovery turned into generated data and a measured failure reduction. Reuse their residual-preserving zero-out intervention as the causal-validity check. Consider 'event-grounded SAE ranking' as an ablation baseline next to our failure-grounded ranking. Possible contact: Rohan Paleja (Purdue).

claim: Prior-art candidate: sparse autoencoders on VLA activations reveal interpretable, steerable features (SAE component of the core claim).
correct_value: Sparse Autoencoders Reveal Interpretable and Steerable Features in VLA Models. Aiden Swann, Lachlain McGranahan, Hugo Buurmeijer, Monroe Kennedy III, Mac Schwager (Stanford). arXiv:2603.19183 (19 Mar 2026). The authors' repo BibTeX lists CoRL 2026 as the venue (not independently verified). Project page: drvla.github.io. Code release announced for 1 Oct 2026: SAE training, π0.5 activation collection, feature-generality metrics.
details: The authors train SAEs on hidden-layer activations of a VLA (π0.5 pipeline) to get a compact, interpretable basis for its computation. Most extracted features correspond to memorized sequences from specific training demonstrations. A smaller set are general, transferable motion primitives and semantic features. They propose a metric that separates general features from episode-specific memorizations. Steering experiments on LIBERO and on DROID hardware show that single SAE features causally drive behavior: amplifying general features produces consistent actions, and removing them sharply degrades performance. They also report that supervised fine-tuning on small datasets increases memorization, while larger and more diverse data gives more transferable features.
project_relevance: THREAT: MEDIUM. This work already establishes SAEs on VLAs and ties feature types to training-data composition, which is close to our planted-gap (withheld-data) premise. A reviewer will ask how our failure axes differ from their memorization features. Required steps: (a) run their generality metric as a filter, so discovered 'failure axes' are not memorized-episode features; (b) show that planted gaps are recovered from failure contrast, not merely visible as data-size effects; (c) move to driving and closed-loop repair. Plan to use their released code (1 Oct 2026). Hugo Buurmeijer and Aiden Swann (Stanford MSL) are the right contacts. Source A's contact line mislabels Buurmeijer as an MMDiff author.

claim: Prior-art candidate: large-scale mechanistic study of VLAs using SAEs, linear probes and contrastive concept identification (the contrastive-diffing and SAE components).
correct_value: Not All Features Are Created Equal: A Mechanistic Study of Vision-Language-Action Models. Bryce Grant, Xijia Zhao, Peng Wang (Case Western Reserve University, CWRU-AISM). arXiv:2603.19233 (Mar 2026). The toolkit repo 'action-atlas' describes the paper as NeurIPS 2026; the venue is not independently verified and the repo BibTeX cites arXiv.
details: The study applies activation injection, sparse autoencoders and linear probes to six VLAs (80M to 7B parameters) across more than 394,000 rollout episodes on four benchmarks. Models named in the toolkit README include X-VLA, SmolVLA, GR00T N1.5, π0.5 and OpenVLA-OFT. The visual pathway dominates action generation. Cross-task activation injection steers robots toward source-task positions (99.8% of X-VLA episodes), which the authors read as spatially bound motor programs. Language sensitivity depends on task structure, not model design. In multi-pathway models, expert pathways encode motor programs and VLM pathways encode goal semantics. 'Contrastive identification' recovers 82+ manipulation concepts, and causal ablation shows 28-92% zero-effect rates. A toolkit (action-atlas) is released.
project_relevance: THREAT: MEDIUM. Their contrastive concept identification over activations is close to our 'contrastive activation distributions' method, and at far larger rollout scale, so a reviewer will cite it against the method component. Our contrast must be explicitly failure-conditioned (success vs failure), tied to ground-truth planted gaps, and run in driving closed loop. Useful caveat: visual-pathway dominance and scene-coordinate-bound motor programs suggest driving failure axes may sit in vision-bridge tokens, so include those layers in the sweep. The action-atlas toolkit may provide ready hooks for π0.5, SmolVLA or OpenVLA-OFT if a robot-VLA pilot is run.

claim: Source A: 'Observing and Controlling Features in VLAs (Buurmeijer et al. - arXiv 2026): shows intermediate VLA layers (OpenVLA, pi0, pi0.5) contain linearly observable state/action features. Validates layer-sweep protocol.' Contact: 'Hugo Buurmeijer & Marco Pavone (Stanford / NVIDIA)'.
correct_value: Observing and Controlling Features in Vision-Language-Action Models. Hugo Buurmeijer, Carmen Amo Alonso, Aiden Swann, Marco Pavone (Stanford). arXiv:2603.05487 (5 Mar 2026; v2 Sep 2026). No venue found.
details: The authors ask whether VLA internal representations support lightweight behavioral steering without retraining. Across four frontier VLAs, spanning autoregressive and transformer-plus-flow-matching architectures, linear 'observers' recover state- and action-relevant information from internal representations. The same directions causally change outputs. They add a 'controller' that minimally modifies representations so observer predictions stay inside prescribed target intervals. Closed-loop experiments with π0.5 in LIBERO and on DROID hardware improve constraint satisfaction while keeping task performance, at about 1% inference overhead.
project_relevance: THREAT: LOW-MEDIUM. It supports the premises of the probe-residual clustering and the layer sweep (linear probes work across VLA architectures), but it steers toward known constraints rather than discovering unknown failure axes. Use their observer and probe protocol as the recipe for the 'nominal probes' whose residuals we cluster. Contact Buurmeijer for observer hooks, as Source A suggests. Do not describe him as an MMDiff author.
discrepancies: Source A lists the models as 'OpenVLA, pi0, pi0.5'. The abstract says 'four frontier VLA models' (autoregressive and transformer-flow-matching); the exact list is unverified, and the closed-loop results are on π0.5 only.
Full author list: Buurmeijer, Amo Alonso, Swann, Pavone. Source A names only Buurmeijer and Pavone.
Source A separately attributes MMDiff and Prisma to 'Hugo Buurmeijer & Sonia Joseph'. Buurmeijer is not an author of either.

claim: Prior-art candidate: mechanistic interpretability and activation steering of VLAs via internal representations.
correct_value: Mechanistic Interpretability for Steering Vision-Language-Action Models. Bear Häon*, Kaylene Stocking*, Ian Chuang, Claire Tomlin (UC Berkeley; *equal contribution). CoRL 2025 (9th Conference on Robot Learning). arXiv:2509.00328. OpenReview: YvsUD8C9QS. Code: github.com/Physical-AI-Safety-Institute/mechanistic-steering-vlas. Project site: vla-mech-interp.github.io.
details: The authors describe this as the first framework for interpreting and steering VLAs through their internal representations. They project feed-forward (FFN) activations and value vectors inside transformer layers onto the token-embedding basis. This finds sparse semantic directions (e.g., speed, direction, 'slow', 'up', 'careful') that are causally linked to action selection. They then steer these activations at inference time, without fine-tuning, reward signals or environment interaction. Evaluation covers π0 (π0-FAST via LeRobot) and OpenVLA (LIBERO), with zero-shot behavioral control in simulation and on a physical UR5.
project_relevance: THREAT: LOW-MEDIUM. It is precedent for 'VLA internals are interpretable and causal' but does no failure discovery, data work or driving. Cite it as the earliest VLA-steering work. Use their vocabulary projection as a cheap, training-free way to name candidate directions, next to SAEs and the VLM gate. Local contact: the Tomlin lab at UC Berkeley (Häon, Stocking) could advise on hooks and closed-loop steering checks.

claim: Source A: 'Multimodal Model Diffing (MMDiff - arXiv 2026): primary inspiration for SAE-based feature discovery; uses multimodal SAEs and contrastive token firing to isolate behavioral features in MLLMs. Operates on static VQA/OCR.' Contact: 'Hugo Buurmeijer & Sonia Joseph (Oxford / Prisma) - Authors of MMDiff & Prisma'.
correct_value: MMDiff: Multimodal Model Diffing for Feature Discovery and Control (arXiv title: 'Multimodal Model Diffing for Feature Discovery and Control'). Lachin Naghashyar, Hunar Batra, Ashkan Khakzar, Phil Torr, Ronald Clark, Christian Schroeder de Witt, Constantin Venhoff (Oxford). arXiv:2608.09928 (10 Aug 2026). Poster at the ICML 2026 EMM-QA workshop (OpenReview 6aJW2yoDjB).
details: MMDiff trains multimodal SAEs for three MLLM families (LLaVA-MORE, PaliGemma 2, InternVL3.5) and uses them in three ways. (i) Feature isolation: diffing a base-LM SAE against its multimodal-adapted counterpart finds features changed by multimodal training. (ii) Task-specific feature detection: per-token contrastive firing analysis isolates causal features. (iii) Control: discovered directions are removed or steered. Removal degrades target behaviors by an average of 12% on spatial tasks and 17% on OCR, and cuts multimodal attack success by 24%, with no VQA impact. Steering improves spatial accuracy by +3.6% and OCR by +1.8% over a single-layer steering baseline. Source A's summary of the method (multimodal SAEs, contrastive token firing, static VQA/OCR-style tasks) is correct.
project_relevance: THREAT: MEDIUM as a method source, LOW as a scoop, since it covers static MLLM tasks and no policies, failures or closed loop. It is the direct template for our 'contrastive activation diffing' (success vs failure firing) and for base-vs-fine-tuned diffing, e.g., a planted-gap policy against a full-data policy. Credit it explicitly as the inspiration. Cite crosscoder sparsity-artifact caveats (Minder et al., NeurIPS 2025, arXiv:2504.02922) when claiming a latent is 'fine-tune specific'. Correct contacts: Constantin Venhoff and Christian Schroeder de Witt (Oxford). For Prisma, contact Sonia Joseph (Prisma, arXiv:2504.19475).
discrepancies: Source A attributes MMDiff to 'Hugo Buurmeijer & Sonia Joseph'. The actual authors are Naghashyar, Batra, Khakzar, Torr, Clark, Schroeder de Witt and Venhoff. Neither Buurmeijer nor Joseph is an author.
Venue: besides arXiv (Aug 2026), MMDiff was an ICML 2026 workshop poster (EMM-QA). It is not a main-conference paper.

claim: Source A: 'RoboART (Predictive Red-Teaming - arXiv 2025): Primary head-to-head baseline. Uses VLMs to score policy degradation across human-enumerated factor lists (lighting, weather).' references.bib: 'RoboART: Predictive Red Teaming and Targeted Data Collection for Robotic Policies', author Anonymous, arXiv:2502.06575.
correct_value: Predictive Red Teaming: Breaking Policies Without Breaking Robots (the pipeline is called RoboART). Anirudha Majumdar, Mohit Sharma, Dmitry Kalashnikov, Sumeet Singh, Pierre Sermanet, Vikas Sindhwani. CoRL 2025, PMLR vol. 305 (OpenReview qAGHsCsA1O). arXiv:2502.06575. Project page: predictive-red-team.github.io.
details: The paper frames 'predictive red teaming': discovering a visuomotor policy's vulnerabilities to environmental factors and predicting the resulting performance drop without hardware evaluation. The RoboART pipeline (1) edits nominal observations with generative image editing to vary environmental factors (e.g., lighting, visual distractors, object locations), and (2) predicts performance under each variation with a policy-specific anomaly detector run on the edited observations. Across more than 500 hardware trials in twelve off-nominal conditions for visuomotor diffusion policies, predicted and real success rates differ by less than 0.19 on average. Fine-tuning on data collected under conditions predicted to be adverse boosts baseline performance 2-7x. The setting is manipulation, not driving.
project_relevance: THREAT: HIGH-MEDIUM. It is our primary baseline, and it already shows 'discover vulnerabilities, collect targeted data, fix'. The only remaining gap is that factors are pre-enumerated and discovery happens in input-edit space, not in policy activations. The paper must show that activation-based discovery recovers planted gaps outside the factor list (interactional or multi-agent confounders that image edits cannot express), at better precision and recall. It must also match RoboART's targeted-data gains per unit of data. For fairness, give RoboART a VLM-proposed factor list as well, and port it to CARLA camera frames with the same retraining budget. Fix the references.bib entry.
discrepancies: Title in references.bib is wrong. The actual title is 'Predictive Red Teaming: Breaking Policies Without Breaking Robots'.
Authors listed as 'Anonymous'. The real authors are Majumdar, Sharma, Kalashnikov, Singh, Sermanet and Sindhwani.
Venue: published at CoRL 2025 (PMLR 305), not only arXiv.
Source A says it 'uses VLMs to score policy degradation'. Degradation is predicted by a policy-specific anomaly detector on generatively edited observations, not scored by a VLM.
Source A lists 'weather' as an example factor. The paper's setting is robot manipulation, with factors such as lighting, distractors and object locations.

claim: Prior-art candidate: failure-aware data curation that links closed-loop failures back to training data.
correct_value: CUPID: Curating Data your Robot Loves with Influence Functions. Christopher Agia, Rohan Sinha, Jingyun Yang, Rika Antonova, Marco Pavone, Haruki Nishimura, Masha Itkina, Jeannette Bohg (Stanford / TRI). CoRL 2025. arXiv:2506.19121. Code: github.com/agiachris/cupid. Project: cupid-curation.github.io.
details: CUPID gives an influence-function formulation for imitation-learning policies. From a set of evaluation rollouts (successes and failures), it estimates each training demonstration's influence on the policy's expected return. It uses this to (1) filter out demonstrations that hurt closed-loop performance and (2) pick which newly collected trajectories will most improve the policy. Training on less than 33% of the data, curated this way, gives state-of-the-art diffusion policies on RoboMimic, with similar gains on hardware. Hardware experiments also show it can identify robust strategies under distribution shift, isolate spurious correlations and improve post-training of generalist policies.
project_relevance: THREAT: MEDIUM, on the 'failure → data' half of the claim. A reviewer will ask why influence functions or data attribution are not used instead. The key argument: planted gaps are missing data, and attribution can only rank data that is present, so it cannot name an absent slice. Activation discovery plus generation targets coverage that is missing. If compute allows, run CUPID-style attribution as a remediation baseline, or show that it flags no coherent slice for planted gaps. Also useful for the 'spurious correlation' controls.

claim: Repo LITERATURE_REVIEW/bib: 'SAFE: Zero-Shot Failure Prediction in Vision-Language-Action Models' (author Anonymous, arXiv:2506.09937), described as 'monitoring activation trajectories across transformer decoder layers, predicting impending crashes or execution stops'.
correct_value: SAFE: Multitask Failure Detection for Vision-Language-Action Models. Qiao Gu, Yuanliang Ju, Shengxiang Sun, Igor Gilitschenski, Haruki Nishimura, Masha Itkina, Florian Shkurti. NeurIPS 2025 (Advances in NeurIPS 38, pp. 40041-40076). arXiv:2506.09937. Code: github.com/vla-safe/SAFE.
details: SAFE observes that VLA internal feature spaces contain task-generic 'failure regions'. It trains lightweight detectors (MLP/LSTM) on internal features from both successful and failed rollouts, and calibrates alarms with functional conformal prediction. The goal is detecting failures of generalist VLAs on unseen tasks. On OpenVLA, π0 and π0-FAST (manipulation, in simulation and on real robots), it reports the best accuracy / detection-time trade-off; the HF daily summary cites ROC-AUC up to about 0.89 on held-out tasks in simulation. The output is a scalar failure score: it detects that a failure is coming but does not characterize failure types or data gaps.
project_relevance: THREAT: LOW-MEDIUM. It supports the premise that failure information lives in VLA internals. A reviewer may argue that clustering SAFE's feature space already yields failure modes, so run 'cluster the SAFE detector's embedding' as a representation-stratification baseline. Note the 2026 wave of internal-state failure detectors a reviewer could also cite: VLA-FAIL (arXiv:2606.21386), Hide-and-Seek (2605.30834), FARM (2609.11445), Tri-Info (2606.19998). None of them do discovery with repair. Fix the references.bib entry.
discrepancies: Title is wrong in references.bib. The actual title is 'SAFE: Multitask Failure Detection for Vision-Language-Action Models'.
Authors are 'Anonymous' in the bib. The real authors are Gu, Ju, Sun, Gilitschenski, Nishimura, Itkina and Shkurti.
Venue: NeurIPS 2025, not only arXiv.
It is not zero-shot in the sense of training-free: detectors are trained on success and failure rollouts and generalize to unseen tasks.
The domain is robot manipulation, not driving crashes.

claim: Prior-art candidate: LLM-driven generation of safety-critical CARLA scenarios, then fine-tuning the driving policy to reduce collisions (the targeted-generation-closes-failures component).
correct_value: ChatScene: Knowledge-Enabled Safety-Critical Scenario Generation for Autonomous Vehicles. Jiawei Zhang, Chejian Xu, Bo Li. CVPR 2024. arXiv:2405.14062. Code: github.com/javyduck/ChatScene.
details: An LLM agent breaks a textual description of a safety-critical scenario into sub-descriptions (behavior, geometry, spawn positions). It retrieves matching Scenic code snippets from a curated knowledge base and assembles executable Scenic programs for CARLA. The generated scenarios cause 15% more collisions than prior baselines against RL-based ego agents. Fine-tuning those agents on the scenarios reduces collision rates by 9%. Scenario content comes from LLM knowledge or text prompts, not from the policy's internals. A CVPR 2026 successor, TrafficAlign, reports 36.1% collision reduction after fine-tuning on region-aligned generated scenarios.
project_relevance: THREAT: MEDIUM for Stage 4. It already shows generation that closes failures in closed loop in CARLA. Our novelty must be that the scenario parameters come from activation-discovered axes, not from LLM priors. Add a strong 'text-only' baseline: ChatScene-style LLM-proposed scenarios with the same generation budget. Show that ours closes the planted gaps while text-only generation does not. Reuse the ChatScene Scenic retrieval/composition pipeline as the generator behind the describability gate.

claim: Prior-art candidate: academic automatic data engine for autonomous driving (issue identification → curation → retraining → verification).
correct_value: AIDE: An Automatic Data Engine for Object Detection in Autonomous Driving. Mingfu Liang, Jong-Chyi Su, Samuel Schulter, Sparsh Garg, Shiyu Zhao, Ying Wu, Manmohan Chandraker (NEC Labs America / Northwestern / Rutgers / UCSD). CVPR 2024. arXiv:2403.17373.
details: AIDE uses vision-language models and LLMs to automate the AV perception data loop. It identifies issues, focusing on rare or novel object categories in a long-tailed distribution. It then curates relevant unlabeled data by retrieval, improves the detector through auto-labeling, and verifies the model on generated diverse scenarios, repeating this for continual self-improvement. It also sets up an open-world detection benchmark on AV datasets and reports better performance at lower annotation cost. Issue identification is driven by outputs and categories, not by representations. The setting is perception, not planning or control.
project_relevance: THREAT: LOW-MEDIUM. It is the academic precedent for the '8-stage data engine' in Source A's Group C, and a reviewer may cite it against the loop framing. Differentiate: our trigger is unsupervised structure in a driving policy's activations, evaluated against ground-truth planted gaps and closed-loop driving metrics, not missing detector categories. Cite it next to Tesla and Mobileye as a data-engine precedent.

claim: Prior-art candidate: SAEs and linear probes applied to internal states of a driving model (motion forecasting).
correct_value: Words in Motion: Extracting Interpretable Control Vectors for Motion Transformers. Omer Sahin Tas, Royden Wagner (KIT MRT). ICLR 2025 (OpenReview J9eKm7j6KD). arXiv:2406.11624. Code: github.com/KIT-MRT/future-motion.
details: The paper analyzes hidden states of transformer-based motion forecasting models for autonomous driving. It uses linear probes to show that human-interpretable motion features (natural-language-style descriptors of motion, e.g., direction and speed) are encoded. From these it derives control vectors that steer forecasts at inference time, and uses sparse autoencoders to make the control vectors more interpretable. Digest summaries report high probe accuracy and zero-shot generalization. It concerns motion forecasting, not closed-loop planning, and does not address failures or data gaps. These details come from repository and digest summaries; check the paper for exact probe targets and datasets.
project_relevance: THREAT: LOW-MEDIUM. The paper cannot claim 'first SAE or probe interpretability in driving models'. Cite this as prior driving-model interpretability. Differentiate: closed-loop VLA planner, failure-conditioned discovery, planted-gap evaluation and repair.

claim: Concurrent-work candidate: mining rare, safety-critical driving scenes from a frozen driving VLM's hidden states with a sparse autoencoder whose neurons name why each frame was flagged.
correct_value: GitHub repo 'long-tail-driving-scene-discovery' (CCC917111), by Yike Chen, Zihua Chen, Yusong Zhao, a capstone project at The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen. Repo created 21 Sep 2026. MIT license. No arXiv preprint or peer-reviewed paper found.
details: The project trains a tail-guided AbsTopK SAE (k=512) on layer-28 MLP (down_proj) activations of NVIDIA Cosmos-Reason1-7B, using nuScenes keyframes. The loss combines reconstruction upweighted on tail samples, suppression of the tail subspace on normal samples, and a margin push on tail samples, so it is supervised by tail labels. Ground truth is a manually verified nuScenes split where 'long-tail' means scenes needing extra defensive driving. It reports long-tail precision 0.902, recall 0.798 and F1 0.847, against F1 0.02-0.32 for raw Cosmos, Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3-VL-2B prompting. Neurons are named post hoc (e.g., 'Rain / wet road', 'Wheelchair user ahead').
project_relevance: THREAT: MEDIUM-LOW, as a signal that 'SAE on driving-VLM hidden states for long-tail discovery' is already being done by students. It is not a policy or failure study: supervised tail labels, a perception VLM, open-loop nuScenes, no repair. Do not cite it as peer-reviewed. Watch for an arXiv version. The paper should state that our discovery is label-free with respect to the gaps and targets policy failures in closed loop. Their precision/recall framing against manually verified labels is similar to our planted-gap metrics.

claim: Prior-art candidate: layer-wise probing of a driving VLA's internal representations on Bench2Drive (layer-sweep component).
correct_value: Depth-Wise Probing and Pruning of the Planning Token in a Driving Vision-Language-Action Model. Harisankar Babu, Benjamin Coors, Christopher Lang, Hendrik Berkemeyer, Tamim Asfour, Simon Foell (Robert Bosch GmbH / Karlsruhe Institute of Technology). arXiv:2608.07361 (7 Aug 2026). The awesome-efficient-vla list gives the venue as the DriveX Workshop at ECCV 2026 (not independently verified).
details: The study targets ORION, a driving VLA that compresses planning into a single planning token decoded by a frozen generative planner. A 'trajectory-space logit lens' decodes the planning token from each of the 32 decoder layers with the native planner, and linear probes predict navigation commands. Navigation commands are 97.7% linearly decodable after the first decoder layer, while planning compatibility improves progressively up to layer 32. Pruning layers ranked by input/output cosine similarity removes 8 of 32 layers with about a 5% error increase (2.06 m to 2.17 m) and a 1.33x decoder speedup. Learned readouts (residual MLP adapters, cross-attention resamplers) recover much early-layer performance. Evaluation is on the Bench2Drive validation set across five ability categories.
project_relevance: THREAT: LOW-MEDIUM. It is the most direct precedent for a layer sweep inside a driving VLA on Bench2Drive, which is our stack, so cite it for methodology. Its finding that planning-relevant information matures late while command information is early should guide which SimLingo layers to hook. It does no failure discovery.

claim: Prior-art candidate: interpretability-based auditing of driving VLAs that links behavioral counterfactuals to internal representations and surfaces failure modes.
correct_value: What Do They See? Interpreting Complex Road Scenarios Through the Eyes of Vision-Language-Action Models for Safe and Trustworthy Autonomous Vehicle Learning. Kalpana Panda, Wesley Maia, Vinti Agarwal, Ross Greer. arXiv:2607.16938 (Jul 2026). No venue found.
details: The paper proposes Counterfactual Vision Action Analysis (CVAA). Generative inpainting removes individual detected objects from front-view images to build a 'Counter-nuScenes' set. The authors measure how driving VLAs' planned trajectories change and compare intermediate representations across the factual and counterfactual conditions. Critical objects (vehicles, pedestrians) strongly influence decisions. Models also sometimes respond strongly to irrelevant objects, a mismatch between internal representations and human-interpretable scene elements that the authors present as potential failure modes. The analysis is open-loop on nuScenes with no data remediation. These details come from digest summaries.
project_relevance: THREAT: LOW-MEDIUM. It overlaps our 'behavioral audit to representation' story and the describability framing for driving VLAs, but it uses human-chosen object ablations, is open-loop and does no repair. It can serve as an extra baseline family: object-ablation attribution as a behavioral way to find failure factors. Cite it in related work on driving-VLA interpretability.
